items.passage:
Dear Parents,

My name is Grace Han, and I am the librarian at Maple Hill Elementary School. Every Thursday afternoon, our library runs a reading hour for first and second graders. Many of these young students are just beginning to read on their own, and they make the most progress when an adult sits beside them and listens. This semester, however, the number of children who join the reading hour has nearly doubled, and our two staff members cannot give each child enough attention. That is why I am writing to you. We are looking for parents who can spend one Thursday afternoon a month reading with small groups of students. No special training is needed; a short guide will be provided on your first day. If you are interested, please fill out the attached form and return it to your child's homeroom teacher by March 20. Your time could make a real difference to a young reader.

Sincerely,
Grace Han
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 저학년 학생 독서 지도 자원봉사를 요청하려고
학부모 대상 독서 교육 연수를 홍보하려고
도서관 직원 추가 채용 계획을 알리려고
items.exp: 참여 학생이 두 배로 늘어 직원 둘로는 부족하니 한 달에 한 번 목요일 오후에 학생들과 함께 책을 읽어 줄 학부모를 찾는다고 했어요. 그래서 자원봉사 요청이 목적이에요. 짧은 안내서를 준다는 말은 있지만 연수를 홍보하는 글은 아니에요.

items.passage: Emma had spent the whole morning decorating a cake for her grandmother's seventieth birthday. She had covered it with cream roses and written "Happy Birthday, Grandma" in careful blue letters. On the way to the party, however, the car stopped suddenly at a red light, and the box slid off the seat. When Emma opened it, the roses were crushed and the letters had turned into a blue blur. Her eyes filled with tears. "It's ruined," she whispered. "Everything I worked for is gone." At the party, she placed the box on the table without a word. Her grandmother lifted the lid, looked at the messy cake for a long moment, and then laughed warmly. "This reminds me of the first cake I ever baked for your grandfather," she said. "It fell on the floor, and he still said it was the best one he had ever eaten." Everyone laughed, and Emma felt the heavy weight in her chest disappear. She smiled and cut the first slice.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Emma의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 케이크가 망가져 눈물을 글썽이며 속상해하다가, 할머니의 따뜻한 웃음과 이야기에 가슴의 무거운 짐이 사라지고 미소 지었어요. 그래서 upset → relieved가 맞아요. 처음에 케이크를 자랑스러워했어도 질투하는 장면은 없어요.

items.passage: Many parents believe that the best way to show love is to do everything for their children. They make the beds, pack the school bags, and clean up after every meal, hoping their children can focus on studying. But this kindness can take away something important. When children never have real tasks at home, they come to see the house as a place that serves them rather than a place they help to run. Household chores, even simple ones like watering plants or setting the table, teach children that their actions matter to others. A ten-year-old who is responsible for feeding the family dog learns that someone depends on him every day. These small duties build habits of responsibility that later carry over to schoolwork and friendships. So parents should stop seeing chores as a burden to remove from their children's lives. Instead, they should hand them age-appropriate tasks and treat them as true members of the household team.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 자녀의 학업 시간을 확보하기 위해 집안일을 줄여 주어야 한다.
자녀가 반려동물을 키우며 생명의 소중함을 배우게 해야 한다.
집안일을 잘한 자녀에게 적절한 보상을 해 주어야 한다.
부모가 먼저 집안일에 모범을 보여야 한다.
자녀에게 나이에 맞는 집안일을 맡겨 책임감을 길러 주어야 한다.
items.exp: 마지막 두 문장에서 집안일을 없애 줄 짐으로 보지 말고 나이에 맞는 일을 맡겨 가족의 일원으로 대하라고 주장해요. 개 밥 주기는 책임감을 보여 주는 예일 뿐이고, ①은 필자가 비판하는 부모의 생각이에요.

items.passage: Imagine a student who has a speech next week. Every night she lies in bed picturing herself forgetting her lines, her classmates laughing, and her teacher frowning. By the time the speech day arrives, she has already lived through the disaster a dozen times in her mind. Then she gives the speech, and it goes reasonably well. Some words come out a little fast, but no one laughs. Looking back, she realizes that the worst part of the experience was not the speech itself but the week before it. This is what too much worry does to us. It makes us feel the pain of an event long before the event happens, and often for an event that never happens at all. In this sense, constant worrying is like [paying interest on a loan you may never take out]. We give away our calm, day after day, for a problem that exists only in our imagination.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [paying interest on a loan you may never take out]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: suffering in advance over troubles that may not actually come
preparing carefully for problems that are certain to happen
borrowing confidence from others to overcome fear
spending too much time practicing for a simple task
ignoring warning signs until a problem becomes serious
items.exp: 걱정은 일이 일어나기 전부터, 그리고 일어나지도 않을 일 때문에 고통을 느끼게 한다고 했어요. 빌리지도 않을 돈의 이자를 낸다는 것은 오지 않을 수도 있는 문제로 미리 괴로워한다는 뜻이에요. ②는 '반드시 일어날 문제'라는 점에서 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: In the deserts of North America lives a small animal that may go its whole life without drinking a single drop of water. The kangaroo rat survives mostly on dry seeds, yet it does not die of thirst. Part of its secret lies in how its body handles food. When the animal digests seeds, chemical reactions inside its cells produce a small amount of water, and the kangaroo rat makes the most of every drop. Its kidneys are extremely efficient, so the waste it produces contains very little water. It also loses little moisture when it breathes, because its nose cools the air it breathes out and captures the water before it escapes. In addition, the kangaroo rat spends the hot daytime hours in a cool underground burrow and comes out only at night. Through this combination of body design and behavior, a creature smaller than a human hand manages to thrive in one of the driest places on Earth.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: reasons desert plants produce seeds rich in water
dangers small animals face from desert predators
ways a desert animal survives with almost no drinking water
the role of underground burrows in shaping desert soil
how climate change is reducing water in deserts
items.exp: 캥거루쥐가 물을 거의 마시지 않고도 소화로 생기는 물, 효율적인 신장, 코의 수분 회수, 낮에 굴에서 지내는 습성으로 살아간다는 내용이에요. 굴은 여러 방법 중 하나일 뿐 흙을 만드는 이야기는 없어요.

items.passage: Before the invention of electric refrigerators, ice was a precious product that people bought and sold across oceans. In the early nineteenth century, workers in the northeastern United States cut huge blocks of ice from frozen lakes and ponds during the winter. The blocks were packed in sawdust, which kept them from melting, and stored in thick-walled ice houses. Then they were loaded onto ships and sent to places as far away as the Caribbean and India. Many people at first laughed at the idea of shipping ice to hot countries, believing it would turn to water before it arrived. Surprisingly, a large share of the ice survived the long journey. Over time, the trade grew into a major industry that employed thousands of workers and changed how people kept food and drinks cool. It lasted until machines that could make ice cheaply took its place.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Sawdust Was Used in Early Factories
How Ice Houses Changed Winter Sports
The Invention of the Electric Refrigerator
Cooking Traditions of the Caribbean and India
Frozen Lakes, Distant Markets: The Old Ice Trade
items.exp: 냉장고가 나오기 전 얼어붙은 호수의 얼음을 잘라 먼 더운 나라까지 배로 팔던 얼음 무역의 역사를 다뤄요. 톱밥, 냉장고, 카리브해와 인도는 글에 나오는 낱말을 빌린 오답이에요.

items.passage: Helena Marsh was born in 1872 in a small fishing village in Scotland. As a child, she spent clear nights on the beach watching the stars with her father, a ship's captain who taught her to find her way by them. Because universities in her region did not accept women at the time, she studied mathematics on her own with books borrowed from the local church. In 1896, she took a job at a city observatory, where her first duty was to copy numbers from photographs of the night sky. While doing this work, she noticed that the brightness of certain stars changed in regular patterns, and she recorded more than two hundred such stars. Her findings were first published under the name of the observatory's director. It was not until 1921 that she received full credit for her work. Marsh continued to work at the observatory until her death in 1950, and a scholarship for young women in science was later created in her name.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 어린 시절 아버지와 함께 별을 관찰했다.
밝기가 규칙적으로 변하는 별을 200개 넘게 기록했다.
items.exp: 당시 그 지역 대학은 여성을 받지 않아 교회에서 빌린 책으로 혼자 수학을 공부했다고 했어요. 그래서 대학에서 수학을 전공했다는 ②가 틀려요. 나머지는 글 내용과 맞아요.

items.passage: Many teenagers believe that staying up late to study ①[helps] them get better grades. However, research suggests the opposite. When we sleep, the brain sorts through the information ②[collected] during the day and stores the important parts in long-term memory. A student who cuts sleep short may finish more pages of a textbook, but much of what he reads ③[disappearing] before the test. Lack of sleep also makes ④[it] harder to concentrate in class the next day. Students who are tired tend to reread the same sentence several times without understanding it. In addition, sleep plays a role in mood. Teenagers who regularly sleep less than seven hours are more likely to feel stressed and easily ⑤[annoyed]. So if you want to do well on your next exam, the smartest thing you can do the night before may be to close your books and go to bed on time.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③은 but 뒤 절의 주어 much of what he reads에 이어지는 동사 자리인데 동사가 없어요. disappearing을 disappears로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 동명사 주어라 단수 helps, ④는 가목적어 it, ⑤는 feel의 보어 annoyed로 맞아요.

items.passage: Wetlands such as marshes and swamps were once seen as useless land. For centuries, people drained them to make room for farms and towns. Today, however, scientists recognize that wetlands provide services that are hard to ①[replace]. One of the most important is flood control. During heavy rains, wetlands act like giant sponges, ②[absorbing] large amounts of water and releasing it slowly. As a result, nearby rivers are less likely to overflow. Wetlands also ③[clean] water. As water moves slowly through the plants and soil, many harmful substances are trapped and broken down. In addition, wetlands are home to a ④[narrow] variety of wildlife, from insects and frogs to birds that stop there during long migrations. Because of these benefits, many countries now try to protect the wetlands that remain and even ⑤[restore] ones that were lost.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 곤충, 개구리에서 철새까지 다양한 생물이 산다고 했으니 narrow가 아니라 wide나 rich처럼 '다양하고 풍부한'의 뜻이어야 해요. 대체하기 어려운 역할, 물을 흡수, 물을 깨끗하게, 잃은 습지 복원은 모두 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: Dictionaries are often thought of as rule books that tell us what words must mean. In reality, most dictionary makers see their job differently. They do not decide how words should be used; they observe how people actually use them and record what they find. When enough speakers begin to use an old word in a new way, the dictionary eventually adds the new meaning, even if some people complain that it is "wrong." For example, the English word "nice" once meant "foolish," and only after centuries of changing use did it come to mean "pleasant." In this sense, a dictionary is less like a law book and more like a photograph of a language at a certain moment. It shows where the language is at the time, but it cannot stop the language from moving. The real authority over the meaning of words, then, belongs to ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 사전 편찬자는 뜻을 정하지 않고 사람들이 실제로 쓰는 방식을 기록하며, 충분히 많은 화자가 새 뜻으로 쓰면 사전이 따라간다고 했어요. 그래서 낱말 뜻의 진짜 권한은 말하는 사람들에게 있어요. ④는 글에서 권한이 없다고 한 쪽이에요.

items.passage: We often assume that the more information we include, the better we understand something. Yet consider a map. A map that showed every tree, every stone, and every crack in the road would be as large and as confusing as the land itself, and no traveler could use it. A map is useful precisely because its makers have chosen to leave most things out, keeping only the roads, rivers, and towns that a traveler needs. Thinking works in a similar way. When a scientist explains why apples fall, she does not mention the color of the apple or the mood of the person watching it. Those details are real, but they are not relevant to the question. Students who try to memorize every fact in a chapter often understand it less well than those who can tell which facts matter. Understanding, in other words, depends not only on what we know but also on ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: our ability to decide what we can safely ignore
how much detail we manage to remember
the number of sources we have checked
our willingness to accept others' views
the time we spend observing the world directly
items.exp: 지도는 대부분을 빼야 쓸모 있고, 과학자도 상관없는 세부는 말하지 않으며, 중요한 사실을 가려내는 학생이 더 잘 이해한다고 했어요. 그래서 이해는 무엇을 무시해도 되는지 판단하는 능력에 달려 있어요. ②는 모든 것을 외우려는, 글이 비판하는 태도예요.

items.passage: Before a game or a workout, many athletes still hold long, still stretches, such as bending down to touch their toes for thirty seconds. However, sports scientists now recommend a different kind of warm-up for the minutes right before activity. ① Instead of standing still, athletes are advised to move through exercises like light jogging, leg swings, and arm circles. ② These movements gradually raise body temperature and increase blood flow to the muscles that are about to be used. ③ As a result, the muscles become more flexible and ready for the quick, powerful actions that most sports require. ④ Many athletes also listen to their favorite music before a game, believing that it helps them focus and feel confident. ⑤ Some studies have even found that long, still stretches right before activity can briefly reduce muscle power, which is another reason to choose an active warm-up.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 경기 직전에는 가만히 하는 스트레칭 대신 움직이는 준비 운동을 하라는 글이에요. ④는 경기 전 음악을 듣는다는 내용으로 경기 준비라는 점은 같지만 준비 운동 방식과는 관계가 없어요.

items.passage:
Have you ever wondered why your smartphone screen responds to your finger but not to the tip of a plastic pen? The answer lies in electricity, and in a simple difference between your skin and plastic.

(A) A plastic pen or a gloved hand, however, does not conduct electricity, so it causes no change in the charge. That is why special gloves for smartphone users have threads that carry electricity sewn into their fingertips.

(B) Most smartphone screens are covered with a thin, invisible layer that holds a small electric charge across its entire surface. Beneath this layer lies a grid of tiny sensors that constantly measure the charge.

(C) Because the human body conducts electricity, a fingertip that touches the screen draws away a little of this charge at that point. The sensors detect the change, and the phone calculates exactly where it happened.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 화면에 전하를 띤 층과 센서가 있다는 (B)가 먼저 오고, (C)의 this charge가 (B)의 전하를 받아 손가락이 전하를 빼앗는 원리를 설명해요. 마지막으로 however로 전기가 통하지 않는 펜과 장갑을 대조하는 (A)가 와요.

items.passage: When a famous painting becomes damaged by age, dirt, or accidents, it is sent to a restorer, an expert whose job is to repair it. ( ① ) In the past, restorers often repainted damaged areas freely, sometimes changing colors or even adding details they thought the artist should have included. ( ② ) As a result, some old paintings we see in museums are partly the work of later hands. ( ③ ) They use special paints that can be dissolved without harming the original layers, so later experts with better tools can undo their work if necessary. ( ④ ) Restorers also keep detailed records and photographs of every change they make. ( ⑤ ) In this way, the goal of restoration has shifted from making a painting look perfect to protecting what the original artist actually created.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Today, however, most restorers follow a very different rule: anything they add must be easy to remove in the future.
items.exp: ③ 앞까지는 과거 복원가들이 마음대로 덧칠했다는 내용이고, ③ 뒤 They use special paints that can be dissolved는 오늘날 복원가들의 방식이에요. 그래서 Today, however로 전환하며 '쉽게 지울 수 있어야 한다'는 규칙을 말하는 문장이 ③에 들어가야 해요.

items.passage: In many modern apartment buildings, neighbors live only a few meters apart yet hardly know each other's names. A team of researchers wanted to find out what helps neighbors form connections. They compared two buildings of similar size. In the first, residents shared a small laundry room on each floor, where they often met while waiting for their clothes to dry. In the second, every apartment had its own washing machine, so residents rarely ran into one another. The conversations in the laundry rooms were usually short and simple, about the weather or a lost sock. Yet after a year, residents of the first building were far more likely to say they could ask a neighbor to watch their children or lend them some money in an emergency. The brief, unplanned meetings had slowly built a feeling that others could be counted on, something the second building lacked.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Frequent but (A) ___ meetings in shared spaces can create (B) ___ among neighbors who would otherwise remain strangers.
items.exp: 세탁실에서의 짧고 계획되지 않은 만남은 casual, 위급할 때 이웃에게 부탁할 수 있다는 '믿을 수 있다는 느낌'은 trust로 바꿔 쓸 수 있어요. 만남은 공식적이거나 계획된 것이 아니었으니 formal, planned는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Money is supposed to be perfectly interchangeable. A ten-thousand-won bill you earned at a part-time job can buy exactly the same things as one you found on the street. Logically, then, people should treat all their money the same way. In reality, however, most of us do not. We tend to sort money into separate mental "boxes" depending on where it came from or what we plan to use it for, and we follow (a)[different] rules for each box.

Consider a simple example. Suppose you receive an unexpected gift of money from a relative. Many people feel (b)[free] to spend such money on things they would never normally buy, like expensive concert tickets or a new gadget. The same people may be very careful with money from their regular paychecks, even though the two amounts have the same value. Because the gift feels like "extra" money, spending it seems to (c)[cost] less.

This habit can be both harmful and helpful. On the negative side, it can make us (d)[wise] with tax refunds or bonuses that could have paid off debts. On the positive side, it can be used as a tool for saving. People who put money into a box labeled "for college" or "emergency fund" often find it harder to spend on daily wants. By giving money a clear purpose, they create a mental barrier that protects their savings.

Understanding how we label money can therefore help us make better choices. Before spending, it is worth asking whether we are treating a won as a won, or (e)[letting] its label decide for us.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How to Earn More Money from Part-Time Jobs
The Danger of Borrowing from Relatives
Saving Is Impossible Without a Budget
Not All Won Are Equal: The Labels We Put on Money
items.exp: 돈은 똑같은 가치인데도 사람들이 출처나 용도에 따라 마음속 상자로 나누어 다르게 쓴다는 내용이에요. 그래서 '모든 원이 똑같지는 않다: 돈에 붙이는 이름표'가 제목으로 알맞아요. 선물이나 저축은 예로 나온 낱말일 뿐이에요.

Understanding how we label money can therefore help us make better choices. Before spending, it is worth asking whether we are treating a won as a won, or (e)[letting] its label decide for us.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: On the negative side, 즉 나쁜 점으로 빚을 갚을 수 있었던 환급금이나 보너스를 함부로 쓰게 만든다는 흐름이에요. 그래서 (d) wise는 careless나 wasteful로 바꿔야 해요. 나머지는 모두 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Before sunrise, Leo and his grandfather loaded the small boat with fishing rods, a bucket of bait, and two sandwiches. It was Leo's first fishing trip, and he had promised his friends a photo of a huge fish. As the boat moved slowly across the misty lake, Leo kept asking when they would catch something. His grandfather only smiled and said, "The lake decides that, not us." When they finally stopped near a group of tall reeds, Leo threw (a)[his] line into the water with a big splash.

(B)
Slowly, Leo began to notice things he had missed. A heron stood perfectly still at the edge of the reeds. Tiny circles appeared on the surface where insects landed. For the first time all morning, (b)[he] forgot about the photo. Just then, the tip of his rod bent sharply. "Grandpa!" he shouted. The old man leaned over and helped (c)[him] reel in the line slowly.

(C)
It was a fish, but a small one, no longer than Leo's hand. Leo looked at it, then at his grandfather. "Should we keep it?" he asked. "That's your choice," Grandfather replied. Leo thought quietly for a long moment, then carefully put the fish back into the lake and watched it disappear. On the way home across the calm water, (d)[he] didn't mention the photo once. Instead, he asked when they could come back.

(D)
An hour passed, then another. Nothing. Leo checked his line again and again, pulling it out of the water each time to see if the bait was still there. "Maybe there are no fish here at all," he complained. Grandfather handed him a sandwich. "Every time you pull your line out, the fish swim away," (e)[he] said gently. "Try keeping still and just watching the water for a while." Leo sighed, but he did as he was told.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 낚싯줄을 던진 뒤, 몇 시간 동안 아무것도 잡히지 않아 할아버지가 가만히 지켜보라고 조언하는 (D)가 와요. 그 조언대로 주변을 보다가 입질이 오는 (B), 잡은 작은 물고기를 놓아주는 (C) 순서예요.

items.exp: (e)는 Leo에게 샌드위치를 건네며 가만히 지켜보라고 조언한 할아버지예요. (a), (b), (c), (d)는 모두 Leo를 가리켜요.

items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Leo는 친구들에게 큰 물고기 사진을 약속했다.
할아버지는 언제 물고기를 잡을지는 호수가 정한다고 말했다.
Leo는 갈대 가장자리에 서 있는 왜가리를 보았다.
Leo는 미끼를 확인하려고 낚싯줄을 여러 번 물 밖으로 꺼냈다.
items.exp: (C)에서 Leo는 작은 물고기를 조심스럽게 호수에 다시 놓아주었어요. 그래서 집으로 가져갔다는 ④가 틀려요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Rivera,

I am a resident of Oakwood Apartments and a regular user of the Oakwood Community Center. I am writing about the center's weekend schedule. At present, the center closes at 5 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. For many residents who work long hours during the week, the weekend is the only time we can use the gym and the study room. Every Saturday afternoon, I see people waiting in line for the treadmills, and many leave without exercising at all. Students preparing for exams also have to pack up their books just when they have settled in to study. I understand that staffing costs money, but even two more hours would help a great deal. Would you consider keeping the center open until 7 p.m. on weekends? Many of my neighbors have told me they agree, and we would be happy to sign a request if needed.

Sincerely,
Daniel Cho
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 주민 센터 체육관 기구 추가를 건의하려고
items.exp: 주말에 오후 5시에 문을 닫아 주민들이 운동과 공부를 제대로 못 한다며 주말에 오후 7시까지 열어 줄 수 있는지 묻고 있어요. 그래서 운영 시간 연장 요청이 목적이에요. 서명은 필요하면 하겠다는 말일 뿐 독려하는 글은 아니에요.

items.passage: On my first day as a volunteer at the animal shelter, I stood outside the door for a full minute before going in. I had never had a pet, and the barking from inside made my hands sweat. "What if the dogs don't like me?" I thought. The manager handed me a leash and pointed to a large brown dog named Biscuit. He looked huge, and I was sure he would pull me over. I almost asked for a smaller dog. But when I opened the cage, Biscuit sat down quietly and pushed his head gently into my hand. During our walk, he stayed right beside me and kept looking up as if to check that I was still there. When we returned, he rolled onto his back and waited for me to rub his belly. I laughed out loud for the first time that day. Walking home, I was already counting the days until my next visit.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음에는 문 앞에서 머뭇거리고 손에 땀이 날 만큼 망설였지만, Biscuit과 산책한 뒤 소리 내어 웃고 다음 방문을 손꼽아 기다려요. 그래서 hesitant → delighted가 맞아요. 처음부터 지루해한 것은 아니므로 ①은 틀려요.

items.passage: When a friend comes to us with a problem, our first instinct is often to tell them what we did in a similar situation. "When I had trouble with my roommate, I just talked to her directly, and everything was fine," we say, sure that we are being helpful. But our experience was shaped by our own personality, our own roommate, and countless details our friend does not share. What worked for us may fail completely for someone who is shyer, or whose roommate is less reasonable. Offering our own solution in this way can be like [handing someone a map of your own city]. The map may be accurate and carefully drawn, but it describes streets they will never walk on. A more helpful approach is to ask questions first: What is the roommate like? What has the friend already tried? Only then can we help them find a route that fits where they actually are.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [handing someone a map of your own city]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: sharing travel tips that a friend has asked for
explaining a problem in more detail than necessary
refusing to help a friend until they ask directly
drawing a clear plan to avoid future arguments
giving advice that suits our situation but not theirs
items.exp: 우리의 경험은 우리 성격과 상황에서 나온 것이라 친구에게는 맞지 않을 수 있다고 했어요. 자기 도시의 지도를 건네는 것은 정확하지만 상대가 걸을 일 없는 길을 알려 주는 것, 곧 내 상황에 맞는 조언을 주는 것이에요. ①은 '여행'이라는 겉뜻만 빌린 오답이에요.

items.passage: When an experiment does not turn out as expected, many scientists simply put the results in a drawer and move on. Journals prefer to publish exciting discoveries, so studies showing that something does not work often go unread. Yet these so-called failed results carry real value. Suppose a research team spends two years testing whether a certain plant extract can kill harmful bacteria and finds that it cannot. If the team never shares this result, other researchers may waste the same two years repeating the same test. Worse, if only the few studies that happened to show a positive effect are published, people may come to believe that the extract works when it actually does not. A clear report of what did not work tells others which paths are closed and makes the overall picture more accurate. Knowing where the answer is not is, in its own way, a step toward finding where it is.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 실패한 실험 결과도 공유하면 과학 발전에 가치가 있다.
과학 학술지는 흥미로운 발견을 더 많이 실어야 한다.
같은 실험을 여러 번 반복해야 정확한 결과를 얻는다.
식물 추출물은 해로운 세균을 없애는 데 효과가 없다.
연구자는 실험 전에 결과를 충분히 예측해야 한다.
items.exp: 효과가 없다는 결과도 공유해야 다른 연구자가 시간을 낭비하지 않고 전체 그림이 정확해진다는 내용이에요. 식물 추출물은 예로 든 가상의 실험이라 ④는 요지가 아니고, ②는 필자가 문제로 본 학술지의 태도예요.

items.passage: If you walk through a field of clover or a bean garden late at night, you may notice that the plants look different from how they did at noon. Their leaves, which were spread wide in the sunlight, are now folded up or hanging down. This daily movement, sometimes called plant sleep, has puzzled observers for thousands of years. The plants are not tired, of course. The movement is controlled by special cells at the base of each leaf. When these cells take in or lose water, they swell or shrink, and the leaf rises or falls. Remarkably, this cycle continues even when the plants are kept in a dark room for several days, which shows that it is driven by an internal clock rather than by light alone. Scientists have suggested several possible benefits, such as keeping the leaves warmer at night or protecting them from insects, but the exact reason is still being studied.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the reasons insects attack garden plants at night
a daily leaf movement in plants and what drives it
how farmers use light to speed up plant growth
the importance of water for healthy bean gardens
differences between plant cells and animal cells
items.exp: 밤이 되면 잎을 접는 식물의 움직임과, 잎 아래 세포의 수분 변화와 체내 시계가 이를 이끈다는 내용이에요. 곤충과 물은 글에 나온 낱말을 빌린 오답이에요.

items.passage: In the middle of the nineteenth century, every town in the United States set its clocks by the sun. When the sun was highest in the sky, it was noon, so the time in one town could be several minutes different from the time in a town just a few dozen kilometers to the east or west. For most people, this caused few problems. But for the growing railroads, it was a nightmare. Each railway company used its own time, and a single station might display several clocks showing different hours. Passengers missed trains, and the risk of accidents increased. Finally, in 1883, the railroads agreed to divide the country into a small number of time zones, each with one standard time. Many towns accepted the new system quickly because daily life now depended on train schedules. In this way, the needs of trains, not the movement of the sun, came to decide what time it was.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why the Sun Was a Perfect Clock
Train Accidents and Their Hidden Causes
How Towns Competed to Build Railway Stations
When Railroads Set the Clocks: The Birth of Time Zones
The Long History of Measuring Noon
items.exp: 해를 기준으로 제각각이던 시간이 철도 때문에 문제가 되자 1883년 철도 회사들이 시간대를 정했다는 내용이에요. 그래서 '철도가 시계를 맞추었을 때: 시간대의 탄생'이 알맞아요. ①은 오히려 해의 시간이 문제였다는 글과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Hillcrest Youth Robotics Day 2027

Build, test, and race your own robot! Hillcrest Science Hall invites middle and high school students to a full day of hands-on robotics.

• When: Saturday, May 15, 2027, 10:00 a.m. – 4:00 p.m.
• Where: Hillcrest Science Hall, 2nd floor
• Who: Students aged 13 to 18 (teams of 2 or 3)
• Fee: $15 per person (lunch included)

Program
• Morning: Robot-building workshop with university mentors
• Afternoon: Obstacle race and awards

Notes
• All robot kits are provided. Please do not bring your own parts.
• Register online at www.hillcrestsciencehall.org by May 5.
• The top three teams will receive science book gift cards.
items.q: Hillcrest Youth Robotics Day 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 상위 세 팀은 과학 도서 상품권을 받는다.
items.exp: 참가비는 1인당 15달러이고 점심이 포함되어 있다(lunch included)고 했어요. 그래서 점심이 포함되지 않는다는 ③이 틀려요.

items.passage: One of the best ways to learn something is to teach it to someone else. When students know that they will have to explain a topic to a classmate, they study it differently. Instead of simply ①[memorizing] facts, they try to understand how the ideas connect, because they expect questions they will have to answer. The act of explaining also reveals gaps in their knowledge. A student may feel confident about a math rule until a friend asks why it works, and suddenly she realizes that she ②[has] never really understood it. Teachers who ③[use] this method often pair students up and ask them to take turns explaining a lesson. Even students ④[who] usually stay quiet in class tend to become more active when they are given this role. The method works because it turns learners into people ⑤[which] feel responsible for someone else's understanding as well as their own.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 선행사 people이 사람이므로 관계대명사 which가 아니라 who를 써야 해요. ①은 전치사 of 뒤 동명사, ②는 주어 she에 맞는 현재완료 has, ③은 Teachers에 맞는 복수 동사, ④는 사람 선행사 students를 받는 who로 맞아요.

items.passage: After a big meal, many people feel like lying down on the sofa. However, a short walk may be a ①[better] choice. When we eat, especially foods rich in rice, bread, or sugar, the level of sugar in our blood rises. Our muscles can ②[use] some of this sugar as fuel when they are active. Even a slow walk of ten to fifteen minutes after eating can therefore help ③[lower] the rise in blood sugar. This is especially helpful for people who are at risk of diabetes. A gentle walk may also ④[ease] the uncomfortable full feeling some people get after eating, as it helps food move through the stomach. The good news is that this habit requires no special equipment or training. Because it is so ⑤[difficult] to add to daily life, a walk after dinner is one of the simplest health habits anyone can start today.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 특별한 장비나 훈련이 필요 없어 누구나 오늘 시작할 수 있는 가장 간단한 습관이라고 했으니, 일상에 더하기 어렵다는 difficult가 아니라 easy가 와야 해요. 나머지 낱말은 모두 식후 걷기의 효과를 설명하는 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage: When people listen to music, they usually pay attention to the notes: the melody they hum, the chords that move them, the rhythm that makes them tap their feet. But experienced musicians know that the moments without sound are just as important. A short pause before the final chord of a song makes listeners lean in, waiting for what comes next. A gap in the middle of a fast drum pattern gives the beat its energy. In written music, these moments are marked with special symbols called rests, and a player who ignores them is making a mistake, just like one who plays a wrong note. Without them, music would become a continuous stream of sound with no shape at all, much like a page of writing without spaces or periods. In this sense, a great piece of music is built not only from sound but also from ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 노래 끝 화음 전의 멈춤, 드럼 패턴 속의 빈틈, 쉼표 등 소리가 없는 순간이 음표만큼 중요하다고 했어요. 그래서 음악은 소리뿐 아니라 침묵으로도 만들어진다는 말이 들어가요. harmony는 소리 쪽에 속해 글의 요점과 반대예요.

items.passage: We often think of a tradition as something that must be kept exactly as it was received, like an old vase that is safe only as long as no one touches it. From this point of view, any change is a kind of damage. But traditions that last for centuries rarely work this way. Consider a folk song passed down through generations. Each singer adds a slightly different rhythm or replaces a word that no longer makes sense, and because of these small changes, the song continues to speak to new listeners. A song that was frozen in its original form, by contrast, might be admired in a museum but no longer sung by anyone. The same is true of holiday customs, festival foods, and even old games. They stay alive because people keep finding new reasons to practice them. A tradition, therefore, survives not by being protected from the present but by ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: being recorded carefully in museums and books
being taught only by those who know its original form
being separated from the changing tastes of each age
being reshaped by each generation that takes part in it
being shared with as many foreign visitors as possible
items.exp: 민요를 부르는 사람마다 조금씩 바꾸기 때문에 새 세대에게도 살아 있고, 그대로 굳은 노래는 더 이상 불리지 않는다고 했어요. 그래서 전통은 참여하는 각 세대가 다시 빚어 가면서 살아남아요. ①과 ③은 글이 비판하는 '보존' 쪽의 생각이에요.

items.passage: Astronauts who spend several months on a space station often return to Earth a few centimeters taller than when they left. This happens because of the way gravity affects the human spine. ① On Earth, gravity constantly presses down on the soft discs between the bones of the back, squeezing them slightly. ② In space, where this pressure disappears, the discs expand, and the spine stretches out. ③ Astronauts also eat specially packaged meals, many of which can be prepared simply by adding hot water. ④ The extra height, however, does not last; within a few weeks of returning, gravity presses the discs back to their usual size. ⑤ In the meantime, the stretching can cause back pain, so astronauts do special exercises to protect their spines both in space and after landing.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 우주에서 중력이 사라져 척추 사이 디스크가 늘어나 키가 커지는 현상을 설명하는 글이에요. ③은 우주인의 식사에 관한 내용이라 같은 우주 생활 소재지만 키와 척추 이야기의 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
Hailstones are balls of ice that fall from thunderstorms, sometimes even on hot summer days. How can ice form when the ground is so warm?

(A) It begins when strong upward winds carry raindrops high into the storm cloud, where the air is far below freezing. There, the drops freeze into tiny balls of ice.

(B) Eventually, the stones grow too heavy for the winds to hold up, and they fall to the ground. The stronger the upward winds, the longer this process continues, which is why the largest hailstones come from the most powerful storms.

(C) These ice balls do not fall right away. The same winds push them up again and again, and each trip through the cloud adds a new layer of frozen water, much like the layers of an onion.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?

items.passage: Many people assume that deaf people all over the world use a single, shared sign language. ( ① ) In reality, sign languages grew naturally within separate deaf communities, just as spoken languages developed separately in different regions, and there are now more than three hundred of them. ( ② ) What is more, the borders between sign languages often do not match the borders between spoken languages. ( ③ ) Such cases show that a sign language is not simply a spoken language turned into hand shapes. ( ④ ) Each one is a complete language with its own grammar and vocabulary. ( ⑤ ) For example, many sign languages use the space in front of the signer's body to show where people and objects are, a feature that has no direct match in spoken grammar.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

For instance, American Sign Language and British Sign Language are so different that their users often struggle to understand each other, even though people in both countries speak English.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 같은 영어권인데도 수어가 서로 다르다는 예로, 수어의 경계가 음성 언어의 경계와 맞지 않는다는 ③ 앞 문장을 뒷받침해요. ③ 뒤 Such cases가 바로 이 예를 가리키므로 ③에 들어가야 해요.

items.passage: Before an important shot, many basketball players quietly talk to themselves. Some researchers wanted to know whether the kind of words they use makes a difference. They asked a group of young players to practice free throws while repeating one of two types of phrases. One group used short instructions about their movements, such as "Elbow in" or "Follow through." The other group used general phrases like "I hope I don't miss." After several weeks, the first group had improved their accuracy noticeably, while the second group showed little change. When interviewed, players in the first group said that focusing on a specific action kept their minds from wandering to the crowd or the score. Players in the second group, on the other hand, admitted that their phrases often made them think more about failing. The words athletes say to themselves, it seems, can either guide their bodies or distract them.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Athletes who talk to themselves using (A) ___ instructions about their actions tend to perform better, because such words help them stay (B) ___ on the task.
items.exp: Elbow in처럼 동작에 관한 구체적인 지시를 쓴 선수들이 나아졌으니 (A)는 specific, 마음이 관중이나 점수로 흐르지 않게 해 주었으니 (B)는 focused예요. general은 실패를 떠올리게 한 두 번째 집단의 말이에요.

items.passage:
For much of the twentieth century, city planners believed that wide roads were the key to a successful city. More lanes, they reasoned, would let cars move quickly and reduce traffic jams. Yet in many cities, the opposite happened. Wider roads encouraged more people to drive, and before long the new lanes were just as (a)[crowded] as the old ones. At the same time, streets became harder and more dangerous to cross on foot.

Today, a growing number of planners are trying a different approach. Instead of widening streets, they make them narrower. A four-lane road may be redesigned with two lanes for cars, a bike lane, and a wider sidewalk lined with trees. At first, this may seem likely to (b)[worsen] traffic. However, drivers on narrower streets naturally slow down, because the road feels tighter and more is happening around them. Slower speeds mean fewer serious accidents, and when accidents do happen, people are less (c)[likely] to be badly hurt.

Narrower streets bring other benefits as well. Wider sidewalks give people room to walk side by side, sit on benches, or stop at small shops. When more people walk, local stores tend to have more customers, and the street feels (d)[livelier]. Many residents also report that they feel safer letting their children walk to school.

Of course, a narrower road is not the right choice for every street. But these examples suggest that a street is more than a pipe for moving cars. It is also a place where people meet, shop, and spend time, and designing it only for speed may (e)[improve] what makes city life valuable.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Building More Lanes: The Fastest Cure for Traffic
Less Road, More Life: Rethinking City Streets
Why Children Should Walk to School
The Rising Cost of Repairing Old Roads
How Bike Lanes Became Popular Around the World
items.exp: 넓은 도로가 오히려 교통과 안전을 나쁘게 했고, 도로를 좁히면 속도가 줄고 걷는 사람과 상점이 늘어난다는 내용이에요. 그래서 '도로는 줄이고 삶은 늘리기'가 알맞아요. ①은 글이 반박하는 예전 생각이에요.

items.passage:
(A)
The bell above the door rang as Mina stepped into Haddon's Books, a narrow shop that smelled of dust and old paper. Her English teacher had asked the class to read a classic novel, and the new copies at the big bookstore were too expensive. Behind the counter sat Mr. Haddon, a white-haired man who had run the shop for nearly fifty years. He pointed (a)[her] toward a tall shelf at the back without a word. After searching for twenty minutes, Mina found a worn copy of the novel with a faded blue cover. It cost only two dollars.

(B)
The next afternoon, Mina returned to the shop and placed the letter on the counter. Mr. Haddon put on his glasses and began to read. Halfway through, his hands started to shake. "Clara was my wife," he said quietly. "She passed away three years ago. I sold boxes of her books without looking inside them." (b)[She] had never seen an adult cry before, and she did not know what to say, so she simply waited while he read to the end.

(C)
That evening, as (c)[she] turned the first page, a folded sheet of paper fell into her lap. It was a letter written in neat handwriting and dated 1978. "Dear future me," it began. "I hope you still read every night and still believe that books can change a life." It was signed "Clara." Mina read it three times. She felt that the letter did not belong to her, so (d)[she] decided to take it back to the shop.

(D)
When he finally looked up, Mr. Haddon tried to give Mina her two dollars back, but she shook her head. "Then let me give you something else," (e)[he] said, smiling for the first time. "Come here any Saturday and read whatever you like, for free." From that day on, Mina spent every Saturday afternoon in the quiet shop, and Mr. Haddon always kept a chair ready for her.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 책을 산 뒤, 그날 저녁 책을 펼쳐 편지를 발견하는 (C)가 와요. 다음 날 그 편지를 가게에 가져가 보여 주는 (B), 다 읽은 뒤(When he finally looked up) 고마움을 전하는 (D) 순서예요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Howard,

My name is Daniel Kim, and I am a second-year student at Westbrook High School. Every weekday morning, about thirty students from the Pine Valley area take the Route 12 bus to school. The first bus leaves Pine Valley at 7:50 a.m. and reaches the school gate at 8:25, only five minutes before our first class begins. When the traffic is heavy, which happens almost every Monday, many of us arrive late even though we left home on time. Some students have even started walking forty minutes to school instead. I understand that changing a timetable is not simple, but I am writing to ask whether your company could add one earlier bus, departing around 7:30 a.m. I have attached a list of signatures from students and parents who would use it. Thank you for considering our situation.

Sincerely,
Daniel Kim

items.passage: I stepped off the train at Central Station and reached for my backpack, but my hand found only empty air. My laptop, my passport, and the notebook with every phone number I needed were inside it. The train doors had already closed, and I watched the train slide away into the dark tunnel. My heart pounded, and I could hardly breathe. I ran to the information desk, trying to explain in broken sentences what had happened. The officer listened calmly, picked up a phone, and spoke to someone for a minute. Then he smiled. "A passenger found a blue backpack on that train and gave it to the driver. It will be at the next station in ten minutes." I let out a long breath, and my shoulders finally dropped. When the bag was placed in my arms, everything was still inside. I thanked the officer again and again.

items.passage: In many classrooms, the question "Does everyone understand?" is followed by silence, and the teacher moves on. But silence rarely means understanding. Students often stay quiet because they fear looking slow in front of their classmates, or because they cannot yet put their confusion into words. If teachers want honest feedback, they should build it into the lesson instead of waiting for brave volunteers. For example, at the end of each class, students can write on a small card one thing they found unclear. The cards are anonymous, so no one feels embarrassed. Reading them takes only a few minutes, yet it shows the teacher exactly which points need to be explained again. When confusion is treated as a normal part of learning rather than a weakness, students begin to learn more deeply. Teachers should make it safe and easy for students to reveal what they do not know.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?

학생들은 이해하지 못한 내용을 수업 후 스스로 복습해야 한다.
교사는 수업이 끝날 때마다 쪽지 시험으로 학생들의 성취도를 평가해야 한다.
학생들은 친구들 앞에서 질문하는 것을 두려워하지 말아야 한다.

items.passage: Every weekend, a new bakery in my neighborhood hands out free cookies, and a long line forms outside its door. People wait for twenty or thirty minutes to receive a cookie that costs about one dollar in the shop. Economists would say these customers are not really getting something for nothing. They are paying, but not with money. Time is a resource just like cash, and an hour spent in line is an hour that cannot be used for work, rest, or family. Because no coins change hands, however, this cost is easy to ignore. We notice a price printed on a label, but we rarely count the minutes that slip away while we wait. In the case of the free cookie, [the price tag was hidden in the clock]. Before chasing anything labeled "free," it is worth asking what we are giving up to get it.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the price tag was hidden in the clock]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the bakery secretly raised the price of its cookies
customers did not know when the free event would end
the real cost was paid in time rather than in money
the cookie was worth less than the time spent baking it
people checked the time too often while waiting in line
items.exp: 공짜 쿠키를 받으려고 줄을 선 사람들은 돈 대신 시간으로 값을 치렀다는 것이 글의 핵심이에요. 그래서 가격표가 시계 속에 숨어 있었다는 말은 진짜 비용을 시간으로 냈다는 뜻이에요. ④는 빵을 굽는 시간을 말하고 있어 글과 관계가 없어요.

items.passage: Many songbirds migrate at night, using the stars and the faint glow of the horizon to find their way. Over the past century, however, cities have filled the night sky with artificial light. Bright towers and streetlights can confuse these travelers, drawing them toward urban areas where they circle buildings until they are exhausted. Some crash into glass windows that reflect the lights or the sky. Researchers estimate that hundreds of millions of birds die from building collisions in North America alone each year. The good news is that the problem has a simple partial solution. When cities turn off or dim unnecessary lights during the busiest migration seasons, the number of birds found under buildings falls sharply. Several cities now run "lights out" programs in spring and fall, asking office buildings to switch off decorative lighting late at night.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the role of stars in the history of human navigation
ways birds change their songs in noisy cities
the growing number of bird species in urban parks
why tall buildings use reflective glass windows
the harm of artificial night light to migrating birds and a solution
items.exp: 도시의 인공 불빛이 밤에 이동하는 새들을 혼란스럽게 해 건물 충돌로 죽게 만든다는 문제와, 이동 철에 불을 끄는 해결책을 함께 다루고 있어요. ④의 반사 유리는 일부 내용일 뿐 글 전체의 주제가 아니에요.

items.passage: Electric cars are much quieter than cars with gasoline engines, especially at low speeds. At first, this seemed to be nothing but an advantage: fewer noisy streets and calmer neighborhoods. Soon, however, safety experts pointed out a problem. Pedestrians, particularly people with visual impairments, rely on the sound of engines to know when a car is approaching. A car that glides silently through a parking lot can surprise someone stepping off the curb. As a result, many countries now require electric vehicles to produce an artificial sound when they move slowly. Engineers design these sounds carefully so that they are easy to notice but not annoying. Some resemble a soft hum, while others rise in pitch as the car speeds up. In this way, a machine that was built to be quiet has been given a voice again, for the sake of the people around it.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Electric Cars: Faster Than You Think
Why Quiet Cars Were Taught to Make Noise
The End of Traffic Noise in Our Cities
How Engine Sounds Affect Drivers' Moods
Designing Cars for Drivers with Poor Eyesight
items.exp: 조용한 전기차가 보행자, 특히 시각 장애인에게 위험해서 저속에서 인공 소리를 내도록 하게 되었다는 내용이에요. ⑤는 운전자가 아니라 보행자를 위한 것이라는 점에서 틀려요.

items.passage: Tomas Reiler was born in 1868 in a small village in the Swiss Alps. As a boy, he worked with his father, who guided travelers across mountain passes. At the age of nineteen, he bought a heavy wooden camera from a traveling merchant and taught himself how to use it. Carrying glass plates that weighed more than twenty kilograms, he climbed peaks that few photographers had ever reached. His images of glaciers, taken between 1890 and 1925, were first sold as postcards to tourists. Reiler never married and spent his final years in Geneva, where he died in 1941. Long after his death, scientists discovered the true value of his work: by comparing his photographs with modern pictures of the same places, they could measure how much the glaciers had shrunk. Today, more than three thousand of his glass plates are kept at a museum in Bern.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 어린 시절 아버지와 함께 여행자들의 산길 안내 일을 했다.
열아홉 살에 카메라를 구입해 사용법을 독학했다.
그의 빙하 사진은 처음에 관광객용 엽서로 판매되었다.
그가 죽은 뒤 과학자들이 그의 사진으로 빙하의 변화를 측정했다.
그의 유리판 대부분은 제네바의 한 박물관에 보관되어 있다.
items.exp: 마지막 문장에서 3천 장이 넘는 유리판은 베른(Bern)의 박물관에 있다고 했어요. 제네바는 그가 말년을 보낸 곳이에요.

items.passage: The ancient Romans built more than 80,000 kilometers of paved roads across their empire. These roads allowed soldiers to move quickly, and they also carried merchants, messengers, and new ideas. They were not simply flat paths of stone. Workers first dug a deep trench and ①[filled] it with layers of different materials: large stones at the bottom, then gravel, and finally tightly fitted paving stones on top. This structure allowed rainwater to drain away, which kept the road ②[from breaking] apart in winter. The surface was also slightly curved, so water ran off to the sides instead of ③[stay] on top. Along the roads, stone markers ④[showing] the distance to the next town helped travelers plan their journeys. Many of these roads were so well made that parts of them are still used today, nearly two thousand years after they ⑤[were built].
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③은 전치사 instead of 뒤이므로 동명사 staying으로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 dug와 병렬인 과거동사, ②는 keep A from -ing, ④는 markers를 꾸미는 현재분사, ⑤는 roads가 지어진 것이므로 수동태로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: In the 1790s, France built a remarkable system for sending messages across the country without wires or electricity. It was a chain of towers placed on hilltops about ten to fifteen kilometers apart. On top of each tower stood a wooden beam with two movable arms, and different positions of the arms ①[represented] different letters or words. An operator in one tower watched the next tower through a telescope and ②[copied] each signal so that it could be passed along the line. In this way, a short message could travel hundreds of kilometers in less than an hour, a speed that seemed ③[amazing] at a time when letters were carried on horseback. The system, however, had clear limits. It worked only during the day and in good weather, since fog or darkness made the signals ④[invisible]. Even so, it proved that information could move far faster than any rider, and this success ⑤[discouraged] inventors from searching for even quicker ways to communicate.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 신호탑이 정보가 말 탄 사람보다 훨씬 빠르게 이동할 수 있음을 증명했다는 성공은 더 빠른 통신 방법을 찾도록 발명가들을 북돋웠을 것이므로 ⑤ discouraged는 encouraged로 바꿔야 해요. ④ invisible은 안개나 어둠 때문에 신호가 보이지 않는다는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage: Between the ages of two and six, children learn several new words every day. Surprisingly, very few of these words are taught directly. Parents rarely stop to say, "This is the meaning of 'enormous.'" Instead, children figure out meanings from the situations around them. If a mother points at an elephant at the zoo and says, "Look how enormous it is!", the child connects the word with the animal's huge size. Later, hearing "an enormous cake" or "an enormous wave," the child refines the meaning further. Each new sentence adds a small piece of information, and gradually a clear picture forms. In this sense, a young child learns vocabulary much like a detective solves a mystery: not through a single answer handed over by someone else, but by collecting ___ and putting them together.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 아이들은 낱말의 뜻을 직접 배우지 않고, 문장마다 얻는 작은 정보 조각을 모아 뜻을 알아낸다고 했어요. 탐정 비유에 맞게 단서(clues)를 모은다고 해야 자연스러워요. 규칙(rules)을 배운다는 내용은 없어요.

items.passage: Imagine you are told that heavier objects always fall faster. It sounds reasonable, and if you drop a stone and a feather, it even seems true. But how well do you really understand the claim? Philosophers suggest that we understand an idea only when we know its limits. So try a test: drop a stone and a tightly crumpled ball of paper of about the same size. They land almost together, even though the stone is much heavier. Now the simple rule begins to crack, and you start to wonder what really slowed the feather down. Perhaps it was the air. This kind of questioning does not destroy knowledge; it sharpens it. A person who has only repeated a rule knows less than a person who has pushed it until it failed. In short, to truly grasp an idea, we should ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: accept it as long as most experts agree with it
repeat it often enough to remember it clearly
replace it with a simpler rule that is easier to use
search for the cases in which it no longer holds
test it once and trust the result from then on
items.exp: 생각을 이해하려면 그 한계를 알아야 하고, 규칙이 무너질 때까지 밀어붙여 본 사람이 더 많이 안다고 했어요. 따라서 그 생각이 더 이상 들어맞지 않는 경우를 찾아야 한다는 말이 들어가요. ⑤는 한 번만 시험하고 믿는다는 뜻이라 계속 의심하며 한계를 찾으라는 글의 취지와 반대예요.

items.passage: Most households own an electric drill, yet the average drill is used for only a very short time over its entire life. It spends most of its years sitting in a drawer or a garage. This simple fact has inspired a growing number of neighborhoods to open "tool libraries." ① Like a book library, a tool library lets members borrow items such as ladders, saws, and garden tools for a small yearly fee. ② Members save money and storage space, since they no longer need to buy equipment they will rarely use. ③ Modern power tools have become lighter and quieter thanks to improved batteries. ④ The libraries also bring neighbors together, as volunteers often teach free workshops on basic home repairs. ⑤ In this way, a shelf of shared tools can strengthen both household budgets and community ties.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 이웃이 공구를 함께 빌려 쓰는 공구 도서관의 장점을 설명하는 글이에요. ③은 전동 공구 자체의 기술 발전 이야기라서 공구를 나누어 쓰는 흐름과 관계가 없어요.

items.passage:
Almost everyone has cried while cutting an onion. The tears, however, have nothing to do with sadness. They are the result of a clever chemical defense that protects the onion from hungry animals.

(A) When a knife breaks these cells open, the two kinds of substances suddenly mix and produce a gas. This gas quickly rises into the air and drifts toward the face of the person who is cutting.

(B) Inside an onion, certain chemicals and the enzymes that act on them are normally stored in separate parts of each cell. As long as this separation remains, a whole onion is harmless and has only a mild smell.

(C) There, it reacts with the thin layer of water on the surface of the eye and forms a weak acid that stings. The eyes respond by producing tears to wash it away. This is why chilling an onion before cutting, which slows the release of the gas, can save you a few tears.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 양파의 세포 안에 화학 물질과 효소가 따로 저장되어 있다는 (B)가 먼저 오고, 칼이 이 세포들(these cells)을 깨면 두 물질이 섞여 기체가 생긴다는 (A)가 이어져요. 그 기체가 눈에 닿은 곳(There, it)에서 산이 생겨 눈물이 난다는 (C)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: In many parts of Asia, as well as in countries such as Sweden and Canada, people take off their shoes before entering a home. ( ① ) To visitors from elsewhere, this custom may look like nothing more than a matter of good manners. ( ② ) In places with snowy winters or long rainy seasons, shoes carry mud, water, and road salt that can damage floors and carpets. ( ③ ) In homes where people traditionally sit or even sleep on the floor, keeping it clean matters even more. ( ④ ) Today, some researchers add another reason: shoe soles can bring dirt and germs from the street into living spaces. ( ⑤ ) Whether for comfort, cleanliness, or respect, the shoes left by the door say a great deal about how people think of home.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Yet the custom also has very practical roots.
items.exp: 신발을 벗는 것이 단순한 예절로 보일 수 있다는 문장 뒤에, Yet으로 실용적인 이유도 있다고 바꾸어 말한 다음 진흙·물·소금 같은 구체적 이유가 이어져야 해요. 그래서 ②가 알맞아요. ③ 이후는 이미 실용적인 이유를 말하고 있어서 Yet으로 연결되지 않아요.

items.passage: When you feel upset, simply naming the feeling may help calm you down. In one experiment, researchers showed participants photos of angry or frightened faces while scanning their brains. When participants just looked at the photos, a brain area linked to fear and alarm became very active. But when they were asked to choose a word, such as "angry" or "scared," to describe each face, activity in that area dropped. At the same time, a region involved in thinking and self-control became more active. Other studies have found similar effects in daily life: people who write down exactly what they are feeling, such as "nervous," "disappointed," or "lonely," often say they feel less overwhelmed afterward. Putting a feeling into language seems to turn it from a storm we are caught in into an object we can look at.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Giving (A) ___ to our feelings can (B) ___ their hold on the mind.
items.exp: 감정을 낱말로 이름 붙이면(labels) 두려움과 관련된 뇌 영역의 활동이 줄고 덜 압도된다고 했으므로 감정의 힘을 약하게(weaken) 해요. 사진을 그냥 보기만 하는 것(attention)은 오히려 그 영역을 활발하게 했어요.

items.passage:
When a great whale dies in the open ocean, its body usually sinks to the deep sea floor. This event, known as a "whale fall," may sound like an ending, but for countless creatures it is a (a)[beginning]. The deep sea is a dark and cold place where food is extremely (b)[scarce]. Most animals there survive on tiny bits of material drifting down from the surface. A single whale body, which can weigh more than forty tons, therefore delivers a sudden feast equal to thousands of years of normal food supply.

Scientists who have studied whale falls with underwater robots describe several stages. First, large scavengers such as sharks and hagfish arrive and strip away the soft flesh within months. Next, smaller animals like worms and crabs (c)[move] in to feed on the remaining bits and the rich mud around the bones. Finally, over decades, special bacteria break down the fats stored inside the bones. These bacteria support whole communities of creatures, some of which have been found nowhere else. Because of this long process, a single whale fall can support deep-sea life for fifty years or more.

Some researchers worry that as whale numbers fell during centuries of hunting, whale falls became (d)[common], making it harder for these creatures to spread from one skeleton to the next. Protecting whales today, then, may (e)[benefit] not only the whales themselves but also the hidden life that waits for them in the deep.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How a Whale's Death Feeds the Deep Sea
Why Whales Sink After They Die
Robots That Explore the Ocean Floor
Centuries of Whale Hunting in the Open Sea
Sharks: The Cleaners of the Ocean
items.exp: 죽은 고래가 심해로 가라앉아 수십 년 동안 여러 단계에 걸쳐 심해 생물들의 먹이가 된다는 내용이므로 ①이 알맞아요. ②는 첫 문장만, ⑤는 첫 단계만 다룬 제목이에요.

items.exp: 고래잡이로 고래 수가 줄었다면 고래 사체는 드물어졌을 것이고, 그래서 생물들이 다른 뼈로 퍼져 나가기 어려워진 거예요. (d) common은 rare로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
Mina had trained for six months for her first marathon. On the morning of the race, she stood at the starting line among thousands of runners, feeling smaller than ever. The air was cool, and music played from speakers along the road. Her plan was simple: keep a steady pace and finish in under four and a half hours. When the starting gun fired, (a)[she] was carried forward by the crowd, her heart beating with excitement.

(B)
For the first twenty kilometers, everything went according to plan. Around the thirty-kilometer mark, however, Mina's legs suddenly grew heavy, as if they were filled with sand. A sharp pain ran through (b)[her] calf, and she slowed to a walk. Runners passed her one after another, and she began to think about quitting. Just then, a gray-haired woman slowed down beside her. Her shirt read "Marathon No. 41." "Your first one?" the woman asked. Mina nodded, too tired to speak.

(C)
With one kilometer left, Helen slowed down and said, "Now go. This last part belongs to you." Mina ran toward the cheering crowd with all the strength (c)[she] had left. She crossed the finish line in four hours and forty-one minutes, slower than her goal, yet she burst into tears of joy. A minute later, Helen arrived. Mina asked why she had given up her own pace for a stranger. Helen smiled. "Someone did the same for me at my first race, forty marathons ago."

(D)
"I'm Helen," the woman said. "Everyone hits the wall at some point. Don't think about the finish line. Just run to the next lamppost." Mina took a deep breath and began to jog again. Helen ran beside her, counting each lamppost aloud. Although (d)[she] could easily have run much faster, Helen never left Mina's side. Slowly, lamppost by lamppost, (e)[she] found her rhythm again, her heavy legs grew lighter, and the kilometers began to pass.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 출발한 (A) 뒤에 30킬로미터 지점에서 지쳐 걷던 Mina 옆에 한 여성이 다가오는 (B), 그 여성이 Helen이라고 자신을 소개하며 가로등까지만 달리라고 하는 (D), 마지막 1킬로미터와 결승선 장면인 (C)가 차례로 와요. Helen이라는 이름은 (D)에서 처음 소개되므로 (C)가 (D)보다 앞설 수 없어요.

choices: Mina는 첫 마라톤을 위해 6개월 동안 훈련했다.
