items.exp: (C)에서 Mina는 4시간 41분에 들어와 목표(4시간 30분 이내)보다 느렸다고 했어요(slower than her goal).

items.passage:
Dear Members of the Oakdale Community,

As many of you know, the Oakdale Public Library recently received a wonderful gift. A retired teacher who lived in our town for fifty years left her entire collection of more than four thousand books to the library. Among them are rare local history records, old maps, and children's books that are no longer printed. We are deeply grateful, but our small staff cannot sort, clean, and label so many books alone. This is why we are reaching out to you. We are looking for volunteers who can spare two or three hours on Saturday mornings during March. No experience is needed, and our librarians will show you everything. If you are interested, please sign up at the front desk or call us at 555-0148. With your help, these treasures can reach readers much sooner.

Warm regards,
Rachel Moore
Head Librarian
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 도서관에 책을 기증해 줄 것을 부탁하려고
은퇴한 교사의 공로를 기리는 행사를 알리려고
items.exp: 기증받은 4천 권이 넘는 책을 직원만으로 정리할 수 없어 3월 토요일 오전에 도와줄 자원봉사자를 찾는다고 했어요. 책을 기증해 달라는 요청(④)은 없어요.

items.passage: The curtain was about to rise, and Jacob stood frozen behind it. He had practiced his lines a hundred times, but now his mind was completely empty. His hands were cold and wet, and he could hear the audience whispering on the other side. "What if I forget everything?" he thought. Then the lights came up, and he stepped onto the stage. His first line came out a little shaky, but the audience laughed at exactly the right moment. Something inside him loosened. The next line was easier, and the one after that easier still. By the second scene, he was moving freely across the stage, enjoying every word. When the play ended, the audience rose to their feet and clapped for a long time. Jacob bowed, grinning so widely that his cheeks hurt. He could not wait to do it all again the next night.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Jacob의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 막이 오르기 전 손이 차갑고 젖을 만큼 긴장하고 대사를 잊을까 걱정했지만, 관객의 반응에 마음이 풀리고 기립 박수 속에 활짝 웃으며 내일 공연을 기다려요. 그래서 anxious에서 thrilled로 바뀐 것이 알맞아요.

items.passage: Young athletes are often told to imitate the stars they admire. They watch videos of famous players and copy every movement, from the way they hold the bat to the way they celebrate. Imitation can be a useful starting point, but it has limits. Every body is different in height, strength, and flexibility, and a technique that works perfectly for one player may cause pain or poor results for another. Good coaches understand this. Instead of forcing every student into the same form, they study how each athlete moves naturally and build on those strengths. A short player may develop a quicker swing, while a tall one may learn to use a longer reach. In the end, the best coaches do not produce copies of champions. They help each athlete [find the shoes that fit their own feet].
items.q: 밑줄 친 [find the shoes that fit their own feet]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: choose the right equipment before every game
develop a style that suits their own bodies
follow the exact form of famous players
train harder than their teammates every day
accept that natural talent decides success
items.exp: 몸마다 키·힘·유연성이 달라서 좋은 코치는 각 선수가 자연스럽게 움직이는 방식을 바탕으로 기량을 키운다고 했어요. 그래서 자기 발에 맞는 신발을 찾는다는 말은 자기 몸에 맞는 방식을 찾는다는 뜻이에요. ①은 장비라는 겉뜻만 따른 오답이에요.

items.passage: Many workers believe that a long list of tasks is a sign of a productive day. They start the morning by answering every email and finishing small jobs that take only a minute or two. By evening, they have crossed off a dozen items, yet the most important project has barely moved forward. The problem is that small tasks feel satisfying because they are quick and easy to complete. Important work, on the other hand, is often difficult and slow, and its rewards come much later. As a result, people naturally put it off. One useful approach is to spend the first hour of the workday on the single task that matters most, before opening the inbox. Even if the rest of the day is filled with interruptions, that hour of focused effort will push the truly valuable work forward.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 이메일은 하루에 정해진 시간에만 확인하는 것이 좋다.
작은 일을 많이 처리하는 것이 생산성을 높이는 비결이다.
업무 중 방해를 줄이려면 근무 환경을 바꾸어야 한다.
어려운 일은 여러 사람과 나누어 처리하는 것이 효율적이다.
가장 중요한 일을 하루의 첫 시간에 먼저 하는 것이 효과적이다.
items.exp: 사람들은 쉽고 빨리 끝나는 작은 일에 빠져 중요한 일을 미루므로, 받은 편지함을 열기 전 첫 한 시간을 가장 중요한 일에 쓰라고 했어요. ①은 이메일을 언급하지만 글의 중심 내용이 아니고, ②는 글의 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: Deserts are often described as places where nothing grows, but many of them burst into life after a heavy rain. Seeds of desert wildflowers can lie in dry soil for years, waiting. They are covered with a special coating that keeps them from sprouting after a light shower, which would not provide enough water for the plant to survive. Only a soaking rain washes the coating away. Once that happens, the seeds sprout within days, and the plants race through their whole life cycle in a few weeks. They grow, flower, and produce new seeds before the ground dries out again. For a brief period, hills that were brown and empty are covered with yellow, purple, and orange blossoms. Then the flowers disappear, leaving behind seeds that will wait, sometimes for a decade, for the next good rain.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: reasons why deserts receive so little rain
the danger of sudden floods in dry regions
how desert wildflowers survive by waiting for heavy rain
the importance of protecting rare desert animals
ways farmers grow crops in desert soil
items.exp: 사막 야생화의 씨앗이 보호막 덕분에 약한 비에는 싹트지 않고, 큰비가 올 때만 짧은 기간에 한살이를 마친다는 생존 방식을 설명하고 있어요. ①은 사막에 비가 적은 이유를 다루지 않으므로 틀려요.

items.passage: For years, people were told that a strong password must be a short jumble of letters, numbers, and symbols, such as "Tr7#qZ!". The trouble is that such passwords are hard for humans to remember but surprisingly easy for computers to guess. A computer can test billions of short combinations every second. Security experts now recommend a different approach: a long phrase made of several ordinary words, such as "purple river eats cold toast." Because of its length, this kind of password would take a computer far longer to crack, even though every word in it is common. At the same time, the strange picture it creates makes it easy for a person to remember. In other words, what makes a password safe is not how complicated it looks, but how long it is.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why You Should Change Your Password Every Week
Symbols: The Secret to Unbreakable Passwords
Longer, Not Stranger: A Smarter Way to Make Passwords
How Computers Learned to Remember Words
The Danger of Sharing Passwords with Friends
items.exp: 짧고 복잡한 비밀번호보다 평범한 낱말 여러 개로 된 긴 문구가 더 안전하고 기억하기도 쉽다는 내용이에요. ②는 기호가 핵심이라는 옛 생각을 그대로 담고 있어 글과 반대예요.

items.passage:
Harbor Town Kite Festival 2027

Come and fill the sky with color at our seaside kite festival!

• When: Saturday, May 15, 2027, 10:00 a.m. – 4:00 p.m.
• Where: Seagull Beach Park
• Fees: Free entry / Kite-making class $5 per person

Events
• Kite-Making Class (11:00 a.m., 1:00 p.m.): All materials are provided. Limited to 20 people per class.
• Biggest Kite Contest (2:30 p.m.): Kites must be at least 2 meters wide.

Notes
• Kite-making classes can be booked only online at www.harbortownkites.org.
• Kites with metal parts are not allowed for safety reasons.
• In case of rain, the festival will be held on Sunday, May 16.
items.q: Harbor Town Kite Festival 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 연 만들기 수업은 하루에 두 번 열린다.
연 만들기 수업은 현장에서 신청할 수 있다.
items.exp: 연 만들기 수업은 온라인으로만 예약할 수 있다고 했으므로(can be booked only online) 현장 신청이 가능하다는 ④가 일치하지 않아요.

items.passage: For centuries, the color blue was one of the most expensive colors a painter could use. The finest blue pigment ①[was made] from a stone called lapis lazuli, which was found mainly in the mountains of what is now Afghanistan. The stone had to be carried thousands of kilometers to Europe, and turning it into paint was a slow process. Workers ground the stone into powder and then ②[washed] it many times to separate the pure blue from the gray. Because the pigment was so costly, artists often saved it for the most important parts of a painting, ③[such as] the robe of a central figure. Some contracts between painters and their clients even stated exactly how much blue ④[had to use]. Only in the nineteenth century, when chemists found a way to make a similar color cheaply, ⑤[did] blue become available to everyone.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ④는 주어가 쓰여야 할 파랑 물감(blue)이므로 수동태 had to be used로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 안료가 만들어진 것이라 수동태, ②는 ground와 병렬, ③은 예시를 드는 such as, ⑤는 Only 부사구가 앞에 와서 도치된 did로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Many students now take notes on laptops, since typing is much faster than writing by hand. Speed, however, is not always an ①[advantage] when it comes to learning. Because fast typists can record a lecture almost word for word, they often copy what they hear without thinking about it. Students who write by hand cannot keep up with the speaker, so they are ②[forced] to choose what is important and put it into their own words. This extra mental effort helps them ③[understand] the material more deeply. In several studies, students who took handwritten notes performed ④[worse] on questions that required them to explain ideas, even though their notes were shorter. Of course, laptops are useful for many tasks, but students who want to remember a lesson may benefit from ⑤[picking] up a pen.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 손으로 필기하면 내용을 골라 자기 말로 바꾸는 노력 덕분에 더 깊이 이해한다고 했으므로, 설명을 요구하는 문제에서 더 잘했어야(better) 해요. ④ worse를 better로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: Crows are known for their intelligence, and an experiment showed just how sharp their minds can be. In it, researchers wearing a particular mask caught a few wild crows, put small bands on their legs, and let them go. The birds were not harmed, but they clearly did not enjoy the experience. For years afterward, whenever someone walked through the area wearing that mask, crows gathered and screamed angrily at the person. Even crows that had never been caught joined in, apparently having learned from the others which face meant danger. When people wore a different mask, the birds ignored them. The crows, it seems, had not simply reacted to strange-looking humans. They possessed a remarkable ___ for faces, one strong enough to last for years and to be shared with others.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 까마귀들은 특정 가면을 몇 년 동안 기억하고 다른 까마귀에게까지 전했다고 했으므로 오래가는 기억(memory)이 알맞아요. 특정 가면만 알아보고 다른 가면은 무시했다는 점이 얼굴을 기억하는 능력을 보여 줘요. fear는 a remarkable ___ for faces라는 표현과도 맞지 않고, 다른 가면은 두려워하지 않았어요.

items.passage: When people cannot easily judge the quality of a product, they often use its price as a guide. A bottle of wine that costs fifty dollars is assumed to be better than one that costs ten, even by drinkers who could not tell the difference in a blind test. This habit is not entirely foolish. In many markets, higher prices do reflect better materials or more careful work, so treating price as a signal of quality saves shoppers the effort of investigating every purchase. The danger appears when sellers understand this habit. A company with an ordinary product can raise its price, not to cover higher costs, but to create the impression of excellence. Shoppers who follow the price signal then pay more for nothing extra. In such cases, the shortcut that usually protects buyers ends up ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: helping them compare products more quickly
forcing sellers to improve the quality of their goods
being used against the very people who rely on it
making expensive products less attractive to buyers
teaching shoppers to trust their own taste instead
items.exp: 가격을 품질의 신호로 보는 지름길은 보통 소비자를 돕지만, 판매자가 그 습관을 알고 가격만 올리면 소비자가 아무것도 더 얻지 못하고 돈을 더 내게 돼요. 그래서 그것에 의지하는 사람들에게 오히려 불리하게 쓰인다는 ③이 알맞아요. ①은 지름길의 평소 장점일 뿐이고, ②는 품질 향상 없이 가격만 올린다는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: In Japan, many children carry a small box lunch called a bento to school or on picnics. A bento is more than just a meal; it is often a carefully arranged little work of art. ① Parents may shape rice into animals, cut vegetables into flowers, or use seaweed to draw faces. ② The goal is not only to make the food look cute but also to encourage children to eat a balanced variety of dishes. ③ Rice has been grown in Japan for more than two thousand years, mainly in flooded fields. ④ Children who might refuse plain carrots are often happy to eat them when they are shaped like stars. ⑤ For many families, preparing a bento in the morning is also a quiet way of showing love.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 아이들의 도시락 벤토를 예쁘게 꾸미는 이유와 의미를 다루는 글이에요. ③은 일본의 벼 재배 역사에 관한 내용이라 도시락을 꾸미는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
During a thunderstorm, you can estimate how far away the lightning is with nothing more than your own counting.

(A) Sound, on the other hand, is much slower. It travels through air at about 340 meters per second, so the thunder from the same lightning reaches you a few seconds later.

(B) This works because lightning and thunder happen at the same moment, but they travel to you at very different speeds. Light moves so fast that you see the flash almost instantly, no matter where it occurs.

(C) Because of this difference, the delay between the flash and the sound tells you the distance. Every three seconds of delay means the lightning is about one kilometer away. If the delay keeps getting shorter, the storm is coming toward you.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 숫자를 세어 번개까지의 거리를 알 수 있다는 주어진 글 뒤에, 그 원리(This works because)로 빛이 매우 빠르다는 (B)가 와요. on the other hand로 소리는 훨씬 느리다는 (A)가 이어지고, 이 차이(this difference)로 거리를 계산하는 (C)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: For most of human history, people whose eyesight weakened with age simply had to accept it. As we grow older, the lens inside the eye slowly stiffens, making it hard to focus on nearby objects. ( ① ) Reading, sewing, and other close work became difficult, and many skilled workers had to stop working in their forties or fifties. ( ② ) Around the late thirteenth century, however, craftsmen in northern Italy began making the first eyeglasses. ( ③ ) These early glasses had no arms to rest on the ears, so users had to hold them in front of their eyes or balance them on their noses. ( ④ ) Still, the effect on daily life was enormous. ( ⑤ ) As printed books spread in later centuries, the demand for glasses grew even faster, and they slowly became the ordinary tool we know today.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Scholars, monks, and craftsmen, for example, could now continue their close work for many more years.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 안경이 일상에 준 큰 영향(the effect on daily life was enormous)의 구체적 예시이므로 그 문장 바로 뒤인 ⑤에 들어가야 해요. for example과 now라는 말도 안경이 생긴 뒤의 상황을 가리켜요. ③에 넣으면 안경 모양을 설명하는 흐름이 끊겨요.

items.passage: People often hesitate to ask strangers for help because they expect to be turned down. In one study, participants were asked to approach strangers and request a small favor, such as filling out a short survey. Before starting, they guessed how many people they would need to ask before three agreed. On average, they predicted about ten. In reality, they needed to ask only about five. Similar results appeared when people asked to borrow a phone or for directions. The researchers explained that people who are thinking of asking focus on the cost to the stranger, such as time and effort. They forget that saying no is uncomfortable, and that most people actually feel good about helping. Because of this mistake, many of us struggle alone with problems that others would gladly help us solve.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

People tend to (A) ___ how willing strangers are to help, which can make them (B) ___ to ask for assistance.
items.exp: 사람들은 열 명쯤 부탁해야 할 것이라 예상했지만 실제로는 다섯 명이면 되었으니, 낯선 사람이 도와줄 의향을 과소평가(underestimate)한 거예요. 그래서 도움을 청하기를 주저하게(reluctant) 돼요.

items.passage:
Why do some songs give us chills while others leave us cold? Part of the answer lies in a simple ability of the human brain: prediction. As we listen to music, the brain constantly guesses what will come next, based on patterns it has heard before. When a melody rises, we (a)[expect] it to come back down; when a beat repeats, we prepare for the next one. Music that we have heard many times becomes easy to predict, and music in a completely unfamiliar style can be hard to follow at all.

Researchers have found that pleasure in music depends on a balance between these guesses being confirmed and being surprised. When a song follows our expectations exactly, it can feel (b)[comfortable] but quickly becomes boring. When it breaks every expectation, it sounds like noise. The most enjoyable moments often come when the music sets up a pattern, makes us wait a little longer than usual, and then (c)[delivers] the expected note or an even better one. Brain scans show that a chemical linked to reward is released not only at the moment of satisfaction but also during the moment of (d)[anticipation] just before it.

This explains why composers and songwriters often play with delay. A short pause before the final chorus, or a chord that hangs in the air before it resolves, can make the listener's brain lean forward. Understanding this does not make music less magical. Instead, it shows that the joy of listening is something we (e)[avoid] ourselves, by actively guessing and waiting along with every note.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Unfamiliar Music Sounds Like Noise
Guess and Wait: How Prediction Shapes Musical Pleasure
The Brain Chemicals That Make Us Dance
How Composers Write Songs That Never Repeat
Learning to Play an Instrument at Any Age
items.exp: 음악을 들을 때 뇌가 다음을 예측하고, 그 예측이 맞거나 기분 좋게 깨질 때와 기다리는 순간에 즐거움이 생긴다는 내용이에요. ①은 일부 내용만, ④는 작곡가들이 반복과 지연을 이용한다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.exp: 음악의 즐거움은 우리가 능동적으로 예측하고 기다리면서 스스로 만들어 내는 것이라는 흐름이므로 (e) avoid는 create로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
Leo and his best friend Sophie had spent two months building a small water filter for the school science fair. Their idea was to clean muddy river water using only sand, charcoal, and old plastic bottles. The night before the fair, they tested it one last time in Leo's garage. The water that came out was clear, and (a)[he] gave Sophie a high five.

(B)
They rushed to the hall, where the judges were already moving from table to table. Leo's hands shook as he poured a cup of muddy water into the filter. Drops began to fall, but this time they came out brown. A small crack in one bottle was letting the dirty water slip past the charcoal. Leo felt his face turn red. He wanted to hide under the table, but Sophie calmly turned to the judges and explained exactly what had gone wrong and how (b)[she] would fix it.

(C)
Then the head judge stepped onto the stage to announce the winners. Leo and Sophie were not among the top three, but the judge said, "We have a special award this year for the team that best showed how real scientists think." She looked at Leo and Sophie. "When things went wrong, you did not hide the problem. You studied it." Leo walked up to receive the award, and as (c)[he] shook the judge's hand, he realized that a broken filter had taught him more than a perfect one ever could.

(D)
The next morning, however, everything went wrong. While carrying the filter to the bus, Leo slipped on the wet sidewalk, and the bottles crashed onto the ground. Sophie helped him gather the pieces. "It looks okay," she said, putting it back together with tape. Leo was not so sure, but they had no time to rebuild it. All the way to school, (d)[he] held the box tightly on his lap, worried that the filter would fail. Sophie kept telling (e)[him] not to worry. "Whatever happens, we'll figure it out together," she said.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 대회 전날 밤 시험에 성공한 (A) 뒤에, 다음 날 아침 넘어져 필터가 망가지는 (D), 대회장에서 필터가 고장 나지만 Sophie가 침착하게 설명하는 (B), 특별상을 받는 (C)가 차례로 와요. (B)의 They rushed to the hall은 (D)에서 학교로 가는 장면 다음에 이어져요.

The next morning, however, everything went wrong. While carrying the filter to the bus, Leo slipped on the wet sidewalk, and the bottles crashed onto the ground. Sophie helped him gather the pieces. "It looks okay," she said, putting it back together with tape. Leo was not so sure, but they had no time to rebuild it. All the way to school, (d)[he] held the box tightly on his lap, worried that the filter would fail. Sophie kept telling (e)[him] not to worry. "Whatever happens, we'll figure it out together," she said.
items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Leo와 Sophie는 두 달 동안 정수 필터를 만들었다.
필터는 모래, 숯, 오래된 플라스틱 병으로 만들어졌다.
대회장에서 필터를 거친 물은 갈색으로 나왔다.
Leo는 버스를 타러 가던 중 미끄러져 필터를 떨어뜨렸다.
items.exp: (C)에서 두 사람은 상위 3팀 안에 들지 못했다(not among the top three)고 했고, 대신 특별상을 받았어요.

items.passage:
Dear Mr. Harris,

I am writing as a resident of Maple Hill who walks along the Brookside Trail almost every evening. Over the past two months, I have noticed that four of the lamps between the north gate and the wooden bridge no longer work. Once the sun goes down, that section becomes so dark that walkers can hardly see the edge of the path. Last week, an elderly neighbor of mine tripped over a tree root there and hurt her wrist. Many people, including students coming home from evening classes, use this trail as a shortcut, so the problem affects more than a few of us. I understand that the park office has many tasks to handle, but I would be grateful if you could arrange for the broken lamps to be repaired as soon as possible. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,
Laura Bennett
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 산책로의 고장 난 가로등 수리를 요청하려고
산책로에서 다친 이웃의 치료비 지원을 문의하려고
산책로를 지름길로 이용하지 말아 달라고 당부하려고
야간 산책 모임에 공원 관리인을 초대하려고
items.exp: 필자는 산책로의 가로등 네 개가 고장 나 위험하다고 설명한 뒤, 고장 난 가로등을 가능한 한 빨리 수리해 달라고 부탁하고 있어요. 이웃이 다친 일은 수리가 필요한 이유로 든 예일 뿐 치료비 문의가 목적은 아니에요.

items.passage: Minseo had spent two weeks making forty colorful bracelets for the school flea market. She arranged them neatly on her small table and waited for customers. An hour passed, then another. Students walked past her table to the snack stand next door, and only one girl stopped, picked up a bracelet, and put it back. Minseo looked at the full box and sighed. "Maybe nobody wants them," she whispered, and she began to think about packing up early. Just then, a group of girls from the dance club came over. One of them tried on a blue bracelet and shouted, "These would be perfect for our team!" Within ten minutes, they had bought twenty-five bracelets, and more students lined up behind them, curious about the noise. By the end of the day, the box was empty. Minseo counted the money twice, her face glowing, and could not stop smiling.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Minseo의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음에는 두 시간 동안 팔찌가 하나도 팔리지 않아 한숨을 쉬며 일찍 정리할 생각까지 했으므로 낙담한 상태예요. 댄스부 학생들이 대량으로 사 가고 상자가 다 비자 얼굴이 환해지며 웃음을 멈추지 못했으므로 discouraged → thrilled가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Many parents give their children an allowance but then decide exactly how every coin should be spent. They mean well, of course. They want to stop their children from wasting money on cheap toys or sweets that are gone in a minute. However, this kind of control takes away the very lesson that an allowance can teach. Children learn how money works not by hearing rules but by making choices and living with the results. A child who spends all her money on the first day and then cannot buy a ticket to the school fair on Friday learns something no lecture could teach her. Such mistakes are small and cheap when a person is eight years old; they become large and expensive when that person is thirty. So, if you give your children money, let them decide how to use it, and allow them to experience the results of their own decisions, even the bad ones.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 자녀에게 용돈을 주기보다 필요한 물건을 직접 사 주어야 한다.
자녀의 용돈 액수는 나이에 맞게 점차 늘려야 한다.
자녀가 용돈을 낭비하지 않도록 사용 규칙을 정해 주어야 한다.
자녀에게 저축의 중요성을 어릴 때부터 가르쳐야 한다.
자녀가 용돈을 스스로 쓰고 그 결과를 경험하게 해야 한다.
items.exp: 마지막 문장에서 용돈을 어떻게 쓸지 자녀가 정하게 하고, 잘못된 결정이라도 그 결과를 겪게 하라고 주장해요. 사용 규칙을 정해 주는 것은 필자가 오히려 문제로 지적한 통제 방식이에요.

items.passage: When a friend arrives twenty minutes late, we tend to see only the lateness itself: she kept us waiting, so she must not care much about our time. When we are late, however, we see everything that happened before the lateness: the bus that never came, the phone call we had to answer, the fact that we truly meant to be on time. In other words, we judge our own behavior by the intentions we know about, but we judge other people's behavior by the actions we can see. Since we have no access to their good intentions, their mistakes seem to say something permanent about who they are, while ours seem like accidents that can easily be explained away. It is as if we [grade ourselves with a pencil and others with a pen]. Recognizing this habit will not make it disappear, but it may help us give others the same understanding we give ourselves so freely.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [grade ourselves with a pencil and others with a pen]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: excuse our own faults easily while treating others' faults as fixed
keep careful records of both our own and others' mistakes
rely on written evidence rather than memory when judging people
expect others to correct their mistakes faster than we do
judge others more kindly because we cannot see their intentions
items.exp: 연필 자국은 지울 수 있고 펜 자국은 지울 수 없어요. 즉 자신의 실수는 의도를 근거로 쉽게 지워 버리고, 남의 실수는 그 사람의 변하지 않는 모습으로 굳혀 판단한다는 뜻이에요. ⑤는 글과 반대로 남을 더 너그럽게 본다고 해서 틀려요.

items.passage: On a hot summer afternoon, walking down a street lined with large trees can feel very different from walking down one with none. This is not just a feeling. Trees block sunlight before it reaches the pavement, so the ground beneath them stays far cooler than bare asphalt, which can become hot enough to burn bare skin. Trees also release water vapor through their leaves, and this process takes heat from the surrounding air, much like sweat cools the human body. Studies in several cities have found that neighborhoods with plenty of tree cover can be several degrees cooler than nearby areas with few trees. This difference matters. During heat waves, cooler streets mean fewer people suffering from heat-related illness and less electricity used for air conditioning. For city planners, then, planting and protecting trees is not simply a way to make streets look pleasant; it is a practical way to keep residents safe.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: difficulties of growing large trees along busy roads
ways to reduce electricity use during heat waves
the role of trees in keeping city areas cool
reasons asphalt is replacing natural ground in cities
how the human body cools itself through sweating
items.exp: 나무가 그늘을 만들고 잎에서 수증기를 내보내 도시의 거리를 시원하게 하며, 그래서 주민의 안전에 도움이 된다는 내용이에요. 전기 사용 감소나 땀은 이 효과를 설명하는 일부 내용일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: If you had called someone "nice" in the 1300s, you might have started a fight, because at that time the word meant "foolish" or "ignorant." Over the following centuries, its meaning shifted again and again, passing through senses such as "shy" and "careful" before finally settling on "pleasant" and "kind." The word "awful" took a journey in the opposite direction. It once described something that filled people with deep respect and wonder, and only later came to mean "very bad." Such changes are not mistakes made by careless speakers. They happen because a language belongs to the people who use it, and every generation uses words in slightly new ways to suit new situations. Dictionaries record these changes, but they do not control them. In this sense, the words we use every day are less like fixed stones and more like rivers, always moving while keeping the same name.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Dictionaries Decide What Words Mean
Careless Speakers Are Ruining Our Language
Ancient Words That Have Disappeared Forever
How to Choose Kind Words in Conversation
Words on the Move: How Meanings Change over Time
items.exp: nice와 awful의 예를 들어 낱말의 의미가 시대에 따라 계속 바뀐다는 것을 설명하고, 낱말을 흐르는 강에 비유해요. 사전은 변화를 기록할 뿐 결정하지 않는다고 했으므로 ①은 반대 내용이에요.

items.passage: Elena Varga (1871–1943) was a botanical illustrator known for her detailed paintings of mountain wildflowers. Born in a small village in western Hungary, she began drawing plants as a child, using pencils her father brought home from the market. At the age of nineteen, she moved to Vienna to study painting, but she left the art school after two years because she preferred working outdoors to copying works in a studio. For the next three decades, she spent every summer walking through the Alps, painting flowers exactly where they grew instead of picking them. Her work was so accurate that several scientists used her paintings to identify rare species. In 1925, she published a book containing more than three hundred of her illustrations. After her death, her niece donated the original paintings to a natural history museum, where they are still displayed today.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 아버지가 시장에서 사 온 연필로 어린 시절 식물을 그렸다.
열아홉 살에 그림을 공부하기 위해 빈으로 이주했다.
30년 동안 여름마다 알프스를 걸으며 꽃을 그렸다.
꽃을 꺾어 와서 작업실에서 정밀하게 그렸다.
사후에 조카가 원본 그림을 자연사 박물관에 기증했다.
items.exp: 꽃을 꺾지 않고 꽃이 자라는 바로 그 자리에서 그렸다고 했으므로 ④가 일치하지 않아요. 또 작업실에서 작품을 베끼는 것보다 야외 작업을 더 좋아했다고 했어요.

items.passage: When the Statue of Liberty was unveiled in New York in 1886, it did not look green at all. Its thin copper skin ①[shone] a reddish brown, like a new penny. Over the following decades, however, the statue slowly changed color. Copper ②[react] with oxygen, water, and other substances in the air, and these reactions produce a thin layer on its surface. At first, the layer turns dark brown, and then, after many years, it becomes the pale blue-green color ③[that] visitors see today. In the early 1900s, some officials wanted to paint the statue to cover up what they considered damage. Experts, however, explained that the green layer actually ④[protects] the copper underneath from further wear. Thanks to this natural coating, the statue's skin, ⑤[which] is only about as thick as two coins, has survived more than a century of wind, rain, and salty sea air.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: 주어 Copper는 셀 수 없는 단수 명사이므로 ② react는 reacts로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 shine의 과거형, ③은 color를 꾸미는 목적격 관계대명사, ④는 단수 주어 the green layer의 현재 시제 동사, ⑤는 skin을 받는 계속적 용법의 관계대명사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Imagine two friends, Jun and Mia, preparing for a class party. Jun is faster than Mia at both baking cookies and making decorations. It might seem ①[sensible] for Jun to do most of the work himself, since he is better at everything. Yet economists would point out a smarter plan. Jun is much faster at baking but only a little faster at decorating, so his time is ②[least] valuable in the kitchen. If Mia takes over the decorations, Jun can focus on baking, and together they finish ③[sooner] than if Jun tried to do everything alone. This idea, called comparative advantage, explains why countries ④[trade] with each other even when one of them can produce almost everything more efficiently. Each side ⑤[gains] by focusing on what it gives up the least to produce and then exchanging with the other. In the end, working together is better than working alone, even for the more skilled partner.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: Jun은 쿠키 굽기에서 훨씬 빠르고 장식에서는 조금만 빠르므로, 그의 시간은 부엌에서 가장 가치가 커요. 따라서 ②의 least를 most로 바꿔야 해요. ①은 모든 일을 더 잘하니 혼자 하는 게 합리적으로 보인다는 뜻이라 맞아요.

items.passage: We often think of a good friend as someone who agrees with us, supports our choices, and makes us feel good about ourselves. Of course, kindness and support are important parts of friendship. But a friend who only ever agrees with us is offering something closer to flattery than friendship. The ancient philosophers who wrote about friendship believed that a true friend wants what is truly good for us, not just what pleases us at the moment. Sometimes, that means telling us that our plan is foolish or that we have treated someone unfairly. Such words are hard to hear and even harder to say, because they put the relationship at risk. Yet a friend who takes that risk shows that he cares more about us than about our approval of him. In this sense, the deepest friendships are built not on constant agreement but on ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 진정한 친구는 관계가 위험해지더라도 우리의 계획이 어리석다거나 우리가 누군가를 부당하게 대했다고 솔직히 말해 준다는 내용이에요. 그러므로 깊은 우정은 끊임없는 동의가 아니라 정직함 위에 세워져요. comfort나 similarity는 글이 경계하는 '듣기 좋은 동의'에 가까워요.

items.passage: When a scientist announces a surprising result, other scientists do not simply celebrate; they try to do the same experiment themselves. This might look like a lack of trust, but it is actually how science protects itself from error. Any single experiment can go wrong in ways its designers never notice. A machine may be slightly off, a sample may be contaminated, or the result may simply be a matter of chance, the way a fair coin can land on heads five times in a row. The scientist who ran the experiment is often the person least able to spot such problems, because she naturally hopes her idea is right. When researchers in other laboratories, using different equipment and different samples, obtain the same result, these hidden problems become far less likely to explain it. A finding, therefore, earns its place in our knowledge not when it is first announced, but when ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the scientist who discovered it explains it clearly to the public
it is published in a well-known scientific journal
it surprises scientists more than any earlier result
the original experiment is repeated many times by the same researcher
it survives being tested by others working independently
items.exp: 실험자는 자기 생각이 맞기를 바라므로 문제를 알아차리기 어렵고, 다른 연구실이 다른 장비와 시료로 같은 결과를 얻어야 숨은 오류 가능성이 줄어든다고 했어요. 따라서 다른 사람들의 독립적인 검증을 통과할 때 지식이 돼요. ④는 같은 연구자가 같은 장비로 반복하는 것이라 숨은 문제를 걸러 내지 못해요.

items.passage: The way people greet each other varies greatly from one culture to another, and these differences can easily lead to misunderstandings. ① In some countries, a firm handshake and direct eye contact show confidence and honesty. ② In others, looking straight into the eyes of an older person may seem rude, and a gentle bow is considered more respectful. ③ Even the distance people keep between themselves when they greet can differ, with some cultures preferring to stand close and others keeping an arm's length apart. ④ Many people also enjoy learning to say hello in foreign languages, since greeting words are usually the first ones taught in language classes. ⑤ For this reason, travelers who take a few minutes to learn how local people greet one another can avoid giving the wrong impression before they have said a single word.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 문화마다 인사하는 몸짓(악수, 눈 맞춤, 절, 거리)이 달라 오해가 생길 수 있다는 흐름이에요. ④는 외국어 인사말을 배우는 즐거움에 관한 내용이라 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 For this reason은 ③까지의 몸짓 차이를 받아요.

items.passage:
For thousands of years, bakers have known that dough left in a warm place slowly grows larger, but for most of that time no one knew why.

(A) This gas cannot easily escape, however, because it is trapped in a stretchy net formed by proteins in the flour. As more and more gas is caught, tiny bubbles form throughout the dough, and the whole dough rises. Baking then sets these bubbles in place, giving bread its light, soft texture.

(B) The answer is yeast, a tiny living thing too small to see with the naked eye. When it is mixed into dough, it begins to feed on the sugars in the flour.

(C) As it feeds, it produces a gas called carbon dioxide, just as our bodies produce this gas when we breathe out. The warmer the dough, the faster the yeast works.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 아무도 이유를 몰랐다는 주어진 글 뒤에 The answer is yeast로 답을 주는 (B)가 와요. (B)의 효모(it)가 먹이를 먹으며 이산화탄소를 만든다는 (C)가 이어지고, This gas가 빠져나가지 못해 반죽이 부푼다는 (A)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Parents who read aloud to young children are giving them more than a pleasant bedtime routine. ( ① ) Most of the language children hear each day comes from conversation, and everyday conversation uses a surprisingly limited set of words. ( ② ) Even well-educated adults chatting with their families at the dinner table rarely go beyond the most common few thousand words. ( ③ ) Even a simple picture book may contain words such as "enormous," "whisper," or "meadow," which a child might not hear in months of ordinary talk. ( ④ ) Through repeated reading, children meet these words again and again, each time in a story that helps make their meaning clear. ( ⑤ ) As a result, children who are read to regularly often enter school knowing many more words than their classmates.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Books, by contrast, are full of words that people rarely use in conversation.
items.exp: ③ 앞까지는 일상 대화가 적은 수의 흔한 낱말만 쓴다는 내용이고, 주어진 문장이 by contrast로 책은 대화에서 잘 쓰지 않는 낱말로 가득하다고 대조해요. ③ 뒤의 Even a simple picture book은 주어진 문장의 Books를 받아 예를 들어요.

items.passage: Look at a map of Europe, and you will notice that many old towns sit beside rivers, often at a point where the water was shallow enough to cross or where a bridge was first built. This is no accident. In the Middle Ages, travel over land was slow and difficult, and rivers were obstacles that forced travelers to gather at the few places where crossing was possible. Merchants carrying goods naturally passed through these points, and so did farmers bringing their crops and animals. Where so many people met, it made sense to set up a market. Once a market was established, craftsmen and innkeepers arrived to serve the visitors, and their workshops and inns soon turned a simple crossing into a busy town. Many of these towns still carry names that reveal their origin, such as English names ending in "-ford," a word that once meant a shallow place to cross a river.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Many medieval towns developed at river crossings because these places (A) ___ travelers, which created opportunities for (B) ___.
items.exp: 강은 건널 수 있는 몇 안 되는 곳으로 여행자들을 모이게 했고(concentrated), 사람이 많이 모이자 시장이 생겨 상인·장인이 몰려들었어요(trade). scattered는 반대 의미이고, defense나 fishing은 글에 근거가 없어요.

items.passage:
Many people assume that the best way to prepare for an important race is to train harder and harder until the very last day. Sports scientists, however, have found that top athletes usually do the opposite. In the final one to three weeks before a major competition, they reduce the amount of training they do, a practice known as "tapering."

To understand why tapering works, it helps to know what training actually does to the body. Hard exercise causes small amounts of damage to muscles and uses up the energy stored in them. The body (a)[responds] by repairing the muscles and refilling the energy stores, and it often builds them back slightly stronger than before. This improvement, however, happens mainly during rest, not during the workout itself. When an athlete trains hard every day, the body never gets enough time to finish this repair work, so tiredness (b)[accumulates] and the gains from training cannot fully show.

Tapering gives the body the chance to catch up. Studies of swimmers, runners, and cyclists have shown that a well-planned taper can (c)[improve] race performance by around two to three percent. That may sound small, but in top-level sport it is often the difference between winning a medal and finishing fourth.

Importantly, tapering does not mean stopping completely. Athletes who rest entirely for weeks begin to lose fitness. Instead, they cut the total amount of training sharply while keeping a few short, fast sessions, which (d)[maintain] the body's readiness for high speed. The lesson is clear: in the final stage of preparation, (e)[more] training is often what makes an athlete faster.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: The Dangers of Overtraining for Young Athletes
Why Training Less Before a Race Makes Athletes Faster
How Muscles Store Energy During Exercise
Training Every Day: The Secret of Champions
Swimming, Running, and Cycling: Which Is Hardest?
items.exp: 대회 직전 1~3주 동안 훈련량을 줄이는 테이퍼링이 몸의 회복을 도와 기록을 높인다는 내용이므로 ②가 알맞아요. ①은 과훈련의 위험을 다루는 듯하지만 글은 어린 선수가 아니라 대회 준비 전략을 설명해요.

items.passage:
Many people assume that the best way to prepare for an important race is to train harder and harder until the very last day. Sports scientists, however, have found that top athletes usually do the opposite. In the final one to three weeks before a major competition, they reduce the amount of training they do, a practice known as "tapering."

To understand why tapering works, it helps to know what training actually does to the body. Hard exercise causes small amounts of damage to muscles and uses up the energy stored in them. The body (a)[responds] by repairing the muscles and refilling the energy stores, and it often builds them back slightly stronger than before. This improvement, however, happens mainly during rest, not during the workout itself. When an athlete trains hard every day, the body never gets enough time to finish this repair work, so tiredness (b)[accumulates] and the gains from training cannot fully show.

Tapering gives the body the chance to catch up. Studies of swimmers, runners, and cyclists have shown that a well-planned taper can (c)[improve] race performance by around two to three percent. That may sound small, but in top-level sport it is often the difference between winning a medal and finishing fourth.

Importantly, tapering does not mean stopping completely. Athletes who rest entirely for weeks begin to lose fitness. Instead, they cut the total amount of training sharply while keeping a few short, fast sessions, which (d)[maintain] the body's readiness for high speed. The lesson is clear: in the final stage of preparation, (e)[more] training is often what makes an athlete faster.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 글 전체가 대회 직전에는 훈련을 줄여야 더 빨라진다는 내용이므로 (e)의 more를 less로 바꿔야 해요. (d)는 짧고 빠른 훈련이 고속 준비 상태를 유지한다는 뜻으로 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Minho had begged his parents for a dog for three years, so when they finally brought home a small brown puppy named Coco, he could not stop smiling. Every day after school, he took Coco for a walk around the apartment complex. One Saturday afternoon, however, a loud truck horn frightened the puppy, and she slipped out of her collar and ran into the busy street. By the time Minho reached the corner, (a)[he] could not see her anywhere.

(B)
When Minho arrived at the flower shop, out of breath, Mrs. Han led him to the back. There, curled up on an old blanket next to a bowl of water, was Coco. The moment the puppy heard his voice, she jumped up and leaped into his arms, licking his face. Mrs. Han told him that she had been feeding Coco rice and chicken for two days. Minho thanked her again and again. The following weekend, (b)[he] returned to the shop with a card he had drawn himself, and Coco wore a new collar that fit much more tightly.

(C)
For the rest of the day, Minho and his father searched the neighborhood, calling Coco's name until their voices were hoarse. That evening, Minho sat at his desk and made posters with Coco's photo and his mother's phone number. Early the next morning, before the shops opened, (c)[he] taped them to every lamppost and bus stop he could find. Still, the whole day passed without a single call, and he went to bed with tears in his eyes.

(D)
On Monday morning, just as Minho was leaving for school, his mother's phone rang. A woman named Mrs. Han explained that she ran a small flower shop three blocks away. "A little brown dog has been sleeping behind my shop since Saturday," she said. "I saw a poster this morning, and I think (d)[she] might be yours." Minho did not wait to hear the rest. (e)[He] grabbed his jacket and ran out the door.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: Coco를 잃어버린 (A) 뒤에 그날 남은 시간 동안 찾아다니고 포스터를 붙인 (C)가 와요. 그 포스터를 본 꽃집 주인의 전화가 온 월요일 아침 (D)가 이어지고, 꽃집에 도착해 Coco를 만나는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

choices: Minho는 3년 동안 부모님께 개를 키우자고 졸랐다.
Mrs. Han은 이틀 동안 강아지에게 밥과 닭고기를 주었다.
Minho는 아버지와 함께 동네를 돌아다니며 Coco를 찾았다.
Mrs. Han은 작은 꽃집을 운영하고 있었다.
items.exp: (C)에서 포스터에는 Coco의 사진과 어머니의 전화번호를 넣었다고 했으므로 ④가 적절하지 않아요. 실제로 전화도 어머니의 휴대폰으로 왔어요.

items.passage:
Dear Chef Morgan,

My name is Daniel Reyes, and I coordinate programs at the Eastwood Senior Center. Many of our members live alone, and they often tell us that cooking for one person feels like too much trouble. As a result, some of them skip meals or rely on instant food. We would like to help them by holding a monthly cooking class focused on simple, healthy dishes that can be made in small portions. Several of our members have eaten at your restaurant and spoke warmly of the cooking demonstrations you gave at the town festival last fall. We would be honored if you could lead our first class on the second Thursday of next month. The session would last about ninety minutes, and we would gladly cover the cost of all ingredients. I look forward to hearing from you.

Best regards,
Daniel Reyes
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 노인 복지관 회원의 식당 단체 예약을 문의하려고
마을 축제의 요리 시연 일정 변경을 알리려고
노인 복지관 요리 교실의 강사를 맡아 달라고 부탁하려고
요리 교실에 필요한 재료비 지원을 요청하려고
혼자 사는 노인을 위한 도시락 배달 봉사자를 모집하려고
items.exp: 혼자 사는 회원들을 위해 간단하고 건강한 요리 교실을 열려고 하며, 다음 달 둘째 목요일 첫 수업을 이끌어 달라고 요리사에게 부탁하고 있어요. 재료비는 오히려 복지관이 부담하겠다고 했으므로 ④는 틀려요.

items.passage: The fog came down so quickly that within ten minutes I could no longer see the trail markers. I had been hiking alone on the ridge, sure that I knew the way back to the parking lot. Now every rock looked the same, and the path seemed to split in three directions. My phone showed no signal. I sat down on a cold stone, my heart pounding, and tried to remember what my uncle had always told me: if you are lost, stay where you are. The wind grew colder, and I pulled my jacket tighter. Then, through the gray air, I heard a faint jingle of bells. A moment later, an old man with a walking stick and a dog wearing a bell appeared on the path. "Lost in the fog?" he asked with a smile. "Follow us. We walk this ridge every morning." I let out a long breath and felt my whole body relax.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 안개 속에서 길을 잃고 신호도 없어 심장이 두근거리는 상태에서, 길을 아는 노인을 만나 긴 숨을 내쉬며 몸의 긴장이 풀려요. 그러므로 frightened → relieved가 알맞아요.

items.passage: At a concert today, it is common to see hundreds of phones raised in the air, each one recording the stage. People want to keep the moment so they can enjoy it again later. Yet researchers who study memory have found something surprising: people who take photos or videos of an experience often remember it less clearly than those who simply watch. When we know a device is storing the moment for us, our brains seem to pay less attention, as if handing the job of remembering to the machine. In addition, attention spent on holding the phone steady and checking the screen is attention taken away from the music itself. Many of those videos are never watched again. So the people trying hardest to save the concert may be the ones who [leave with the thinnest version of it]. The best record of an experience may be the one we carry inside us by paying full attention.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [leave with the thinnest version of it]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: end up with videos that take up little storage space
keep only a weak memory of the actual experience
miss the end of the concert because they leave early
see the performers from the farthest seats
share fewer videos online than other audience members
items.exp: 공연을 녹화하는 사람은 기기에 기억을 맡겨 주의를 덜 기울이므로 실제 경험을 덜 선명하게 기억한다고 했어요. 따라서 '가장 얇은 판본을 가지고 떠난다'는 경험에 대한 빈약한 기억만 남는다는 뜻이에요. ①은 thin을 파일 크기로 문자 그대로 해석한 오답이에요.

items.passage: In the 1970s, some cities began cutting small ramps into the edges of sidewalks so that people in wheelchairs could cross the street more easily. The ramps were built for a small group, but something unexpected happened. Parents pushing baby strollers started using them. So did travelers pulling suitcases, delivery workers with heavy carts, and children on bicycles. Today, few people even notice these ramps, yet almost everyone benefits from them. The same pattern appears again and again in design. Subtitles on videos, automatic doors, and large buttons in elevators were first made with certain users in mind, but they turned out to make life easier for the general public as well. This suggests that designers should not think of features for people with special needs as extra costs. When we solve a problem for those who struggle the most, we often create something better for everyone.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 공공시설은 다수의 사용자를 기준으로 설계해야 한다.
보행 환경을 개선하는 데에는 많은 비용과 시간이 든다.
새로운 디자인은 사용자의 오랜 습관을 바꾸기 어렵다.
특정 사용자의 어려움을 해결한 설계가 모두에게 이익이 된다.
장애인을 위한 시설은 별도의 공간에 따로 마련되어야 한다.
items.exp: 휠체어 사용자를 위해 만든 보도 경사로를 유모차, 여행 가방, 자전거 이용자까지 모두 쓰게 된 예를 들며, 가장 어려움을 겪는 사람의 문제를 풀면 모두에게 더 나은 것이 만들어진다고 했어요. ①은 오히려 다수 기준 설계를 말해 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: In the middle of the Antarctic winter, temperatures can fall below minus forty degrees, and strong winds blow for days. Yet this is exactly when male emperor penguins stand on the ice, each keeping an egg warm on its feet for about two months without eating. How do they survive? The answer is teamwork. Thousands of penguins press their bodies together in a tight group called a huddle. Inside it, the temperature can rise above twenty degrees, so the birds lose much less heat than they would alone. A huddle is not a fixed crowd, however. Every minute or so, the penguins take tiny steps, and the whole group slowly moves. Birds on the cold outside edge gradually work their way inward, while those in the warm center drift toward the edge. In this way, every penguin gets a turn in the warmth.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the way penguins find food under the ice
reasons why penguin eggs are hard to protect
the long journey of penguins to the sea
how climate change threatens Antarctic animals
how penguins share warmth to survive the winter
items.exp: 황제펭귄이 몸을 맞대어 허들을 만들고 바깥과 안쪽 자리를 조금씩 바꾸며 모두가 따뜻함을 나눈다는 내용이에요. 그래서 ⑤ '펭귄이 겨울을 견디려고 온기를 나누는 방법'이 주제로 알맞아요. ②는 알을 품는다는 배경만 다뤄 주제가 될 수 없어요.

items.passage: "Only 100 left!" "Sale ends tonight!" Messages like these appear everywhere, from online stores to supermarket shelves, and for good reason: they work. When something seems to be running out, people tend to value it more and decide to buy it more quickly. In one simple study, people were asked to rate cookies from two jars. One jar held ten cookies, and the other held only two. Although the cookies were exactly the same, people rated the ones from the nearly empty jar as more delicious and more desirable. Sellers understand this tendency well. By limiting the number of products or the time to buy them, they can make customers feel that they might lose a chance, and the fear of losing it often matters more than the product itself. The next time a store tells you to hurry, it may be worth asking whether you really want the item, or just the feeling of not missing out.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Running Out: Why Scarcity Makes Us Want More
How to Bake Cookies That Everyone Will Love
Online Stores Versus Supermarkets: Which Is Cheaper?
The Hidden Cost of Shopping Late at Night
items.exp: 물건이 얼마 남지 않았다고 느끼면 사람들이 그것을 더 가치 있게 여기고 서둘러 사며, 판매자는 이를 이용한다는 내용이므로 ①이 알맞아요. 쿠키는 이를 보여 주는 실험 예일 뿐이에요.

items.passage:
Greenfield Community Book Swap 2027

Bring the books you have finished and take home new ones!

items.q: Greenfield Community Book Swap 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 책 없이 온 방문객은 1달러에 책을 살 수 있다.
items.exp: 가져올 수 있는 책은 최대 10권(up to 10 books)이므로 ③이 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 시간, 무료 입장, 1달러 구매, 잡지 불가 안내와 모두 일치해요.

items.passage: If you look at the Moon on any night of the year, you will always see the same patterns of light and dark. This is not because the Moon does not spin. It does spin, but it takes exactly as long to turn once as it ①[does] to travel around the Earth. Scientists believe that billions of years ago, the Moon ②[spun] much faster than it does today. The Earth's gravity pulled on the Moon and stretched it slightly, and this pull acted like a brake, slowing the spin until it ③[matched] the time of one trip around the Earth. As a result, one side of the Moon always faces away from us. That side, ④[what] people often wrongly call the "dark side," actually receives just as much sunlight as the side we see. No one saw it until 1959, when a spacecraft flew behind the Moon and took the first photographs ⑤[ever] made of it.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ④는 앞의 명사 That side를 보충 설명하는 계속적 용법의 관계대명사 자리이므로 what이 아니라 which를 써야 해요. ①은 takes를 대신하는 대동사, ②는 과거 시제, ③은 until절의 과거 동사, ⑤는 최상급·first를 강조하는 ever로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: When food scraps are thrown into the trash, most of them end up buried in landfills. You might expect them to simply rot away there, but the conditions in a landfill are ①[harmful] to the process. Food buried under layers of garbage is cut off from oxygen, so it breaks down very slowly and produces methane, a gas that traps far more heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide does. Composting offers a ②[better] way. In a compost pile, food scraps are mixed with dry leaves and turned regularly so that air can ③[reach] every part. With enough oxygen, tiny organisms break the waste down quickly into a rich soil that gardeners can use. Much less methane is released, and the soil helps plants grow without chemical fertilizers. Even people living in apartments can ④[join] in, as many cities now collect food waste separately for composting. Small kitchen choices, it seems, can have a ⑤[minor] effect on the planet.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 음식물 쓰레기를 퇴비로 만들면 메탄이 줄고 비료 없이 식물을 키울 수 있다는 흐름이므로, 부엌에서의 작은 선택이 지구에 큰 영향을 줄 수 있다고 해야 해요. 따라서 ⑤ minor를 major나 large로 바꿔야 해요. ①은 매립지 환경이 분해에 해롭다는 뜻으로 맞아요.

items.passage: Many people believe that the way to be liked in a conversation is to be impressive. Before meeting someone new, they prepare funny stories, interesting facts, and examples of their own success. Research on everyday conversations, however, points in a different direction. In one study, people who asked more questions during a first meeting were liked more by their partners, and the most powerful questions were follow-up questions, such as "What happened next?" or "Why did you choose that?" A follow-up question proves that you were actually listening and that you want to hear more. It gives the other person the pleasure of being understood, something few people enjoy often. Interestingly, the partners rarely remembered how much the question-askers had said about themselves. So if you want others to find you interesting, you should first be ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 질문을 많이, 특히 이어지는 질문을 하는 사람이 더 호감을 얻었고 상대는 그 사람이 자기 이야기를 얼마나 했는지 거의 기억하지 못했다고 했어요. 그러니 남에게 흥미로운 사람이 되려면 먼저 상대에게 관심을 가져야 해요. impressive는 글이 뒤집은 통념이에요.

items.passage: If you wanted to build the fastest possible relay team, you might simply choose the four fastest sprinters you could find. Surprisingly, such teams often lose. In a 4×100-meter relay, the baton must be handed from one runner to the next inside a short zone of about thirty meters. A perfect handoff happens when the next runner starts early and is already near full speed when the baton reaches her, so that the baton itself never slows down. If she starts too early, the two runners cannot meet inside the zone; if she starts too late, the baton loses precious time. Getting this right requires hundreds of hours of practice together, until each runner can judge her teammate's speed almost without thinking. This is why a team of slightly slower runners who have trained together for years can beat a team of stars who met only a month ago. In a relay, the team's final time depends less on the speed of each runner than on ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the physical strength of the final runner
how loudly the crowd cheers for the team
how smoothly the baton travels between them
the number of races each runner has won
the length of the track on which they compete
items.exp: 바통이 속도를 잃지 않고 넘어가려면 함께 오래 훈련해 서로의 속도를 감으로 알아야 하고, 그래서 조금 느려도 오래 함께한 팀이 스타 선수들의 팀을 이길 수 있다고 했어요. 따라서 기록은 각 선수의 속도보다 바통이 얼마나 매끄럽게 이어지느냐에 달려 있어요. ④는 개인의 실력을 말해 글의 논지와 반대예요.

items.passage: Much of what we do each day is not decided by careful thought but triggered by our surroundings. A bowl of fruit placed on the kitchen table, for example, makes people more likely to grab an apple instead of cookies. ① In the same way, a guitar left out of its case in the middle of the living room invites practice, while one stored in a closet is easily forgotten. ② This suggests that one of the simplest ways to build a good habit is to make the first step visible and easy. ③ Likewise, breaking a bad habit often becomes easier when the cue that starts it is moved out of sight, such as keeping a phone in another room while studying. ④ People who change their surroundings in these small ways often find that new habits form with surprisingly little effort. ⑤ Some psychologists, however, have argued that strong willpower is a talent that only a few people are born with.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 주변 환경이 행동을 이끌기 때문에 환경을 바꾸면 습관을 쉽게 만들거나 끊을 수 있다는 흐름이에요. ⑤는 의지력이 타고나는 재능이라는 주장으로, 환경을 통한 습관 형성이라는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
Most volcanoes form near the edges of the huge plates that make up the Earth's surface. Some islands, however, rise from the middle of an ocean, thousands of kilometers from any plate edge.

(A) The plate above, however, does not stay still. It moves slowly, only a few centimeters a year, and carries the volcano away from the hot spot. Cut off from its supply of melted rock, the volcano becomes quiet, and a new one begins to form over the hot spot.

(B) Over millions of years, this process repeats again and again, producing a long chain of islands. The oldest islands, which have had the most time to wear away, are the smallest and lie farthest from the hot spot.

(C) Scientists explain these islands with the idea of a "hot spot," a place deep beneath the plate where unusually hot rock rises and melts. The melted rock pushes up through the plate and slowly builds a volcano on the sea floor, which may eventually rise above the water.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 판 가장자리에서 먼 섬들이 있다는 주어진 글 뒤에 이를 열점(hot spot)으로 설명하는 (C)가 와요. 그 위의 판이 움직여 화산을 열점에서 멀리 옮긴다는 (A)가 이어지고, 이 과정(this process)이 반복되어 섬의 사슬이 생긴다는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: For centuries, farmers have noticed that growing the same crop in the same field year after year causes harvests to shrink. ( ① ) One reason is that each type of plant takes certain nutrients from the soil, and if the same plant is grown again and again, those nutrients slowly run out. ( ② ) Insects and diseases that attack a particular crop can build up in the soil, waiting for their favorite food to return each spring. ( ③ ) By changing crops from year to year, a practice called crop rotation, farmers can solve both problems at once. ( ④ ) Beans and peas, for instance, actually add a valuable nutrient back into the soil, which helps the corn or wheat that is planted after them. ( ⑤ ) This simple method has allowed farmers to keep their land healthy for generations without relying heavily on chemicals.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Another problem has to do with the living things that feed on crops.
items.exp: ② 앞은 영양분이 고갈된다는 첫 번째 문제이고, 주어진 문장은 Another problem으로 작물을 먹고 사는 생물이라는 두 번째 문제를 꺼내요. ② 뒤 문장이 특정 작물을 공격하는 곤충과 병을 구체적으로 설명하고, ③ 뒤의 both problems가 두 문제를 받아요.

items.passage: Can the height of a room change the way we think? In one study, researchers invited people into rooms that were the same in every way except for the ceiling, which was either about 3 meters high or about 2.4 meters high. The participants were then given a set of tasks. Those in the high-ceilinged room were better at finding connections between different ideas and tended to describe objects in broad, general terms. Those in the low-ceilinged room, by contrast, paid closer attention to small details and did better on tasks that required careful checking. The researchers suggested that a high ceiling gives people a feeling of freedom, which encourages their minds to wander, while a low ceiling creates a sense of being enclosed, which helps them focus. This may be worth considering when designing spaces such as art studios or exam rooms.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

The sense of (A) ___ that a tall ceiling provides seems to promote (B) ___ thinking, whereas a lower ceiling helps people concentrate on details.
items.exp: 높은 천장은 자유로운 느낌, 즉 개방감(openness)을 주어 생각이 이리저리 뻗어 나가게 하므로 (A)는 openness예요. 높은 천장 방의 사람들은 서로 다른 생각을 잇고 넓게 묘사했으므로 (B)는 wide-ranging이 알맞아요. precise는 낮은 천장의 효과예요.

items.passage:
Today we usually read a novel as a complete book, from the first page to the last. In the nineteenth century, however, many famous novels first reached readers in small pieces. They were published in parts, one chapter or a few chapters at a time, in monthly magazines or cheap booklets.

This way of publishing was (a)[popular] with both readers and publishers. A whole book was expensive, but a single part cost very little, so even working families could afford to follow a story. Publishers, for their part, could test a new story with a small investment and stop if sales were poor.

Publishing in parts also shaped the stories themselves. Because readers had to wait weeks for the next part, writers learned to end each one at an exciting moment, leaving a question (b)[unanswered]. Long novels were filled with many characters and side plots, which kept readers interested over months. Writers often began publishing before they had finished writing, so they could (c)[respond] to their audience. If readers loved a minor character, that character might get a bigger role in later parts; if sales dropped, a plot could be changed.

Readers, in turn, became part of a shared experience. Families read the newest part aloud together, and people discussed what might happen next with friends and strangers, much as fans today talk about a television series between episodes. In some cases, crowds were said to gather at the docks to (d)[greet] ships carrying the latest part from overseas. Seen this way, the habit of waiting for the next episode is not a modern invention. It is a (e)[recent] pleasure that storytellers have been using for well over a century.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Novels Became Too Expensive for Families
How Magazines Replaced Books in the Nineteenth Century
The Secret Life of Minor Characters in Novels
Reading Aloud: A Lost Family Tradition
Stories in Pieces: How Serial Publishing Shaped the Novel
items.exp: 19세기 소설이 조금씩 나뉘어 연재되면서 독자층이 넓어지고, 장면을 끊는 방식과 이야기 전개, 함께 읽고 이야기하는 경험까지 바뀌었다는 내용이므로 ⑤가 알맞아요. ③과 ④는 글의 일부 세부 내용만 다뤄요.

items.exp: 다음 회를 기다리는 습관이 현대의 발명이 아니고 한 세기도 넘게 이어져 왔다고 했으므로 (e)의 recent를 old(오래된)로 바꿔야 해요. (b)는 궁금증을 남긴 채 끝낸다는 뜻이라 흥미로운 순간에 끊는다는 내용과 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every summer since she was five, Sora had spent her vacation at her grandmother's house in the countryside. Her favorite place there was the garden behind the house, where Grandma grew tomatoes, beans, peppers, and a row of tall sunflowers. Together they watered the plants each evening as the sun went down. But this spring, Grandma fell on the stairs and broke her hip. The doctor said (a)[she] would have to stay in the hospital for several months.

(B)
By the end of August, the garden was full again. Red tomatoes hung heavy on their stems, and the beans had climbed to the top of their poles. Sora filled a basket with the best vegetables and carried it to the hospital. When Grandma saw the basket, her eyes grew wide. "These are from my garden?" she asked. Sora nodded proudly. (b)[She] showed her photos of the sunflowers, which had grown taller than the fence.

(C)
In September, Grandma was finally allowed to go home. Holding a cane in one hand and Sora's arm in the other, she slowly walked out to the garden. For a long moment, Grandma said nothing, and Sora worried that (c)[she] had done something wrong. Then she wiped her eyes and squeezed Sora's hand. "You kept it alive for me," she said softly. That evening, the two of them sat on the back steps, watching the sunflowers turn gold in the setting sun, and Grandma promised to teach (d)[her] how to save the seeds for next year.

(D)
When Sora first visited the house alone in May, she could hardly believe her eyes. Weeds had grown as high as her knees, and the young tomato plants were lying on the dry ground. Sora decided she would not let the garden die. Every weekend, she took the early bus to the countryside, pulled weeds, and watered the plants. Whenever (e)[she] did not know what to do, she called Grandma, who explained from her hospital bed how to tie the tomato stems to sticks.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 할머니가 입원한 (A) 뒤에 5월에 혼자 가서 엉망이 된 정원을 돌보기 시작하는 (D)가 와요. 8월 말 정원이 다시 가득 차 병원에 채소를 가져가는 (B)가 이어지고, 9월에 할머니가 퇴원해 정원을 보는 (C)가 마지막이에요.
