items.q: Harbor City Junior Coding Camp 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
items.exp: 안내문의 Notes에 점심은 포함되지 않으니 직접 싸 오라고 했으므로 ④가 내용과 일치하지 않아요. 7월 19일부터 23일까지 5일간, 12~16세 대상, 회원 100달러, 마지막 날 수료증 내용은 모두 안내문과 같아요.

items.passage: Almost everyone has felt it: you take a big bite of ice cream on a hot day, and a sharp pain suddenly ①[strikes] your forehead. This "brain freeze" does not actually mean that your brain is getting cold. When something very cold touches the roof of your mouth, the blood vessels there quickly narrow and then widen again to bring in warm blood. A nerve ②[that] carries feeling from this area also serves much of the face and forehead. As a result, the brain becomes confused about where the signal is coming from and ③[reports] the pain as if it came from your head. Fortunately, the pain usually disappears within a minute. If you press your tongue against the roof of your mouth, its warmth can help the pain pass more ④[quickly]. Better still, eating cold foods slowly gives your mouth time to adjust and keeps the pain from ⑤[start] at all.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 keep A from -ing(A가 ~하지 못하게 하다) 구문이므로 start를 starting으로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 단수 주어 a sharp pain의 동사, ②는 a nerve를 꾸미는 주격 관계대명사, ③은 becomes와 and로 이어진 동사, ④는 pass를 꾸미는 부사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Some parents worry that learning two languages at once will confuse young children. They fear that the child will mix up words and fall behind in both languages. Research suggests that these worries are largely ①[justified]. It is true that bilingual children sometimes mix words from two languages in a single sentence, but this is a normal stage, not a sign of ②[confusion]. In fact, they usually choose the right language for the right person surprisingly early, speaking one language to their grandmother and another to their friends. Bilingual children may also know ③[fewer] words in each language than children who speak only one, yet when both languages are counted together, their total vocabulary is often similar or even larger. What is more, constantly switching between languages seems to ④[train] the ability to focus attention and ignore distractions. For most families, raising a child with two languages is therefore not a burden but a valuable ⑤[gift].
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 글 전체는 두 언어를 함께 배워도 아이가 혼란을 겪지 않는다는 연구 결과를 소개하므로, 부모들의 걱정은 대체로 근거가 없다는 뜻이 되어야 해요. 따라서 ①의 justified를 unfounded 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요. ②는 섞어 쓰는 것이 혼란의 신호가 아니라는 뜻, ③은 각 언어의 어휘가 적을 수 있다는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage: When we think of archaeology, we often imagine golden treasures or grand temples. Yet many archaeologists are happiest when they find an ancient rubbish heap. Kings built monuments and wrote records to show how they wanted to be remembered, so these sources often praise their victories and hide their failures. A rubbish heap is different. No one ever expected strangers to study it, so no one tried to make it look good. Broken dishes reveal what kind of food people cooked, animal bones show which animals they hunted or raised, and burnt seeds tell which crops they grew. Even the size of the heap can suggest how many people lived nearby. Because it was never meant to be seen, such waste gives a picture of daily life that is far more ___ than any official record. For archaeologists, what people threw away can be worth more than what they proudly kept.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 왕의 기념물과 기록은 승리는 자랑하고 실패는 숨기지만, 쓰레기 더미는 누구도 잘 보이려 꾸미지 않았다는 글이에요. 그래서 공식 기록보다 훨씬 '솔직한(honest)' 일상의 모습을 보여 준다는 ②가 알맞아요. ⑤ official은 글에서 쓰레기와 대비된 공식 기록 쪽의 성격이에요.

items.passage: When Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877, he made a list of the things he thought it would be useful for. Among them were recording letters spoken by busy businessmen, making "talking books" for blind people, and preserving the last words of dying family members. Playing music was on the list, but it was only one idea among many. For years, companies tried to sell the machine as an office tool, with little success. Ordinary people, however, discovered that they loved hearing songs at home, and within a few decades the phonograph had become the center of a huge music industry. This pattern is common in the history of technology. Inventors build a tool with certain uses in mind, but once it leaves the workshop, it meets millions of people with their own needs and ideas. The meaning of an invention, then, is decided less by those who design it than by ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the experts who first test it in the laboratory
the price at which it first goes on sale
the many people who find their own uses for it
the older machines it was meant to replace
the original list of purposes its maker wrote
items.exp: 에디슨은 축음기를 사무용 도구로 생각했지만, 사람들이 집에서 음악을 듣는 데 쓰면서 음악 산업의 중심이 되었어요. 발명품은 작업실을 떠나 각자의 필요를 가진 수많은 사람을 만나므로, 그 의미는 설계자보다 '스스로 쓰임새를 찾는 많은 사람들'이 정한다는 ③이 알맞아요. ⑤는 설계자 쪽이라 글의 결론과 반대예요.

items.passage: Have you ever had a song play over and over in your head for hours, even though you did not want to hear it? Scientists call this experience an "earworm," and nearly everyone has it from time to time. ① Earworms are usually short pieces of songs, often just the chorus, with simple melodies and repeated patterns that are easy for the brain to replay. ② They often appear after we have heard a song several times in a row, or when our minds are relaxed and not busy with a demanding task. ③ Interestingly, one way to stop an earworm is to listen to the whole song, because the brain seems to replay unfinished pieces more often than complete ones. ④ Many songwriters work hard to create catchy melodies, since a song that people can remember easily may sell many more copies. ⑤ Another method is to chew gum or solve a word puzzle, which keeps the parts of the brain used for imagining music busy with something else.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 글은 머릿속에서 노래가 반복되는 현상의 특징, 생기는 때, 멈추는 방법을 차례로 설명해요. ④는 작곡가들이 많이 팔리는 노래를 만들려고 애쓴다는 내용이라 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 Another method는 ③의 one way to stop에 이어지는 표현이에요.

items.passage:
We still call the black center of a pencil its "lead," but pencils have never contained the metal lead. The name comes from a mistake made hundreds of years ago.

(A) Because it left a dark, clean mark, people soon began cutting it into sticks and wrapping them in string or wood to keep their hands clean. These were the first pencils, and the material became so valuable that the place where it was dug up was guarded.

(B) Over time, however, the best supply ran low. In the 1790s, a French inventor solved the problem by mixing powdered graphite with clay and baking it. This method, which allowed makers to control how dark a pencil writes, is still used today.

(C) In the 1500s, people in northern England found a large deposit of a soft black material. Thinking it was a kind of lead, they called it "black lead." Today we know it as graphite, a form of carbon.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 '오래전의 실수'를 (C)가 흑연을 납으로 착각한 이야기로 설명해요. (A)의 it은 (C)의 검은 물질을 가리키고 이것으로 첫 연필을 만들었어요. (B)는 However로 공급이 줄어든 뒤 새 제조법이 나온 마지막 단계라 (C)-(A)-(B)예요.

items.passage: Writing was not invented by poets or storytellers. In ancient Mesopotamia, it seems to have grown out of a much more practical need: keeping track of goods. ( ① ) Farmers and traders used small clay shapes called tokens, each standing for a certain item, such as a cone for a measure of grain or a cylinder for an animal. ( ② ) To make sure no tokens were lost or added along the way, they sometimes sealed them inside a hollow clay ball. ( ③ ) Before closing the ball, people pressed the tokens into its soft surface, so the marks on the outside showed what was inside. ( ④ ) Eventually, people realized that the marks alone were enough, and the tokens themselves were no longer needed. ( ⑤ ) Over time, these marks developed into the signs of one of the world's earliest writing systems.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

A trader who sent ten sheep to a buyer, for example, could send ten tokens along with them as a kind of receipt.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 ② 앞에서 소개한 토큰이 실제로 어떻게 쓰였는지 보여 주는 예(for example)예요. 토큰을 보내는 상황이 먼저 나와야 ② 뒤의 '도중에 토큰이 없어지거나 더해지지 않도록'이 자연스러워요. ③에 넣으면 점토 공과 Before closing the ball 사이가 끊겨요.

items.passage: When people work in the same office, much of their communication happens without effort. A quick question at someone's desk, a comment during lunch, or a glance at a coworker's face can clear up confusion in seconds. When a team works from different places, these small moments disappear. A message that seemed perfectly clear to the writer may be read in a completely different way by someone in another city. As a result, successful remote teams tend to write things down in much more detail. They record decisions in shared documents, explain the reasons behind each task, and describe exactly what they expect and by when. At first, this may feel slow and unnecessary. Over time, however, it reduces mistakes and saves the time that would otherwise be spent fixing misunderstandings.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Because remote teams lack the (A) ___ communication of a shared office, they need to make their messages more (B) ___ in writing.
items.exp: 같은 사무실에서는 책상 앞 질문, 점심시간 대화, 표정 같은 가벼운 소통이 저절로 일어나는데 원격 팀은 이것이 없어요(A: informal). 그래서 결정과 이유, 기대를 훨씬 자세히 글로 남겨야 한다고 했어요(B: explicit). 짧게 쓰라는 내용은 없으므로 ②는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
For a long time, people thought of memory as a kind of video recorder. An event happened, the brain recorded it, and later we simply played the recording back. Research over the past several decades has shown that this picture is (a)[mistaken]. Memories are not stored as complete copies. Instead, the brain keeps scattered pieces, such as a smell, a few words, or a feeling, and rebuilds the event each time we remember it.

This rebuilding process has a surprising result. When a memory is recalled, it becomes (b)[unstable] for a short time before it is stored again. During this period, new information can slip in. In one type of study, people watched a short film of a car accident and were later asked questions about it. When the questions used slightly different words, such as "smashed" instead of "hit," many people later remembered the cars moving faster, and some even recalled broken glass that was never shown. Their memories had been quietly (c)[changed] by the questions themselves.

These findings have important consequences. In courtrooms, a witness who feels completely certain may still be wrong, because confidence and accuracy do not always go together. For this reason, many police departments now (d)[avoid] asking witnesses leading questions. The research also teaches a lesson for everyday life. When two friends remember a shared trip differently, neither may be lying. Each has simply rebuilt the past from his or her own pieces. Recognizing this can make us more (e)[stubborn] when our memories disagree with those of others.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How to Improve Your Memory in Simple Steps
Why Witnesses Should Never Be Trusted
The Brain Works Like a Video Recorder
Car Accidents and Their Effects on Drivers
items.exp: 기억은 녹화본을 재생하는 것이 아니라 조각들로 매번 다시 만들어지며, 그 과정에서 바뀔 수 있다는 글이므로 ③이 제목으로 알맞아요. ④는 글에서 틀렸다고 한 옛 생각이고, ②는 확신과 정확성이 늘 일치하지는 않는다는 내용을 지나치게 일반화했어요.

items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 친구와 기억이 다르더라도 서로 거짓말을 하는 것이 아니라 각자 기억을 재구성했다는 점을 알면, 기억이 엇갈릴 때 더 너그러워질 수 있다는 흐름이에요. 따라서 (e)의 stubborn을 understanding이나 tolerant 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요. (d)는 유도 질문을 피한다는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
The snow had started just after lunch, and by the time Nora left the library, the wind was blowing it sideways across the road. Her house was only two kilometers away, so she decided to walk instead of waiting for a bus that might never come. Within ten minutes, she could hardly see the streetlights. Her boots sank deep into the snow, and the cold wind stung her face. Nora pulled her scarf over her nose and kept moving, but soon (a)[she] realized she had no idea which street she was on.

(B)
When they reached the corner of Pine Street, Nora finally saw the warm yellow light of her own kitchen window. Her mother was standing at the door, holding a flashlight. Nora ran into her arms. Then Nora turned to thank the boy, but he had already disappeared into the snow. (b)[She] promised herself that she would thank him properly. The next week, Nora knocked on the door of the house with the blue mailbox and gave Mr. Tanaka and his son a box of homemade cookies.

(C)
The old man, Mr. Tanaka, was still recovering from a fall and could not walk far, so he asked his son to guide her home. The boy, who was about Nora's age, put on a thick coat and handed her a pair of dry gloves. "Stay right behind me," (c)[he] said. He knew the neighborhood well and led her along the fences, checking each corner before they crossed. Walking behind him, Nora felt (d)[her] fear slowly melt away.

(D)
Feeling her heart beat faster, Nora stopped and looked around. Through the falling snow, she noticed a faint light in a small house with a blue mailbox. She walked up to the door and knocked. An old man opened it, and when Nora explained that (e)[she] was lost, he quickly invited her inside. He gave her a cup of hot tea and called her mother to tell her that Nora was safe. "The roads are too dangerous to drive on," he said. "But we can still help you get home."
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 길을 잃은 Nora가 (D)에서 파란 우편함이 있는 집 노인에게 도움을 받아요. (C)의 Mr. Tanaka는 그 노인이고 아들에게 길 안내를 부탁해요. (B)에서 둘이 Pine Street에 도착하고 다음 주에 감사 인사를 하므로 (D)-(C)-(B)예요.

items.exp: (A)에서 Nora는 오지 않을 수도 있는 버스를 기다리는 대신 걸어가기로 했으므로 ①이 글의 내용과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 (B)의 쿠키, (C)의 부상과 장갑, (D)의 전화 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Carter,

My name is Yuna Seo, and I am the editor of the student newspaper at Eastwood High School. Every year, our paper holds a short story contest for students, and this year we received more than ninety stories, the largest number ever. Many of our writers first fell in love with fiction after reading your novel The Winter Orchard in class, and your visit to our school two years ago is still talked about. For this reason, we would be truly honored if you would agree to serve as the final judge of our contest. Our teachers will choose the ten best stories, so you would need to read only those, each about four pages long. The results will be announced on June 12, and the winning stories will be printed in our summer issue along with your comments. We hope you will consider our request.

Sincerely,
Yuna Seo
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 학교를 방문해 준 것에 대해 감사하려고
단편 소설 대회의 최종 심사를 맡아 달라고 부탁하려고
작가의 신작 소설에 대한 인터뷰를 요청하려고
items.exp: 학생 단편 소설 대회를 소개한 뒤 작가에게 최종 심사위원을 맡아 줄 수 있는지(serve as the final judge of our contest) 정중히 부탁하고 있어요. 따라서 ②가 알맞아요. 2년 전의 학교 방문은 부탁하는 이유로 언급된 것이에요.

items.passage: Mina carefully placed her first clay bowl on the shelf beside the kiln. She had spent three weeks shaping it, but now that it was finished, all she could see were its flaws. One side was thicker than the other, and the rim was not perfectly round. "It will probably crack in the fire," she whispered to herself. When her teacher, Mr. Kent, closed the kiln door, her stomach tightened. For the next two days, she could hardly think about anything else. On Friday, she walked into the studio slowly, ready for bad news. Mr. Kent was holding something wrapped in newspaper. He unwrapped it and handed it to her with a smile. The bowl had survived without a single crack, and the blue glaze had turned into a deep, shining color like the evening sea. Mina turned it over in her hands again and again. "I made this," she said, her face glowing.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Mina의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음에는 그릇이 가마에서 깨질까 봐 속이 조이고 다른 생각을 못 할 만큼 불안했지만, 금 하나 없이 아름답게 완성된 그릇을 보고 '내가 만들었다'며 얼굴이 환해졌어요. 그래서 anxious에서 proud로 바뀐 것이에요.

items.passage: When a friend tells us about a failure or a loss, most of us know what to do: we listen, comfort, and offer help. But when a friend shares good news, many of us respond poorly. We say "Nice" and go back to our phones, or we quickly turn the conversation to our own achievements. Some people even point out problems, such as how busy the new job will make her. Yet how we react to a friend's happy moments may matter as much as how we react to sad ones. When someone tells you she has won a prize or passed a test, stop what you are doing and show real interest. Ask how it happened, how she felt, and what comes next. Let her enjoy telling the story again. Celebrating a friend's success in this way doubles her joy and tells her that you are truly on her side. Do not save your attention only for the bad days.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 친구가 좋은 소식을 전하면 관심을 보이며 함께 기뻐해 주어야 한다.
친구가 어려움을 겪을 때 먼저 다가가 위로해야 한다.
친구와 대화할 때는 휴대 전화를 멀리 두어야 한다.
자신의 성취를 친구에게 지나치게 자랑하지 말아야 한다.
친구의 새 출발에 따르는 문제점을 솔직하게 알려 주어야 한다.
items.exp: 필자는 친구가 좋은 소식을 전할 때 하던 일을 멈추고 어떻게 된 일인지 묻는 등 진심 어린 관심을 보이며 함께 축하하라고 주장해요. ②는 사람들이 이미 잘하고 있다고 소개한 내용이고, ⑤는 잘못된 반응의 예예요.

items.passage: Experienced mountain climbers have a saying: reaching the top is optional, but getting down is required. Many climbing accidents do not happen on the way up. They happen on the way down, when climbers are tired, short of oxygen, and running out of daylight. Climbers who push on to the summit no matter what may use up the strength they need for the long return. For this reason, careful teams set a "turnaround time" before they start. If they have not reached the top by, say, two o'clock, they turn back, even if the summit is only a few hundred meters away. This is painfully hard to do, because the goal seems so close. But wise climbers remember that [the summit is only the halfway point]. A climb is not complete until everyone is safely back at the base.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the summit is only the halfway point]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the top of a mountain is too dangerous to stay on for long
climbers should rest halfway up before trying for the top
a climb succeeds only if climbers keep enough strength to return
most climbers turn back before they reach the highest point
the way down takes exactly as long as the way up
items.exp: 사고는 주로 지친 상태로 내려올 때 일어나므로 정해 둔 시각이 되면 정상 직전이라도 돌아선다고 했어요. 정상은 절반일 뿐이라는 말은 돌아올 힘을 남겨 안전하게 내려와야 등반이 완성된다는 뜻이에요. ⑤처럼 오르내리는 시간이 같다는 내용은 없어요.

items.passage: In high mountains and near the poles, the snow that falls each winter does not always melt in summer. Year after year, it piles up, and the weight of the new snow presses the old snow into thick ice. When this ice becomes heavy enough, it begins to flow slowly downhill like an extremely thick river. This is a glacier. As it moves, a glacier picks up rocks and stones, which freeze into its bottom. These rocks act like the teeth of a giant file, scraping and grinding the ground beneath. Over thousands of years, a glacier can turn a narrow V-shaped river valley into a wide valley shaped like the letter U. When the climate warms and the ice melts away, the valley remains, often with long scratches on its rocks pointing in the direction the ice once traveled. Many famous mountain valleys were shaped in this way.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: reasons why snow melts faster on high mountains
the dangers that glaciers pose to mountain climbers
the way rivers form narrow V-shaped valleys
how melting glaciers raise the level of the sea
how moving glaciers shape the land beneath them
items.exp: 쌓인 눈이 얼음이 되어 흐르는 빙하가 바닥의 암석을 긁고 갈아 V자 골짜기를 U자 골짜기로 바꾼다는 내용이에요. ③의 V자 골짜기는 빙하가 바꾸기 전의 모습으로 잠깐 나올 뿐 글의 중심이 아니에요.

items.passage: If rivers carry fresh water into the ocean, why is seawater salty? The answer begins with rain. As rain falls, it absorbs a small amount of carbon dioxide from the air, which makes it slightly acidic. When this water flows over rocks and soil, it slowly breaks down minerals and carries tiny amounts of salt into rivers. The amount in any river is too small to taste, so river water seems fresh. But rivers have been pouring these minerals into the sea for hundreds of millions of years. Once in the ocean, the water does not stay there forever. The sun heats the surface, and water evaporates into the air, later falling again as rain. The salt, however, cannot evaporate, so it is left behind. In this way, the sea has slowly collected salt from the land, like a pot of soup that grows saltier as it boils.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Rain: Nature's Way of Cleaning the Air
Why the Sea Keeps the Salt That Rivers Bring
How Rivers Lose Their Fresh Water
The Ocean Is Slowly Becoming Fresher
Evaporation: Why Seawater Cannot Be Drunk
items.exp: 빗물이 암석의 광물을 녹여 강을 통해 바다로 나르고, 물은 증발하지만 소금은 남아 오랜 세월 바다에 쌓였다는 내용이에요. 그래서 강이 가져온 소금을 바다가 간직하는 이유라는 제목이 알맞아요. ④는 바다가 점점 짜졌다는 글의 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: Margrethe Holm was born in 1879 in a farming village in eastern Denmark. As a child, she spent most of her free time in the beech woods near her home, where her grandfather taught her the names of birds and plants. She trained as a teacher in Copenhagen and began working at a crowded city school in 1902. Holm noticed that her pupils were often pale and restless after long hours at their desks. In 1911, she opened a small school in a forest outside the city, where children learned reading and arithmetic outdoors in every season. At first, many parents worried that their children would catch colds, but the school soon had a long waiting list. Holm wrote three books about outdoor learning, and teachers from Sweden and Germany came to visit her school. She died in 1958, and the school she founded is still open today.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 어린 시절 할아버지에게 새와 식물의 이름을 배웠다.
1911년에 도시 밖 숲속에 작은 학교를 열었다.
처음부터 모든 부모가 그녀의 학교를 반겼다.
그녀가 세운 학교는 오늘날에도 운영되고 있다.
items.exp: 처음에는 많은 부모가 아이들이 감기에 걸릴까 봐 걱정했다(many parents worried)고 했으므로 ④가 글의 내용과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 할아버지에게 배운 이름, 코펜하겐의 교사 교육, 1911년의 숲 학교, 지금도 열려 있는 학교로 모두 글과 일치해요.

items.passage: For centuries, Koreans have kept their homes warm in winter with a heating system called ondol. Instead of heating the air in a room, ondol heats the floor itself. A fire is built in a fireplace outside the room, often the same one ①[used] for cooking. The hot smoke then travels through passages under a floor of flat stones, ②[warming] the stones before it escapes through a chimney at the other end. Because the stones ③[holds] heat for a long time, the floor stays warm for hours after the fire dies down. This way of heating ④[shaped] daily life in Korean homes. People sat, ate, and slept on the floor, and they took off their shoes before entering so that the warm floor stayed clean. Even today, most Korean apartments have floors heated by hot water pipes, a modern version of the old system. Many say nothing feels as comforting as lying on a warm floor on a cold night, ⑤[which] helps explain why the tradition has lasted so long.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: because절의 주어 the stones가 복수이므로 ③ holds를 hold로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 fireplace를 꾸미는 과거분사, ②는 연속 동작을 나타내는 분사구문, ⑤는 앞 절 전체를 받는 계속적 용법의 관계대명사라 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: The lithium-ion batteries in our phones slowly lose their ability to hold a charge as they age. Each time a battery is charged and used, tiny chemical changes take place inside it, and over hundreds of cycles these changes ①[reduce] its capacity. However, the way we charge our phones can make a ②[difference]. Batteries tend to wear out faster when they are kept at very high or very low charge levels for long periods. Heat is also ③[harmful], so leaving a phone in a hot car or charging it under a pillow can shorten its life. For this reason, many experts suggest keeping the charge roughly between 20 and 80 percent whenever possible. Some phones now offer settings that ④[stop] charging at a certain level to protect the battery. Small habits like these will not make a battery last forever, but they can ⑤[speed] its decline and keep a phone useful for longer.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 좋은 충전 습관은 배터리 성능이 떨어지는 것을 늦춰 휴대폰을 더 오래 쓰게 해 준다는 흐름이에요. 그래서 ⑤ speed는 slow로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: When a weather forecast says there is a 70 percent chance of rain tomorrow, many people hear a promise. If the day stays dry, they complain that the forecaster was wrong. But a forecast of this kind is not a promise at all. It means that on days with conditions like tomorrow's, rain has fallen about seven times out of ten. On the other three days, it stayed dry. So a dry day after a 70 percent forecast is not a mistake; it is one of the outcomes the forecast already included. In fact, forecasters check their work by looking at many such days together. If it rains on roughly 70 percent of them, the forecasts were doing their job well. Understanding this helps us use forecasts wisely. A forecast is best read as a statement of ___, telling us how often to expect rain rather than promising that it will certainly come.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 강수 확률 70퍼센트는 비슷한 조건의 날 열 번 중 일곱 번쯤 비가 왔다는 뜻이고, 비가 꼭 온다는 약속이 아니라고 했어요. 그러니 예보는 가능성을 말하는 진술로 읽어야 하므로 likelihood가 알맞아요. certainty는 빈칸 뒤 'rather than promising that it will certainly come'과 정면으로 어긋나요.

items.passage: We often think of our beliefs as things we have carefully chosen. In reality, many of them were simply handed to us by our family, friends, or the community we grew up in. There is nothing wrong with this at first; no one can examine every idea alone. The problem begins when we never allow these beliefs to be questioned. A person who has heard only one side of an issue may defend it loudly, yet be unable to explain why the other side is wrong. Philosophers have long argued that the deepest understanding comes from facing serious objections and answering them. When someone challenges our view, we are forced to look for reasons, and we either find better ones or discover that we should change our mind. Either way, we gain something. This is why a belief that has never met disagreement ___. It may well be true, but its owner does not really know why.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: is more likely to be false than one that has been tested
should be shared with others as widely as possible
deserves more respect because it has lasted so long
is held more by habit than by real understanding
will eventually be forgotten by the people who hold it
items.exp: 반론을 만나 이유를 찾아보아야 깊이 이해하게 되는데, 그런 과정 없이 물려받은 믿음은 주인이 왜 옳은지 모른다고 했어요. 그래서 진짜 이해보다 습관으로 지니는 믿음이라는 ④가 알맞아요. 빈칸 뒤에서 그 믿음이 참일 수도 있다고 했으므로 거짓일 가능성이 높다는 ①은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: A short nap in the early afternoon can be a powerful tool for staying alert through the rest of the day. ① Many people feel a natural drop in energy after lunch, and a nap of about twenty minutes can restore focus without leaving them groggy. ② Longer naps, however, may let the brain fall into deep sleep, which can leave people feeling heavy and confused when they wake up. ③ Some people enjoy keeping a diary of their dreams, writing down whatever they remember as soon as they open their eyes in the morning. ④ Timing also matters, because napping too late in the day can make it harder to fall asleep at night. ⑤ By keeping naps short and taking them early, people can enjoy the benefits of napping while protecting their nighttime sleep.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 낮잠을 짧게, 이른 오후에 자야 효과가 있다는 흐름이에요. ③은 잠과 관련은 있지만 아침에 꿈 일기를 쓰는 이야기라 낮잠의 길이와 시간에 관한 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
For thousands of years, sailors faced great danger whenever they approached rocky coasts at night. Without any light to guide them, ships often crashed into hidden rocks just a short distance from safe harbors.

(A) To help them, people in ancient times lit large fires on hilltops near the shore. These simple fires, which warned ships where the land began, were the earliest form of what we now call lighthouses.

(B) Towers like this, however, depended on burning wood or oil, which produced a weak and unsteady light. It was not until the 1800s that special lenses were invented to gather light into strong beams that could reach ships many kilometers away.

(C) Later, builders began to raise these fires on tall towers so that their light could be seen from much farther out at sea. One of the most famous of these towers stood in Alexandria, Egypt, more than two thousand years ago.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 선원들의 위험(주어진 글) 뒤에 그들을 돕기 위해 언덕 위에 불을 피웠다는 (A)가 와요. 이어서 these fires를 탑 위로 올렸다는 (C)가 오고, 그 탑을 Towers like this로 받아 렌즈 발명까지 설명하는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Singers in a choir are sometimes asked to hold a single note for longer than one breath can last. ( ① ) A soloist facing such a passage has no choice but to stop for air, which creates a clear break in the music. ( ② ) A choir, however, can solve this problem with a technique called staggered breathing. ( ③ ) Instead of everyone breathing at once, each singer chooses a different moment to drop out briefly, take a quick breath, and return to the note. ( ④ ) Because the other voices keep singing during that moment, the audience hears one long, unbroken sound. ( ⑤ ) A singer who rushes back in at full volume, for example, creates a small bump that careful listeners can easily notice. For this reason, directors often plan the breathing points in advance so that singers standing next to each other do not drop out at the same time.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

For the effect to work, though, each singer must also slip back into the sound gently.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 교대 호흡이 효과를 내려면 다시 부드럽게 들어와야 한다는 추가 조건이에요. ⑤ 뒤의 '예를 들어 크게 다시 들어오면 소리가 튄다'는 문장이 바로 이 조건의 예이므로 ⑤에 들어가야 해요. ④에 넣으면 교대 호흡 방법과 그 결과를 잇는 흐름이 끊겨요.

items.passage: Walk into a neighborhood where the streets are clean and the gardens are neat, and you will probably think twice before dropping a candy wrapper. Walk down a street covered with trash, and the same wrapper may fall from your hand without a second thought. Our behavior is strongly shaped by what we see around us, even when no one is watching. Signs of care in a place send a quiet message that people here follow the rules, while signs of neglect suggest that nobody cares. For this reason, some towns have found that quickly cleaning up graffiti and repairing broken windows helps prevent further damage. Once a place looks cared for, people tend to treat it with care. Small efforts to keep a space in good shape can therefore protect it far more effectively than strict warnings alone.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

People tend to adjust their behavior to the (A) ___ of their surroundings, so keeping a place well maintained can (B) ___ careless actions.
items.exp: 깨끗한 곳에서는 쓰레기를 버리기 망설이고 더러운 곳에서는 쉽게 버린다고 했으니 사람들은 주변의 상태(condition)에 맞춰 행동해요. 그래서 장소를 잘 관리하면 부주의한 행동을 줄일(discourage) 수 있어요.

items.passage:
In the seventeenth century, a Swiss doctor gave a name to a strange illness he saw in soldiers serving far from home. They lost their appetite, could not sleep, and cried for the mountains of their childhood. He called it "nostalgia," from Greek words meaning "return home" and "pain." For a long time afterward, longing for the past was treated as a (a)[weakness], something that kept people from living in the present.

Psychologists today, however, see nostalgia quite differently. In studies, people who were asked to recall a fond memory, such as a family holiday or a childhood friend, later reported feeling more loved and less lonely. Nostalgic memories are rarely about being alone; they are usually filled with the people who cared for us. Recalling them reminds us that we have been part of meaningful relationships, and this can (b)[comfort] us when we feel isolated. Nostalgia also seems to give life a sense of continuity. When we look back, we see that the child we once were and the person we are now are (c)[connected] by a single story.

Interestingly, people tend to feel nostalgic most often during difficult times, such as when they move to a new city or face a stressful change. This suggests that the mind may turn to nostalgia in order to (d)[increase] its distress, much as the body shivers to warm itself in the cold. Of course, living only in the past is not healthy. But a short visit to our memories can give us the (e)[strength] to face what lies ahead.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Looking Back to Move Forward: The Value of Nostalgia
Why Soldiers Long for Their Home Mountains
Living in the Present: The Danger of Old Memories
How Moving to a New City Changes Our Memories
Nostalgia: A Disease That Doctors Finally Cured
items.exp: 예전에는 병이나 약점으로 여겨졌던 향수가 사랑받는 느낌과 삶의 연속성을 주고 힘든 시기에 마음을 지탱해 준다는 내용이에요. ②는 글 첫머리의 일화일 뿐이고, ③은 글이 반박하는 옛 생각에 가까워요.

Psychologists today, however, see nostalgia quite differently. items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 힘든 시기에 향수를 자주 느끼는 것은 몸이 떨어서 체온을 올리듯 마음이 스스로를 돕는 것이라는 흐름이에요. 그러므로 (d) increase는 괴로움을 덜어 준다는 뜻의 reduce나 ease로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every Saturday morning, Leo helped his aunt Rosa at her vegetable stall in the town's farmers' market. On this particular Saturday, it was raining, and only a few shoppers wandered between the stalls. Leo sat on a box behind the table, staring at his phone. "Why don't you arrange the tomatoes so they look nicer?" Rosa suggested. With a sigh, (a)[he] put his phone away and began lining them up by color. Just then, an elderly man with a cane stopped at the stall and began to choose tomatoes slowly, holding each one up to the light.

(B)
By late summer, the seeds had grown into tall plants heavy with golden-yellow tomatoes. Leo picked the best ones and carried them to the market in a basket. He placed them at the front of the table under a handwritten sign: "Hale's Gold." Around noon, Mr. Hale came walking down the row. When (b)[he] saw the sign, he stopped and laughed out loud. "Well, look at that," he said. "They taste just like the ones from my old garden." Leo had never felt so proud of anything in his life.

(C)
The man paid for a bag of tomatoes, but as he turned to leave, the wet paper bag tore open. Tomatoes rolled across the ground in every direction. Without thinking, Leo jumped up and ran after them, picking them up one by one. Then (c)[he] found a sturdy wooden box and packed the tomatoes inside. "Thank you, young man," the man said. "My name is Arthur Hale. I used to grow my own tomatoes, but my knees won't let me garden anymore." Leo noticed how sadly he looked at the vegetables on the table.

(D)
The following Saturday, Mr. Hale returned, this time carrying a small envelope. "These are seeds from my favorite tomatoes," he said to Leo. "My family has saved them for sixty years. I'd like (d)[you] to plant them." Leo hesitated, since (e)[he] had never grown anything before. But Rosa promised to show him how, so he accepted the envelope. That evening, Leo cleared a sunny corner of the backyard and planted the seeds, imagining what they would become.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 노인이 토마토를 고르고, (C)에서 봉투가 찢어져 Leo가 도와주며 노인이 Arthur Hale이라고 자신을 소개해요. (D)에서 다음 토요일에 그가 다시 와서 씨앗을 주고, (B)에서 늦여름에 그 씨앗이 자라 Hale's Gold로 팔려요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every Saturday morning, Leo helped his aunt Rosa at her vegetable stall in the town's farmers' market. On this particular Saturday, it was raining, and only a few shoppers wandered between the stalls. Leo sat on a box behind the table, staring at his phone. "Why don't you arrange the tomatoes so they look nicer?" Rosa suggested. With a sigh, (a)[he] put his phone away and began lining them up by color. Just then, an elderly man with a cane stopped at the stall and began to choose tomatoes slowly, holding each one up to the light.

(B)
By late summer, the seeds had grown into tall plants heavy with golden-yellow tomatoes. Leo picked the best ones and carried them to the market in a basket. He placed them at the front of the table under a handwritten sign: "Hale's Gold." Around noon, Mr. Hale came walking down the row. When (b)[he] saw the sign, he stopped and laughed out loud. "Well, look at that," he said. "They taste just like the ones from my old garden." Leo had never felt so proud of anything in his life.

(C)
The man paid for a bag of tomatoes, but as he turned to leave, the wet paper bag tore open. Tomatoes rolled across the ground in every direction. Without thinking, Leo jumped up and ran after them, picking them up one by one. Then (c)[he] found a sturdy wooden box and packed the tomatoes inside. "Thank you, young man," the man said. "My name is Arthur Hale. I used to grow my own tomatoes, but my knees won't let me garden anymore." Leo noticed how sadly he looked at the vegetables on the table.

(D)
The following Saturday, Mr. Hale returned, this time carrying a small envelope. "These are seeds from my favorite tomatoes," he said to Leo. "My family has saved them for sixty years. I'd like (d)[you] to plant them." Leo hesitated, since (e)[he] had never grown anything before. But Rosa promised to show him how, so he accepted the envelope. That evening, Leo cleared a sunny corner of the backyard and planted the seeds, imagining what they would become.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 가리키는 대상이 나머지 넷과 다른 것은?
items.exp: (b)는 Hale's Gold라는 팻말을 보고 웃은 Mr. Hale을 가리키고, 나머지 (a), (c), (d), (e)는 모두 Leo를 가리켜요.

items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Leo는 비 오는 토요일에 휴대폰을 보며 가판대 뒤에 앉아 있었다.
Leo는 노란 토마토를 'Hale's Gold'라는 팻말 아래 진열했다.
Mr. Hale의 종이 봉투가 찢어져 토마토가 바닥에 굴러갔다.
Mr. Hale은 무릎 때문에 더 이상 정원을 가꾸지 못한다고 말했다.
Leo는 이전에 채소를 길러 본 경험이 많았다.
items.exp: (D)에서 Leo는 무언가를 길러 본 적이 한 번도 없어서 망설였다고 했어요. 그래서 채소를 길러 본 경험이 많았다는 ⑤가 글과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Dear Students of Greenhill High School,

I am Olivia Grant, the manager of Sunny Paws Animal Shelter. Every year, our shelter takes care of hundreds of dogs and cats that have lost their homes. Most of our work is done by a small team of staff members, and lately we have been struggling to give every animal the attention it needs. Many of our dogs have not been on a proper walk in days, and our cats rarely get the chance to play with people. That is why we are looking for students who are willing to spend a few hours each weekend with our animals. You do not need any special experience. We will teach you how to walk the dogs safely and how to care for the cats. If you are interested, please fill out the form on our website by March 15. Your time could make a real difference in an animal's life.

Warm regards,
Olivia Grant
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 보호소 시설 개선을 위한 기부를 요청하려고
주말 동물 돌봄 자원봉사에 지원하도록 요청하려고
items.exp: 직원이 부족해 동물들이 충분히 산책하거나 놀지 못한다고 설명한 뒤, 주말마다 몇 시간씩 동물과 함께할 학생을 찾는다며 웹사이트에서 신청하라고 했어요. 산책 방법은 봉사자에게 가르쳐 주겠다는 내용일 뿐 글의 목적이 아니에요.

items.passage: The last bus to the village had left ten minutes before I reached the station. I stood alone on the empty platform in a small mountain town where I did not speak the language. My phone battery was almost dead, and the only hotel I had seen was closed. The wind grew colder as the sky turned dark. I tried asking a man passing by for help, but he only shook his head and hurried away. My heart was pounding, and I wondered if I would have to spend the night on the bench. Then an old woman selling chestnuts at the corner waved at me. Using hand signs and a few simple words, she made me understand that her son drove to my village every evening. Twenty minutes later, I was sitting in the warm front seat of his truck, holding a paper bag of hot chestnuts. I let out a long breath and finally smiled.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 마지막 버스를 놓치고 말도 통하지 않는 곳에서 휴대폰도 꺼져 가며 가슴이 두근거렸지만, 할머니의 아들 트럭을 타고 긴 숨을 내쉬며 미소 지었어요. 그래서 panicked에서 relieved로 바뀐 것이에요.

items.passage: Many people believe that as long as they do not break the law, they are good citizens. If something is legal, the reasoning goes, no one can blame them for doing it. But laws were never meant to describe everything a good person should do. A law cannot force you to thank a bus driver, to keep a promise made to a friend, or to give up your seat to an elderly passenger. It sets only the minimum that a society can enforce with fines and prisons, the line below which behavior becomes unacceptable. Above that line lies a large area that the law leaves to each person's conscience: kindness, honesty, and fairness in daily life. A person who asks only "Is this allowed?" has stopped asking the more important question, "Is this right?" In this sense, [the law is a floor, not a ceiling].
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the law is a floor, not a ceiling]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: laws should be made stricter so that people behave better
obeying the law is only the lowest standard of right behavior
people who break small rules deserve severe punishment
good citizens should try to change laws they disagree with
the law protects people at the bottom of society first
items.exp: 법은 사회가 벌금과 감옥으로 강제할 수 있는 최소한만 정하고, 그 위의 친절·정직·공정은 각자의 양심에 맡겨진다고 했어요. 그러므로 법은 바닥(최소 기준)일 뿐 천장(최고 기준)이 아니라는 뜻인 ②가 알맞아요. ①은 법을 더 엄격하게 하자는 내용으로 글에 없어요.

items.passage: Many people read only the headlines of news articles before sharing them online. This seems harmless, since a headline is supposed to tell us what the story is about. But headlines are written to catch attention in a few words, and they often leave out important details. A headline saying "Coffee Linked to Longer Life" may describe a study that found only a small connection in one group of people. Readers who stop at the headline may believe something far stronger than what the research actually showed. When they share it, the exaggerated message spreads to many others. Reading the full article takes only a few extra minutes, but it allows us to see who did the research, how it was done, and what its limits are. Before we pass a story on to others, we should make sure we understand more than its title.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 뉴스 제목은 기사 내용을 정확히 요약해야 한다.
건강 관련 기사는 전문가에게 확인을 받아야 한다.
온라인 기사를 공유하는 것은 가급적 피해야 한다.
연구 결과는 다양한 집단을 대상으로 검증되어야 한다.
기사를 공유하기 전에 제목만이 아니라 본문 전체를 읽어야 한다.
items.exp: 제목만 읽으면 연구 결과를 과장해서 믿고 퍼뜨리기 쉬우니, 공유하기 전에 기사 전체를 읽고 이해해야 한다는 것이 요지예요. ①은 제목이 세부 내용을 빠뜨린다는 부분만 빌린 오답이에요.

items.passage: A vacuum flask can keep tea hot for hours on a cold day or keep juice cool on a summer afternoon. How can one bottle do both jobs? The secret is that it does not create heat or cold at all; it simply slows down the movement of heat. Heat travels in three main ways: through direct contact, through moving air or liquid, and as invisible rays. A vacuum flask blocks all three. It has two thin walls with almost no air between them, so heat cannot easily pass from one wall to the other by contact or by moving air. The walls are also coated with a shiny, mirror-like layer that reflects heat rays back toward where they came from. Finally, a tight cap stops warm air from escaping at the top. Because heat moves in or out so slowly, whatever is inside stays close to its starting temperature for a long time.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the history of the vacuum flask's invention
why hot drinks cool down faster in winter
how a vacuum flask keeps drinks hot or cold by slowing heat flow
the best materials for making drink containers
ways to keep food fresh without using electricity
items.exp: 보온병은 열을 만들지 않고, 두 겹 벽 사이의 진공·반짝이는 막·꽉 닫히는 뚜껑으로 열의 이동을 느리게 해 안의 온도를 지킨다는 내용이에요. 그래서 ③이 알맞아요. ②의 겨울에 음료가 빨리 식는 이유는 글에서 다루지 않아요.

items.passage: Deserts are known for their burning heat, but travelers who spend a night in one are often shocked by how cold it becomes. In some deserts, the temperature can drop by more than 20°C after sunset. The main reason is the lack of water in the air. Water vapor works like a blanket, trapping heat near the ground and releasing it slowly. In humid places, this blanket keeps nights fairly warm. In a desert, however, the air is so dry that the heat collected during the day escapes quickly into the sky once the sun goes down. Clear skies make the effect even stronger, since there are no clouds to hold the warmth in. The dry sand also cannot store much heat. So the same dryness that makes deserts so hot during the day is what makes them surprisingly cold at night.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How Desert Animals Stay Cool in the Day
Clouds: The Main Cause of Desert Heat
Why Sand Holds Heat Longer Than Soil
Dry Air: The Reason Desert Nights Turn Cold
Planning a Safe Trip Across the Desert
items.exp: 사막의 공기에는 수증기가 거의 없어 낮 동안 모인 열이 해가 지면 빠르게 빠져나가므로 밤이 춥다는 내용이에요. ③은 모래가 열을 많이 저장하지 못한다는 글의 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage:
Lakeside Youth Photo Contest 2027

Show us your town through your camera! The Lakeside Cultural Center invites young photographers to share their view of everyday life in our community.

• Who: Students aged 13 to 18 living in Lakeside
• Theme: "Small Moments in Our Town"
• Deadline: Friday, May 21, 2027, 6 p.m.
• Entry Fee: Free

How to Enter
• Each person may submit up to two photos.
• Upload your photos with a short title on our website.
• Photos taken with smartphones are welcome.

Prizes
• First Prize: $300 gift card
• Second Prize: $150 gift card

Notes
• Edited photos that change the original scene will not be accepted.
• Winners will be announced on June 4 and their photos will be displayed at the center for one month.
items.q: Lakeside Youth Photo Contest 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: Lakeside에 사는 13세에서 18세 학생이 참가할 수 있다.
한 사람당 사진을 두 장까지 제출할 수 있다.
스마트폰으로 찍은 사진도 제출할 수 있다.
items.exp: 수상자는 6월 4일에 발표하고, 5월 21일은 사진 제출 마감일이에요. 그래서 ⑤가 안내문과 일치하지 않아요.

items.passage: Reading aloud is often seen as something only young children do, but it can help learners of any age. When you read a text silently, your eyes can easily skip over words ①[that] you do not fully understand. Reading aloud forces you to slow down and pay attention to every word. It also ②[involving] more of your senses at once. You see the words, say them, and hear them, and this combination makes the information easier to remember. For language learners, reading aloud has another benefit: it gives them a chance ③[to practice] pronunciation and rhythm. Many students feel shy about ④[hearing] their own voices at first, but this feeling usually disappears with practice. Even a few minutes of reading aloud each day can make a noticeable difference. Teachers who have tried it in class often report that their students become more ⑤[confident] speakers and more careful readers over time.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: 주어 It 뒤에 문장의 동사가 와야 하므로 ② involving을 involves로 고쳐야 해요. ④는 전치사 about 뒤의 동명사, ⑤는 become 뒤의 보어 형용사로 맞아요.

items.passage: Have you ever noticed how many prices end in .99? A shirt costs $19.99 instead of $20, and a snack is $2.99 instead of $3. The difference is only one cent, yet stores use this trick because it ①[works]. When people look at a price, they tend to read from left to right and pay the most attention to the first number. As a result, $19.99 feels closer to $19 than to $20, even though the real difference is ②[huge]. Shoppers then see the item as a better deal and are more ③[likely] to buy it. Interestingly, some expensive stores do the opposite and use round numbers such as $200. A round price can feel ④[simple] and confident, which matches the high-quality image these stores want to create. In both cases, the numbers on a price tag are chosen ⑤[carefully] to influence how customers feel.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: $19.99와 $20의 차이는 1센트밖에 되지 않는다고 했으므로 실제 차이는 아주 작아요. 그래서 ② huge는 tiny 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: In most team sports, a referee watches the players and decides when a rule has been broken. Ultimate, a team sport played with a flying disc, works differently. In many games, even at high levels of competition, there is no referee on the field. When players believe they have been fouled, they make the call themselves, and the players involved discuss what happened and settle the matter on the spot. If they cannot agree, the play is simply done over. Newcomers often expect this system to fall apart, since every player has a reason to make calls that favor their own team. Yet it works surprisingly well, largely because the sport's culture treats fair play as part of the game itself. Players are taught from the very beginning that winning through a false call is not really winning at all. In Ultimate, the role of the referee is filled by each player's ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 심판 없이 선수들이 스스로 반칙을 선언하고, 거짓 판정으로 이기는 것은 진짜 승리가 아니라고 배운다고 했어요. 그래서 심판의 역할을 대신하는 것은 각 선수의 정직함(honesty)이에요. ④의 경험은 처음부터 공정함을 배운다는 내용과 관련이 없어요.

items.passage: Imagine two birthday presents. One is an expensive scarf bought online in a few seconds. The other is a simple card with a poem your friend wrote by hand, crossing out words and starting over several times. Many people say the card touches them more, even though it cost almost nothing. Why? Part of the answer is that we read gifts as messages. Money can be spent quickly and without much thought, but time cannot be saved up or bought back. When someone gives up hours to make something for us, the gift shows that we were important enough to receive a piece of their limited life. This is also why a home-cooked meal can feel more special than a fancy restaurant dinner, and why a short visit can mean more than a long text message. What makes such gifts precious is ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the time and effort they show the giver was willing to spend
the high price that the giver paid in the store
the great skill with which they were made
the surprise they create on special occasions
the practical use the receiver can make of them
items.exp: 돈은 쉽게 쓸 수 있지만 시간은 되돌릴 수 없어서, 누군가 우리를 위해 몇 시간을 들였다는 것 자체가 마음을 전한다고 했어요. 그래서 주는 사람이 기꺼이 들인 시간과 노력을 보여 준다는 ①이 알맞아요. ②는 거의 돈이 들지 않은 카드가 더 감동적이라는 내용과 반대이고, ③의 솜씨는 고쳐 쓰며 만든 시 이야기와 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: For a long time, public libraries charged small fines for books returned late, believing that the fear of paying would make people bring books back on time. ① In recent years, however, many libraries have stopped charging these fines, and the results have surprised some librarians. ② Instead of keeping books longer, most users returned them about as quickly as before, and some libraries even saw long-missing books come back once the fear of a large fine was gone. ③ The fines, it turned out, had also been driving away the very people libraries most wanted to serve, such as children and low-income families who could not afford to pay. ④ Most libraries today also lend e-books, which disappear from the reader's device automatically when the borrowing period ends. ⑤ Without the fines, these readers began visiting again, and libraries found that the small amount of money they lost was worth far less than the trust and use they gained.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 도서관이 연체료를 없앴더니 반납이 늦어지지 않았고, 연체료 때문에 떠났던 아이들과 저소득 가정이 다시 찾아왔다는 글이에요. ④는 전자책이 자동으로 반납된다는 내용으로, 연체료 폐지의 효과라는 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 these readers는 ③의 아이들과 저소득 가정을 가리켜요.

items.passage:
Water is heavy, and sending it into space by rocket costs a great deal of money. For astronauts living on a space station for months, carrying all the water they need from Earth is simply not practical.

(A) This system can turn almost every drop of used water back into clean water. Astronauts often joke that today's coffee is made from yesterday's coffee, and in a way, they are right.

(B) Instead, the station recycles nearly all of its water. Moisture from the astronauts' breath and sweat is collected from the air, and even urine is gathered and processed by a special system.

(C) Thanks to such recycling, the station needs far fewer deliveries from Earth. Scientists also hope to use similar technology one day to help areas on Earth that suffer from water shortages.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 물을 지구에서 다 실어 나를 수 없다는 주어진 글 뒤에 Instead로 재활용을 소개하는 (B)가 와요. (B)의 a special system을 This system으로 받는 (A)가 이어지고, such recycling으로 정리하는 (C)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: In face-to-face conversation, people take turns speaking with remarkable timing. ( ① ) Usually, one person begins to talk only a fraction of a second after the other stops, and this smooth rhythm happens without any planning. ( ② ) Even a delay of half a second, which is common on many internet connections, can upset this rhythm. ( ③ ) When a speaker pauses, the listener waits, hears nothing, and starts talking just as the speaker's next words arrive. ( ④ ) Both people stop, apologize, and wait again, and the conversation feels awkward. ( ⑤ ) Over time, these small interruptions can even make people seem less friendly or less focused than they really are. Knowing the cause can help us be more patient and allow a little extra time before we reply.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Video calls, however, often break this natural pattern because of tiny delays in sound.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 however로 대면 대화의 자연스러운 주고받기와 대조하며 화상 통화의 지연 문제를 처음 꺼내요. ② 뒤의 Even a delay of half a second는 이 지연을 이어받는 내용이므로 ②에 들어가야 해요.

items.passage: In one study, a group of city workers was asked to take a thirty-minute walk during their lunch break for several weeks. Half of them walked along busy streets lined with shops and traffic, while the other half walked through a park with trees and grass. Both groups walked the same distance at the same speed. At the end of the study, the park walkers reported feeling much calmer and less tired in the afternoon than the street walkers did. Their heart rates were also lower after the walks. The researchers concluded that the exercise alone could not explain the difference. Being surrounded by natural scenery seemed to give the mind a chance to rest from the constant noise and demands of the city, which made the walk more refreshing.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Walking in (A) ___ settings was found to reduce stress more than walking in busy streets, which suggests that the (B) ___ of a walk matters as well as the physical activity.
items.exp: 같은 거리와 속도로 걸었는데도 공원(녹지)에서 걸은 사람들이 더 차분하고 덜 피곤했으므로 (A)는 green이에요. 운동만으로는 차이를 설명할 수 없고 주변 자연 풍경이 영향을 주었으니 (B)는 걷는 환경(environment)이에요. 거리와 속도는 두 집단이 같았으므로 length, speed는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
How can we understand the everyday life of a community that is very different from our own? One answer comes from anthropology, the study of human cultures. Many anthropologists use a method called participant observation. Instead of simply sending out surveys or watching from a distance, they live with the people they study for months or even years, joining in their daily work, meals, and celebrations.

This method has a clear (a)[advantage]. People often describe their lives differently from how they actually live them. A villager asked about farming might give a short, simple answer, but by working in the fields beside him, an anthropologist can see the many small decisions and shared habits that he would never think to (b)[mention]. Over time, the researcher also gains trust. People begin to act naturally instead of behaving politely for a stranger, and the anthropologist is able to observe real life rather than a (c)[performance].

Participant observation, however, is not without problems. The longer researchers stay, the more they may come to share the views of the community, which can make it harder to (d)[notice] things that seem normal to everyone there. Their very presence may also change how people behave. For this reason, anthropologists try to balance being an insider and an outsider. They take part in daily life but keep careful notes and regularly step back to ask what they might be missing. In the end, this method shows that understanding a culture requires not only observing people but also (e)[avoiding] their experiences.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Surveys: The Best Tool for Studying Cultures
Living Among People: The Power and Limits of Participant Observation
How Farming Shaped Early Human Societies
items.exp: 인류학자가 사람들과 함께 살며 관찰하는 참여 관찰의 장점(실제 삶과 신뢰)과 한계(공동체 시각에 물듦, 존재 자체의 영향)를 함께 설명하는 글이에요. ⑤는 내부자와 외부자 사이의 균형을 잡는다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.exp: 참여 관찰은 사람들의 일상에 함께 참여하는 방법이므로, 문화를 이해하려면 관찰뿐 아니라 그들의 경험을 함께 나누어야 한다는 결론이 자연스러워요. 그래서 (e) avoiding은 sharing으로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
For thirty years, the Moreno family had run a small noodle restaurant on the corner of Elm Street. Grandpa Luis made the broth every morning, and his granddaughter Sofia helped out after school. One evening, Sofia's father, Carlos, sat at an empty table with a pile of bills in front of him. A new fast-food chain had opened across the street, and fewer customers came in each week. "We may have to close by the end of the year," (a)[he] said quietly.

(B)
Sofia began to photograph each bowl before it left the kitchen and posted the pictures online with short stories about her grandfather. She wrote about how (b)[he] had learned the recipe from his own mother in a tiny village and had carried it across the ocean. Within a few weeks, people started coming in and asking for "the grandfather's noodles." Some of them said they had read every story Sofia posted.

(C)
One Saturday, a long line formed outside the door before the restaurant even opened. Grandpa Luis stood behind the counter, surprised, as customers greeted (c)[him] by name. Carlos looked at the full tables and then at his daughter. "You saved this place," he said. Sofia shook her head. "No, Dad. Grandpa's soup did. I just told people about it." That night, after the last customer had left, the family stayed late, laughing and cleaning together, and Grandpa Luis quietly began planning tomorrow's broth.

(D)
Sofia could not sleep that night. She kept thinking about the regular customers who had told her how much they loved her grandfather's soup. The next morning, she watched (d)[him] stir the broth for hours, adding spices one by one as (e)[he] had always done. "Nobody makes noodles like this anymore," she thought. "People just don't know about us." An idea came to her, and she took out her phone.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 가게가 문을 닫을 위기라는 말을 듣고, (D)에서 Sofia가 잠 못 이루다 할아버지를 보며 아이디어를 떠올려요. (B)에서 사진과 이야기를 올리자 손님이 늘고, (C)에서 가게 앞에 긴 줄이 생겨요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Howard,

My name is Daniel Reyes, and I have lived in the Greenfield neighborhood for over ten years. Until last spring, the community center ran a free bike repair workshop every Saturday morning. Volunteers taught residents how to fix flat tires, adjust brakes, and replace chains. My two children learned to take care of their own bikes there, and I often saw retired neighbors chatting with teenagers over a box of tools. Since the workshop closed, many of those bikes have been left in garages, waiting for repairs that nobody knows how to do. I understand that the center lost its volunteer coordinator, but several parents, including me, are willing to help organize the sessions. I am writing to ask you to consider bringing the Saturday workshop back. We would be happy to meet with you to discuss how we can support it.

Sincerely,
Daniel Reyes
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 토요일 자전거 수리 작업장의 재운영을 요청하려고
커뮤니티 센터의 주차 공간 확충을 건의하려고
기증할 자전거 부품의 전달 방법을 문의하려고
작업장 이용 시간 변경에 대해 항의하려고
items.exp: 필자는 문을 닫은 토요일 자전거 수리 작업장을 다시 열어 달라고 부탁하고 있어요(I am writing to ask you to consider bringing the Saturday workshop back). 학부모들이 운영을 돕겠다고 했지만 강사로 지원하는 글은 아니므로 ①은 답이 아니에요.

items.passage: Jiwoo stood at the edge of the deep end, her toes curled over the cold tiles. For three weeks at the summer swimming class, she had practiced only in the shallow part of the pool, where she could always touch the bottom. Now the coach wanted everyone to swim one full length across the deep water. The blue below her looked endless, and her heart pounded so hard that she could hear it. "What if I sink?" she whispered. The coach smiled and promised to walk along the side of the pool the whole way. Jiwoo took a deep breath and pushed off. Kick, pull, breathe. Before she knew it, her hand touched the far wall. She turned around and saw her classmates clapping. Jiwoo pulled off her goggles, grinning so widely that her cheeks hurt. She had done it all by herself.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Jiwoo의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 깊은 물을 내려다보며 심장이 쿵쾅거리고 가라앉을까 봐 속삭이는 모습에서 겁에 질린 마음이 드러나요. 끝까지 혼자 헤엄쳐 벽을 짚고 친구들의 박수 속에 활짝 웃었으므로 자랑스러운 마음으로 바뀌었어요. 그래서 frightened → proud가 알맞아요.

items.passage: When a student gets a math problem wrong, many teachers simply mark it with a red X and write the correct answer next to it. This seems efficient, but it hides the most valuable part of the mistake. A wrong answer is rarely random. It usually comes from a reasonable but incomplete idea, such as forgetting a step or using a rule in the wrong situation. If students only see the right answer, they may copy it without ever discovering where their thinking went off track. Instead, teachers should invite students to explain, out loud or in writing, how they arrived at their wrong answers. In doing so, students often find the error themselves, and teachers learn what kind of help each student really needs. A few minutes spent listening to a mistake can prevent the same mistake from happening again and again.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 교사는 학생에게 오답에 이르게 된 풀이 과정을 설명하게 해야 한다.
교사는 틀린 문제의 정답을 학생에게 즉시 알려 주어야 한다.
학생은 수학 문제를 풀 때 여러 가지 방법을 시도해야 한다.
교사는 학생의 실수를 다른 학생 앞에서 지적하지 말아야 한다.
학생은 틀린 문제를 정답이 나올 때까지 반복해서 풀어야 한다.
items.exp: teachers should invite students to explain ... how they arrived at their wrong answers에 필자의 주장이 드러나 있어요. 정답만 적어 주는 방식은 오히려 비판하고 있으므로 ②는 반대 내용이에요.

items.passage: You have paid for a concert ticket weeks in advance. On the day of the concert, you wake up with a bad cold, and it is pouring rain. You would much rather stay home, but you go anyway, telling yourself, "I already paid for it." Economists call money like this a sunk cost: it is gone, and nothing you do now can bring it back. Whether you go or stay, the ticket price has already been spent. The only real question is which choice will make the rest of your evening better. Yet many of us keep watching boring movies, finishing meals we do not enjoy, and continuing projects that are clearly failing, simply because we have already put money or time into them. In such moments, we are [letting yesterday's receipt make today's decision]. A wiser approach is to look forward, not back.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [letting yesterday's receipt make today's decision]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: planning our spending carefully before we buy anything
keeping records so that we can get our money back
allowing past costs that cannot be recovered to control present choices
trusting the advice of people who have paid for the same thing
choosing whatever is cheapest without thinking about quality
items.exp: 이미 써 버려 되찾을 수 없는 돈(sunk cost) 때문에 원하지 않는 선택을 계속하는 상황을 비유한 표현이에요. 그래서 되찾을 수 없는 과거의 비용이 현재 선택을 좌우하게 둔다는 ③이 알맞아요. ②는 영수증이라는 낱말만 빌린 오답이에요.

items.passage: In spring, many birds begin singing loudly just before sunrise, creating what scientists call the dawn chorus. Why do they choose this early hour? One explanation is related to sound itself. In the early morning, the air is usually cool and still, so songs can travel farther and more clearly than later in the day. Another reason is that the light is too dim for hunting insects, which are hard to find until the sun warms them. Instead of wasting this time, birds use it to send messages. A male's strong song at dawn tells rivals that he has survived the cold night and is still guarding his territory. It also shows nearby females that he is healthy enough to spend energy on singing before eating breakfast. In other words, the dawn chorus is not just a beautiful sound; it is a carefully timed form of communication.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: ways birds find insects in the dark
how cold weather affects birds' health
the role of females in choosing nesting sites
why sound travels differently in cities
reasons why birds sing intensely around sunrise
items.exp: 새들이 해 뜨기 직전에 노래하는 까닭(소리가 멀리 퍼짐, 먹이 사냥이 어려운 시간, 경쟁자와 암컷에게 보내는 신호)을 설명하는 글이에요. ①은 어둠 속 먹이 찾기만 다루어 글 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: When people imagine a public library, they often picture quiet rooms full of books. Today, however, many libraries play a much wider role in their communities. In some towns, the library is the only place where anyone can stay for hours without having to buy anything. Job seekers use its computers to write résumés, parents bring toddlers to free story times, and elderly residents join classes to learn how to video-call their grandchildren. Teenagers gather there after school to study together in a safe, warm space. For people who live alone, a short conversation with a librarian may be the only social contact they have that day. In this way, libraries are becoming something like a shared living room for the whole town. Their value cannot be measured only by how many books are borrowed.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Fewer People Borrow Books Today
How to Find Books Quickly in a Library
Libraries: The Town's Shared Living Room
Quiet Please: Rules Every Library Needs
items.exp: 도서관이 책을 빌리는 곳을 넘어 구직자, 부모, 노인, 청소년이 모이는 마을의 공동 거실이 되고 있다는 내용이에요. 대출 권수가 줄어든 이유는 다루지 않으므로 ①은 답이 아니에요.

items.passage: Ines Calloway (1884–1957) was an American designer who changed the way children play outdoors. She was born in a small town in Ohio, the daughter of a carpenter, and spent her childhood building toys from scraps of wood in her father's workshop. After studying engineering at a state college, she worked for several years designing bridges. In 1912, she noticed that city children had nowhere safe to play except the busy streets. She began designing playgrounds with wooden climbing frames, sand areas, and low slides, testing each idea by watching local children use them. Her first playground opened in Cleveland in 1915 and was so popular that more than thirty cities asked for her plans. Calloway refused to sell the designs and shared them for free. In her later years, she wrote a guidebook for parents and teachers on the value of outdoor play.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 어린 시절 아버지의 작업장에서 장난감을 만들었다.
대학에서 공학을 공부한 후 몇 년간 다리를 설계했다.
아이들이 놀이 시설을 이용하는 모습을 관찰하며 아이디어를 시험했다.
첫 놀이터의 설계도를 여러 도시에 판매했다.
말년에 야외 놀이의 가치에 관한 안내서를 썼다.
items.exp: 30개가 넘는 도시가 설계도를 요청했지만 Calloway는 설계도를 팔기를 거절하고 무료로 나눠 주었다고 했어요(refused to sell the designs and shared them for free). 그래서 ④가 글의 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: In many cultures, the way a gift is wrapped matters almost as much as the gift itself. In Japan, for example, people sometimes use a square cloth called furoshiki, which ①[can be folded] around objects of different shapes and reused many times. The careful folding shows that the giver spent time ②[thinking] about the receiver. In other places, the color of the paper carries meaning. Red, ③[which] is linked to luck and happiness in China, is a popular choice for celebrations, while white may be avoided because it is associated with funerals. Even the act of opening a gift differs. In some countries, it is polite to open a present immediately and show delight, but in ④[other], receivers wait until the giver has left so that no one ⑤[feels] embarrassed. These small customs remind us that a gift is not just an object but a message.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ④는 앞의 some countries와 짝을 이루어 '다른 나라들'을 뜻하는 대명사가 와야 하므로 others로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 천이 접히는 것이라 수동태, ②는 spend time -ing, ③은 계속적 용법 관계대명사, ⑤는 단수 주어 no one에 맞춘 feels로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Some cafés and museums let visitors decide how much to pay. At first glance, this policy seems ①[certain] to succeed, since customers could simply pay nothing and walk away. Surprisingly, most people do not take advantage of it. Studies of such businesses show that customers usually pay an amount that is ②[close] to the normal price, and some even pay more. One reason is fairness: people feel ③[uncomfortable] taking something valuable without giving something back. Another reason is the way others see us. Paying too little in front of a cashier or other customers can feel ④[embarrassing], so people tend to pay a reasonable amount. Still, the system does not work everywhere. It succeeds best in small places where customers feel a personal ⑤[connection] to the business and its staff, and it often fails in large, busy places where no one knows anyone else.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 손님이 한 푼도 안 내고 갈 수 있으니 처음 보기에는 이 제도가 실패할 것처럼 보인다는 흐름이에요. 따라서 ①의 certain to succeed는 certain to fail처럼 바꿔야 해요(certain을 unlikely로 바꿔도 돼요). 뒤의 Surprisingly가 처음 예상과 반대 결과임을 보여 줘요.

items.passage: Young children learning English often say things like "I goed to the park" or "I saw two mouses." Parents may worry that these mistakes are a step backward, especially because the same child may have said "went" correctly a few months earlier. In fact, these errors are a sign of progress. At first, children simply copy whole words they hear, so "went" is just one more word to remember. Later, they notice that many past forms end in "-ed" and many plurals end in "-s," and they begin applying this pattern to every new word, even to words that do not follow it. Nobody around them says "goed," so they could not have copied it from anyone. They created it themselves. The mistake shows that the child is no longer just repeating sounds but has discovered a ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 아이들은 과거형에 -ed, 복수형에 -s가 붙는 패턴을 알아차리고 모든 낱말에 적용하다가 goed 같은 말을 스스로 만들어 낸다고 했어요. 따라서 아이가 단순 반복을 넘어 규칙을 발견했다는 rule이 알맞아요. sound는 단순히 소리를 따라 하는 단계를 가리키므로 답이 아니에요.

items.passage: Managers often see idle workers or empty machines as a sign of waste. If a delivery company's trucks are full every hour of the day, it seems to be running perfectly. Yet such a company has a hidden weakness. When a truck breaks down or a holiday rush suddenly doubles the number of orders, there is no extra truck and no free driver to take on the load. Deliveries pile up, customers grow angry, and a small problem spreads through the whole system. A company that keeps a few trucks and workers in reserve looks less efficient on an ordinary day, but it can absorb shocks that would cripple its fully loaded rival. Engineers designing bridges follow the same logic, building them to carry far more weight than they normally hold. In both cases, spare capacity is not wasted; a system with nothing left over is ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the most reliable choice for any growing business
efficient only until something unexpected happens
unable to make a profit even on ordinary days
easier to manage because nothing is left idle
a sign that its workers are not being paid enough
items.exp: 여유 트럭·인력이 없는 회사는 평소엔 완벽해 보이지만 고장이나 주문 폭주 같은 돌발 상황에 무너진다고 했어요. 따라서 남는 것이 없는 시스템은 예상치 못한 일이 생기기 전까지만 효율적이라는 ②가 알맞아요. ③은 평소에도 이익을 못 낸다는 뜻이라 글과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: In long-distance cycling races, riders rarely ride side by side for long. Instead, they form lines, one behind another, because of a simple effect called drafting. ① The rider at the front pushes through the air and leaves a pocket of calmer air behind him. ② A cyclist who stays close behind in this pocket faces much less wind and can use up to a third less energy at the same speed. ③ Modern racing bicycles are made of light materials such as carbon, and some weigh less than seven kilograms. ④ This is why team members take turns at the front, sharing the hardest work so that everyone saves strength for later. ⑤ Near the finish line, a team often shields its fastest rider inside the line until the final sprint, when the rider at last moves out into the wind.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 앞 선수 뒤에 붙어 바람 저항을 줄이는 드래프팅과 그 활용을 설명하는 글이에요. ③은 경주용 자전거의 재료와 무게에 관한 내용이라 공기 저항을 나눠 받는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
At sea level, water boils at 100°C. Many people assume that this number never changes, but the boiling point of water actually depends on the pressure of the air above it.

(A) A pressure cooker solves this problem by doing the opposite. Its tightly sealed lid traps steam inside the pot, which raises the pressure and allows the water to reach about 120°C before it boils.

(B) On a high mountain, for example, the air pressure is lower, so water starts boiling at a lower temperature, sometimes around 85°C. Climbers often find that their rice or noodles stay hard even after boiling for a long time.

(C) At this higher temperature, food cooks much faster. Tough meat or dried beans that would need hours in an ordinary pot can be ready in less than half the time, which also saves fuel.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 공기 압력에 따라 끓는점이 달라진다는 주어진 글 다음에, 높은 산에서는 낮은 온도에서 끓어 음식이 덜 익는다는 예(for example)인 (B)가 와요. (A)의 this problem이 (B)의 덜 익는 문제를 받아 압력솥을 소개하고, (C)의 this higher temperature가 (A)의 약 120°C를 가리켜요.

items.passage: Many of the clothes we wear today are made from synthetic materials such as polyester and nylon. These fabrics are cheap, light, and dry quickly, but they have a hidden cost. ( ① ) Every time they are washed, the rubbing of fabric against fabric breaks off thousands of tiny plastic threads called microfibers. ( ② ) As a result, they flow with the wastewater into rivers and eventually into the ocean. ( ③ ) There, small sea creatures such as plankton mistake them for food, and the plastic moves up the food chain to fish and, finally, to our dinner tables. ( ④ ) Fortunately, there are simple ways to reduce the problem. ( ⑤ ) Washing clothes less often, using cold water, and choosing shorter cycles all lower the number of fibers released.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Each of these fibers is far too small to be caught by most washing machine filters or water treatment plants.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 these fibers는 바로 앞의 microfibers를 가리키고, 필터에 걸러지지 않는다는 내용이 As a result, 폐수와 함께 강과 바다로 흘러간다는 결과로 이어져요. 그래서 ②가 알맞아요.

items.passage: In many parks, you can see narrow dirt trails cutting across the grass, often right next to a paved path. These trails appear because people choose the shortest or easiest way, and after enough feet have walked the same route, the grass wears away. Traditionally, park managers treated such trails as damage. They put up fences or signs telling people to stay on the official paths, but walkers often ignored them. Some planners now take a different approach. When a new park or campus opens, they plant grass everywhere and wait several months before building any paths. Then they look at where the grass has been worn down and pave those lines. The result is a set of paths that people actually use, because the paths were, in a sense, designed by the walkers themselves.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Instead of (A) ___ in advance where people should walk, some planners let the routes people actually take (B) ___ where paths are built.
items.exp: 예전에는 공식 길을 미리 정해 두고 따르게 했지만, 이제는 잔디가 닳은 자리를 보고 그곳에 길을 낸다고 했어요. 그래서 (A)는 미리 정한다는 deciding, (B)는 실제 다닌 길이 길의 위치를 정한다는 determine이 알맞아요. 새 방식은 오히려 사람들의 움직임을 관찰하므로 observing은 (A)에 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
When you look up at the night sky, it is natural to think that you are seeing the stars as they are right now. In fact, you are looking at the past. Light is the fastest thing in the universe, but it still needs time to travel. Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, so the Sun you see is the Sun of eight minutes ago. For distant stars, the delay is much (a)[longer]. The light from some of the stars visible to the naked eye left them hundreds or even thousands of years ago. This means that a star you see tonight might have already changed greatly, or even disappeared, and you would have no way of knowing it yet.

Far from being a problem, this delay is a great (b)[gift] to astronomers. Because light from more distant objects is older, powerful telescopes work like time machines. By observing galaxies that are extremely far away, scientists can see what the universe looked like when it was very (c)[young]. Comparing these faraway galaxies with nearby ones allows them to study how galaxies form and develop over billions of years, a process far too (d)[quick] for any human to watch directly. In a sense, the sky is a history book in which every page was written at a different time. The farther we look, the earlier the chapter we read. So the next time you gaze at the stars, remember that the night sky is not a single photograph but a (e)[collection] of messages sent across time.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Starlight: A Window into the Universe's Past
Why Stars Shine Brighter in Winter
How to Build Your Own Telescope at Home
The Sun: The Closest Star to Earth
items.exp: 별빛이 도달하는 데 시간이 걸리므로 밤하늘을 보는 것은 과거를 보는 것이고, 이 덕분에 천문학자들이 우주의 역사를 연구한다는 글이에요. ⑤는 별이 사라졌을 수도 있다는 일부 내용만 다루어 제목으로 알맞지 않아요.

items.exp: 은하가 수십억 년에 걸쳐 형성되고 발달하는 과정은 사람이 직접 지켜보기에는 너무 느린 것이므로 (d)의 quick을 slow로 바꿔야 해요. (b)는 Far from being a problem과 이어져 '선물'이 자연스러워요.

items.passage:
(A)
Minho had been the best player in his school's chess club for two years. He rarely lost, and younger members often gathered around his table to watch him play. One afternoon in September, a new student named Jaden walked into the club room. He was quiet and seemed a little nervous, but he politely asked Minho for a game. Minho agreed, expecting an easy win, and (a)[he] was right. Jaden lost in fewer than twenty moves.

(B)
In December, the club held its annual tournament, and in the final round Minho found himself facing Jaden. The game lasted almost two hours. Jaden played carefully and set a clever trap that Minho had never seen before. It was clear that (b)[he] had been preparing for this moment for months. Minho noticed the trap just in time, however, and went on to win. When the game ended, Jaden reached out to shake his hand, and Minho said, "Thank you." Jaden looked surprised. Minho smiled, and (c)[he] explained that their games had taught him to love learning again.

(C)
Instead of leaving, Jaden took out a small notebook and wrote down every move of the game. The next day, he came back and asked for another game. Again he lost, and again he wrote everything down. This went on for weeks, and Minho began to find it strange. "Why do you keep playing me if you always lose?" (d)[he] asked one day. Jaden smiled and answered, "Because losing to you teaches me more than beating anyone else."

(D)
Those words stayed with Minho for days. He realized that he himself had stopped learning long ago. He had been playing only against weaker members and feeling proud of his easy victories. That evening, (e)[he] opened his own old notebook, which had been gathering dust for months, and began studying his past games. He also started to play online against stronger opponents. He lost often, and it was painful, but slowly his game improved.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Jaden이 첫 판에 진 뒤, 떠나지 않고(Instead of leaving) 공책에 수를 적는 (C)가 이어져요. Jaden의 말(Those words)이 Minho에게 남아 다시 공부하게 되는 (D)가 온 다음, 12월 대회 결승에서 두 사람이 만나는 (B)로 끝나요.
