items.passage:
Dear Editor,

I am a teacher at Riverside Middle School, and I am writing about the article "Students Turn Empty Lot into Garden," which appeared in last Saturday's paper. I was delighted to see our students' hard work recognized, and many parents have told me how much they enjoyed the story. However, I noticed an error that I hope you can fix. The article said that the garden project was led by students from Riverside High School, but it was actually planned and carried out by our eighth graders at Riverside Middle School. The students are proud of what they achieved, and some of them were disappointed that their school's name was not mentioned. I would be grateful if you could print a correction in an upcoming issue so that their efforts are properly credited.

Sincerely,
Laura Kim
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 학생들의 정원 가꾸기 활동을 기사로 다뤄 줄 것을 제안하려고
기사에 잘못 실린 학교 이름의 정정을 요청하려고
기사에 대한 학부모들의 감사 인사를 전하려고
신문사의 학교 방문 취재 일정을 문의하려고
items.exp: 기사에 정원 프로젝트를 고등학교 학생들이 했다고 잘못 실렸다고 지적한 뒤, 다음 호에 정정 기사를 실어 달라고 부탁하고 있어요. 그래서 ②가 알맞아요. 기사는 이미 실렸으므로 ①은 답이 아니고, 학부모 반응은 글의 도입에 쓰인 내용일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: For almost two weeks, Sungmin had spent every evening at the dining table, working on a thousand-piece jigsaw puzzle of a harbor at sunset. Piece by piece, the boats, the orange sky, and the tiny houses on the hill had come together. On Friday night, only one gap remained, right in the middle of the setting sun. Sungmin searched the box, then the floor, then under every chair. He shook out the tablecloth and even checked his pockets. Nothing. "After all that work," he muttered, dropping onto the sofa and pushing his hair back with both hands. Just then, his sister's cat, Mochi, rolled over on the rug beside him. Something small and orange was stuck to the fur on her back. Sungmin carefully pulled it free, ran to the table, and pressed it into place. The picture was complete. He grinned and lifted Mochi into the air. "You were hiding it all along!"
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Sungmin의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 마지막 한 조각을 아무리 찾아도 없자 Sungmin은 소파에 주저앉아 투덜대지만, 고양이 털에 붙은 조각을 찾아 퍼즐을 완성하고 활짝 웃어요. 그래서 frustrated → delighted인 ④가 알맞아요. 처음부터 자신만만하다가 걱정하게 된 것이 아니므로 ⑤는 틀려요.

items.passage: When a neighbor's noise keeps us awake, many of us choose one of two responses. We either suffer in silence, growing angrier each night, or we go straight to the building manager or even the police. I believe that, in most cases, the first step should be a polite conversation with the neighbor. Often the people making the noise simply do not know how far the sound travels. A family whose child runs around at nine o'clock may have no idea that the person below goes to bed early for work. A friendly knock and a calm explanation give them a chance to fix the problem without feeling attacked. In contrast, a complaint through a third party makes neighbors feel accused and can turn a small problem into a long conflict. Talking face to face may feel uncomfortable at first, but it is usually the quickest way to quiet nights and good relations.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 이웃 간 소음 문제는 먼저 이웃과 직접 정중하게 대화해 풀어야 한다.
건물을 지을 때 층간 소음을 막는 설계를 의무화해야 한다.
소음 문제는 관리인을 통해 공식적으로 처리해야 한다.
밤늦은 시간에는 아이들이 뛰지 않도록 가르쳐야 한다.
이웃의 소음은 서로 이해하고 참으며 지내야 한다.
items.exp: 필자는 소음 문제가 생기면 참거나 관리인·경찰에 바로 알리기보다 먼저 이웃과 정중하게 대화해야 한다고 주장해요. 제3자를 통한 항의는 갈등을 키운다고 했으므로 ③은 반대이고, 말없이 참는 것도 화만 키운다고 했으므로 ⑤도 답이 아니에요.

items.passage: Imagine you are reading a book at home and someone walks into the room every few minutes to tell you something small: the weather has changed, a friend liked your photo, a store is having a sale. You would soon find it impossible to follow the story. Yet this is exactly what happens when our phones are allowed to send us alerts all day. Each notification is [a guest who never knocks]. It arrives whenever it wants, regardless of what we are doing, and it expects our attention right away. After an interruption, it can take several minutes to return fully to a task. Multiply that by dozens of alerts a day, and a large part of our focus is lost. The solution is not to throw away our phones but to decide for ourselves when we will open the door, by turning off unnecessary alerts and checking messages at set times.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a guest who never knocks]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a friendly reminder that helps us manage our daily schedule
a message that we must answer before anyone else does
a visitor whose news is usually more important than our work
an alert that we can easily ignore without any effect
an interruption that enters our attention without asking permission
items.exp: 바로 뒤에서 알림은 우리가 무엇을 하든 상관없이 원할 때 찾아와 즉시 주의를 요구한다고 설명해요. 즉 허락 없이 주의를 비집고 들어오는 방해라는 뜻이에요. 알림 하나하나가 집중력을 빼앗는다고 했으므로 ④는 반대 내용이에요.

items.passage: Suppose a country ranks all of its schools by their students' average test scores. When researchers look at the very top of the list, they often find many small schools. This might suggest that small schools are simply better. Strangely, however, the very bottom of the list is also full of small schools. The reason has little to do with teaching. In a school with only twenty students, a few unusually strong or weak students can push the average far up or down. In a school with two thousand students, such cases are balanced by many others, so the average stays close to the middle. The same thing happens with coins. Toss one five times, and getting heads every time is not so rare; toss it five hundred times, and the result will almost always be close to half heads. Small groups naturally produce extreme results, so we should be careful about reading too much into them.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: advantages of small schools over large ones
ways to make tests fairer for all students
why small groups tend to show extreme results
the role of luck in coin-tossing games
how teachers can raise students' average scores
items.exp: 작은 학교가 순위의 맨 위와 맨 아래에 모두 많은 이유는 학생 수가 적으면 몇 명만으로도 평균이 크게 흔들리기 때문이라고 설명하고, 동전 던지기 예를 더해 작은 집단은 극단적인 결과를 내기 쉽다고 정리해요. 그래서 ③이 주제예요. ①은 글이 부정하는 해석이고, ④는 예시만 빌린 오답이에요.

items.passage: In the early years of professional basketball, there was no limit on how long a team could hold the ball. A team that took the lead could simply pass the ball around and refuse to shoot, while the other team chased it helplessly. Fans paid to see exciting play but often watched players standing still. In one famous game in 1950, the final score was just 19 to 18. To solve the problem, the professional league in the United States introduced a new rule in 1954: a team had to attempt a shot within 24 seconds of getting the ball. The effect was dramatic. Scores rose sharply, games became faster, and more fans came to watch. Today, almost every basketball league in the world uses some form of this shot clock. A single rule about time turned a slow, cautious game into the fast sport we know today.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Fans Prefer Defense to Offense
The Lowest Scores in Basketball History
How Players Train to Shoot Faster
Rules That Protect Players from Injury
items.exp: 공을 오래 돌리며 시간을 끌던 농구에 24초 안에 슛해야 한다는 규칙이 생기면서 경기가 빨라지고 관중이 늘었다는 글이에요. 그래서 ①이 제목으로 알맞아요. ③은 19 대 18이라는 예시 하나만 다룬 오답이에요.

items.passage: Tomas Lindqvist was born in 1902 in a small fishing village in northern Sweden. As a boy, he spent hours watching the wooden bridge near his home shake in winter storms, and he became determined to build bridges that would stand firm. After studying engineering in Stockholm, he worked for a railway company for ten years. In 1938, he designed his first steel bridge, which crossed a wide river and was praised for its light and simple shape. During his career, he completed more than forty bridges across Scandinavia. Lindqvist believed that bridges should be beautiful as well as strong, and he often worked closely with local artists to choose their colors. In his later years, he taught at a technical university, where he wrote a textbook that some students still use today. He died in 1978, leaving his notebooks to the library of his home village.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 어린 시절 집 근처 나무다리가 겨울 폭풍에 흔들리는 것을 지켜보았다.
스톡홀름에서 공학을 공부한 후 철도 회사에서 10년간 일했다.
1938년에 설계한 첫 철교는 가볍고 단순한 형태로 칭찬받았다.
다리의 색을 정할 때 지역 예술가들의 의견을 거의 듣지 않았다.
items.exp: 'he often worked closely with local artists to choose their colors'라고 했으므로 다리 색을 정할 때 지역 예술가들과 긴밀히 협력했어요. 나머지는 모두 글의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: When the first steam-powered road vehicles appeared in Britain in the nineteenth century, many people ①[were] alarmed. The heavy machines frightened horses, damaged roads, and seemed likely to cause accidents. In 1865, Parliament passed a law ②[requires] such vehicles to travel no faster than four miles per hour in the countryside and two miles per hour in towns. Even more surprisingly, a person had to walk about sixty yards ahead of each vehicle, ③[carrying] a red flag to warn riders and horse-drawn carriages. Because of these rules, the new machines could hardly move faster than a person on foot, ④[which] made them almost useless for long trips. Some historians believe that the law slowed the development of motor vehicles in Britain while inventors in other countries ⑤[moved] ahead. It was not until 1896 that the speed limit was raised and a person walking in front was no longer required.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ②는 문장의 동사 passed가 이미 있고 a law를 뒤에서 꾸며야 하므로 requires가 아니라 현재분사 requiring(또는 that required)이 되어야 해요. ①은 복수 주어 many people에 맞는 were, ③은 동시 동작의 분사구문, ④는 앞 절 전체를 받는 관계대명사, ⑤는 while절의 과거 동사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: When students are put into groups for a project, teachers often hope that everyone will contribute equally. In reality, this rarely happens without some planning. Without clear roles, a few active members tend to ①[take over] the work, while others quietly fall behind. This is not always because some students are lazy; often, they simply do not know where they can be ②[useful]. Giving each member a specific role, such as researcher, writer, or presenter, can solve much of this problem. When people know exactly what is expected of them, they feel more ③[responsible] for the result. Roles also make it easier to notice when someone needs help, since each part of the work has a clear owner. Teachers who rotate roles between projects allow students to ④[develop] a wider range of skills. In short, clear roles turn a group of individuals into a real team, where cooperation is ⑤[discouraged] by design rather than left to chance.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 분명한 역할이 개인들을 진짜 팀으로 만든다고 했으므로 협력은 우연에 맡겨지지 않고 계획적으로 '장려되는' 것이에요. ⑤ discouraged를 encouraged로 바꿔야 해요. ① 몇몇이 일을 떠맡는다, ③ 책임감을 더 느낀다 등 나머지는 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: In many cultures, a gift is never just a gift. When someone gives you a present, you usually feel that you should give something back, perhaps not right away, but someday. In Korea, neighbors who receive a plate of rice cakes traditionally return the plate with some food of their own on it rather than empty. Similar customs exist around the world, from wedding gifts that are carefully recorded so they can be matched later to holiday cards sent in reply to cards received. Anthropologists point out that these exchanges are not mainly about the objects themselves. They create a chain of small debts that keeps people connected over time. If everyone paid back every gift immediately and exactly, the relationship would end there. In this sense, gift-giving works because it leaves people slightly ___ to each other.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 선물 교환은 '작은 빚의 사슬'을 만들어 사람들을 계속 이어 주며, 즉시 정확히 갚으면 관계가 끝난다고 했어요. 그러니 선물은 사람들을 서로에게 약간 '빚진' 상태로 남겨 둔다는 indebted가 알맞아요. equal은 정확히 갚아 끝나는 상태에 가까워 반대예요.

items.passage: Imagine two drivers who leave the same party late at night, both a little too tired to drive safely. Each takes his eyes off the road for a moment on the way home. The first driver reaches home without any problem. The second, at exactly that moment, fails to see a child who has run into the street and injures her. Most of us would judge the second driver far more harshly, and the law would likely punish him much more severely. Yet if we ask what each driver actually did, the answer is the same: they made identical choices, and only the presence of the child made the difference. Philosophers call this puzzle "moral luck." We like to believe that people should be blamed only for what is under their control, but in practice our judgments ___. The puzzle does not mean that the second driver is innocent; rather, it suggests that the first is not as blameless as we tend to think.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: depend entirely on the intentions people had in mind
become stricter when people are honest about mistakes
are shaped mainly by the laws of the country we live in
are strongly influenced by outcomes no one could have chosen
focus on how often a person has made the same choice
items.exp: 두 운전자는 똑같은 선택을 했는데 아이가 우연히 나타났느냐에 따라 평가가 크게 달라진다고 했어요. 통제할 수 있는 것에만 책임을 묻는다고 믿지만 실제로는 아무도 선택하지 않은 결과에 크게 좌우된다는 ④가 알맞아요. ①은 의도만으로 판단한다는 뜻이라 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: The umbrella has a much longer history than most people think. ① Over three thousand years ago, umbrellas were used in ancient Egypt and China, but mainly to provide shade from the sun rather than protection from rain. ② In those societies, they were often a sign of high rank, carried by servants to shade kings and nobles. ③ Today, folding umbrellas are so cheap that many people simply buy a new one when they forget theirs at home. ④ The Chinese are believed to have been among the first to make umbrellas waterproof, by coating paper with wax or oil. ⑤ In Europe, umbrellas for rain did not become common until the eighteenth century, when they slowly changed from a luxury item into an everyday object. At first, men who carried them in the streets of London were laughed at, but by the end of the century, the umbrella had become a familiar part of city life.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 우산이 햇빛 가리개에서 신분의 상징, 방수 우산, 유럽의 일상용품으로 변해 온 역사를 시대 순으로 다루는 글이에요. ③은 오늘날 접이식 우산이 싸다는 내용이라 역사의 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
In the early 1800s, a French army officer named Charles Barbier invented a system of raised dots that soldiers could read with their fingers in the dark, without lighting a lamp that might reveal their position.

(A) Over the next few years, Braille reshaped it into cells of just six dots, each standing for a letter, a number, or a punctuation mark. The system that bears his name is still used by blind readers around the world.

(B) The army, however, found the system too difficult and soon gave it up. Barbier believed it could still be useful to another group of people, so he presented it at a school for blind children in Paris.

(C) There, a young student named Louis Braille quickly saw both its promise and its problems. Each symbol used up to twelve dots, too many to feel with a single fingertip, and the dots stood for sounds rather than letters.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 군대가 이 체계를 너무 어렵다고 포기하자 바바에가 맹아 학교에 소개했다는 (B)가 먼저 와요. (C)의 There는 (B)의 파리 맹아 학교를 가리키며 루이 브라유가 장단점을 알아보고, (A)에서 브라유가 그것을 여섯 점 체계로 바꾸었으므로 (B)-(C)-(A)예요.

items.passage: Sand dunes may look like they stay in one place, but many of them are actually moving. ( ① ) The movement begins with the wind. ( ② ) When wind blows across a dune, it picks up loose grains of sand on the gentle side facing the wind and carries them up toward the top. ( ③ ) Most grains do not fly far; they bounce along the surface in short hops. ( ④ ) When they reach the top, they pile up until the sand becomes too steep and slides down the other side, which is much steeper. ( ⑤ ) Some dunes move more than ten meters a year, burying roads and even whole villages in their path. For this reason, people living near deserts often plant rows of grasses and shrubs to hold the sand in place.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

As this process repeats over and over, the whole dune slowly travels in the direction of the wind.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 this process는 모래가 바람을 받는 쪽에서 꼭대기로 옮겨져 반대편으로 미끄러져 내리는 과정을 가리켜요. 그 과정이 반복되어 모래 언덕 전체가 이동한다는 내용 뒤에 '해마다 10미터 넘게 움직이는 언덕도 있다'가 이어져야 자연스러우므로 ⑤가 알맞아요.

items.passage: What happens when people find a lost wallet? In a large study, researchers handed in more than 17,000 "lost" wallets at banks, hotels, and post offices in 40 countries, telling the staff that they had found them on the street. Each wallet held a card with an email address so that the owner could be contacted. Some wallets contained no money, while others contained about thirteen dollars. Most economists predicted that wallets with money would be returned less often, since keeping the cash would be tempting. The results showed the opposite. In almost every country, wallets with money were returned more often than empty ones, and in the countries tested with larger amounts, return rates rose even further. Follow-up surveys suggested a reason: keeping someone else's money would make people feel like thieves, and that feeling grew stronger as the amount increased.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Contrary to what many experts expected, people were (A) ___ likely to return a lost wallet that contained money, partly because keeping it would damage their view of themselves as (B) ___ people.
items.exp: 돈이 든 지갑이 빈 지갑보다 더 자주 돌아왔으므로 (A)는 more, 남의 돈을 가지면 도둑처럼 느껴진다는 것은 자신을 정직한 사람으로 보는 생각이 깨진다는 뜻이므로 (B)는 honest예요. 경제학자들의 예측과 같은 less는 결과와 반대예요.

items.passage:
For most of history, painters could not simply pick up their colors and walk outside. Paint had to be made by hand in the studio, by grinding colored minerals into powder and mixing them with oil. The mixture dried quickly, so artists stored it in small bags made from pig bladders, which were (a)[difficult] to carry and often burst. As a result, most landscapes were painted indoors from sketches and memory.

This changed in 1841, when an American painter named John Goffe Rand invented a small, squeezable metal tube for paint. The tube kept paint fresh for a long time and could be closed again after use. Before long, paint makers were selling ready-made colors in tubes, and artists could pack a whole box of them into a bag. For the first time, painting outdoors became truly (b)[practical].

Young French painters, later known as the Impressionists, took full advantage of this freedom. They set up their easels in fields, on riverbanks, and in busy city streets, trying to capture the changing light of a particular moment. Working outside forced them to paint (c)[quickly], with short, visible brushstrokes, because the sun and shadows would not wait. Their bright, rough paintings shocked many critics, who were used to the smooth surfaces of studio work. Pierre-Auguste Renoir is often quoted as saying that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. The story shows that new art does not come only from new ideas; sometimes a simple tool (d)[limits] what artists can imagine and do, opening the way to a new (e)[style].
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How the Impressionists Were Rejected by Critics
A Small Tube That Changed the History of Painting
Why Studio Paintings Look Smoother Than Outdoor Ones
The Art of Grinding Minerals into Colors
Light and Shadow: The Science Behind Landscapes
items.exp: 1841년에 발명된 물감 튜브 덕분에 야외 그림이 가능해졌고, 이것이 인상주의라는 새로운 화풍으로 이어졌다는 글이에요. 그래서 '회화의 역사를 바꾼 작은 튜브'가 알맞아요. ①·③은 글의 일부 내용만 다뤄요.

items.exp: 단순한 도구가 새로운 화풍으로 가는 길을 열었다고 했으므로 도구는 화가가 상상하고 할 수 있는 것을 '넓혀 준다'는 뜻이 되어야 해요. (d) limits를 expands로 바꿔야 해요. (a) 돼지 방광 주머니는 들고 다니기 어려웠고, (c) 빛이 기다려 주지 않아 빨리 그려야 했다는 것은 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Clara had been practicing for the city youth orchestra audition for nearly six months. The violin she played was old and a little worn, but it was special to her because it had belonged to her mother as a girl. Two days before the audition, Clara left the instrument on a chair while she went to get a glass of water. At that moment, her little brother Leo came running into the room, chasing the cat. (a)[He] bumped into the chair, and the violin fell to the floor with a terrible crack. Its neck had snapped.

(B)
The next evening, Clara knocked on Mr. Ortiz's door, hardly daring to hope. (b)[He] smiled and handed her the violin. The neck was back in place, and only a thin line showed where the break had been. "It is not as perfect as before," he said, "but a crack is not always the end of a story." Clara played a scale. To her surprise, the sound was as warm as ever, perhaps even a little richer.

(C)
At the audition, Clara walked onto the stage with the repaired violin. Her hands were shaking at first, but as soon as she began to play, she forgot about the crack and thought only of the music. A week later, a letter arrived: she had been accepted into the orchestra. On the night of her first concert, she saved a seat in the front row for Mr. Ortiz, and (c)[he] clapped louder than anyone in the hall.

(D)
Clara picked up the pieces and burst into tears. Leo, pale and silent, kept saying that he was sorry. Their mother called the music shop downtown, but the repairman there said the violin could not be fixed in less than three weeks. Then she thought of their neighbor, Mr. Ortiz, a retired carpenter who had repaired instruments for local musicians for years. Clara carried the broken violin next door. (d)[The old man] turned it over slowly in his hands, studying the break. Finally, (e)[he] looked up and said, "Come back tomorrow evening."
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 바이올린 목이 부러진 (A) 뒤에는 Clara가 울고 이웃 Ortiz 씨를 찾아가 '내일 저녁에 오라'는 말을 듣는 (D)가 와요. 'The next evening'으로 고친 바이올린을 받는 (B)가 이어지고, 그 바이올린으로 오디션에 합격하는 (C)가 마지막이에요.

items.exp: (D)에서 시내 악기점 수리공은 3주 안에는 고칠 수 없다고 했어요. 그래서 일주일 안에 고칠 수 있다는 ⑤가 글과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 각각 (A), (A), (B), (C)의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Members of the Lakeside Skating Club,

I hope you have all enjoyed a wonderful season on the ice. I am writing to let you know about an important change. Last week, our technicians found a serious problem with the cooling system under the main rink at Lakeside Ice Arena. To repair it safely, the arena will be closed from January 10 to January 24. During this period, no lessons or free skating sessions can be held there. Fortunately, the Northgate Sports Center has agreed to share its rink with us. All Tuesday and Thursday practices will move there at the usual times, and a free shuttle bus will leave our parking lot thirty minutes before each practice. Please check your email for the updated schedule. We are sorry for the trouble and look forward to welcoming you back soon.

Best regards,
Ellen Moore
Club Director
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 새 냉각 장치 구입을 위한 기부를 부탁하려고
빙상장 수리로 인한 임시 휴관과 연습 장소 변경을 알리려고
스케이트 클럽의 시즌 마무리 행사에 초대하려고
items.exp: 냉각 장치 고장으로 빙상장이 1월 10일부터 24일까지 문을 닫고(the arena will be closed), 그동안 화요일·목요일 연습은 Northgate 스포츠 센터로 옮긴다고 알리고 있어요. 그래서 ③이 알맞아요. 셔틀버스는 바뀐 장소로 가는 방법을 안내한 것이에요.

items.passage: Hana had been on the whale-watching boat for almost three hours, and all she had seen was gray water. The guide kept pointing at the horizon, but every time, it turned out to be just a wave. Hana yawned, leaned against the rail, and checked the time on her phone again. Her little brother had fallen asleep on a bench, and she was beginning to wish she had stayed in bed too. Then, without warning, the sea beside the boat seemed to explode. A huge humpback whale shot out of the water, twisted in the air, and crashed back down, sending cold spray over the deck. Hana's mouth fell open. She grabbed her brother's arm to wake him, unable to take her eyes off the spot where the giant had disappeared. "Did you see that?" she cried.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Hana의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 세 시간 동안 회색 바다만 보며 하품하고 시간을 확인하는 모습에서 지루함이 드러나요. 그러다 혹등고래가 물 위로 솟구치자 입이 떡 벌어지고 눈을 떼지 못하며 소리쳤으므로 놀라워하는 마음으로 바뀌었어요. 그래서 bored → amazed가 알맞아요.

items.passage: At the start of a long race, almost every runner feels fresh and strong. The crowd is cheering, and it is tempting to rush ahead of the others. Yet runners who start too fast usually pay for it later. Their bodies burn through stored energy early, and in the final kilometers their legs grow heavy and their pace drops sharply. Experienced marathoners therefore follow an old piece of advice: [run the first half with your head, the rest with your heart]. In the early stage, they hold back on purpose, checking their watches and keeping a steady pace even when they feel they could go faster. Only later, when their bodies begin to hurt and quitting starts to look attractive, do they rely on sheer determination to push through to the finish line.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [run the first half with your head, the rest with your heart]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Plan the route carefully before the race and ignore the crowd.
Start with careful control and finish by relying on willpower.
Run fast at the beginning while you still have plenty of energy.
Think about your family and friends throughout the race.
Change your pace often so that other runners cannot follow you.
items.exp: 경험 많은 선수들은 초반에는 일부러 속도를 억제하며 시계를 보고 일정한 속도를 지키고, 후반에 몸이 아플 때는 순수한 의지로 버틴다고 했어요. 그래서 '처음에는 신중하게 조절하고 끝은 의지력으로 달린다'가 알맞아요. 초반에 빨리 달리라는 ③은 글의 조언과 반대예요.

items.passage: Many parents let their children win every game they play together, whether it is a card game, a race in the park, or a round of chess. They want their kids to feel happy and confident. Yet always letting a child win may take away an important lesson. Losing is unpleasant, but it teaches children that effort does not always bring immediate success and that disappointment can be handled. A child who never loses at home may cry or quit when a classmate beats him at school. This does not mean that parents should play as hard as they can against a five-year-old. Instead, they can adjust the game so that the child wins sometimes and loses sometimes, and then talk calmly about how losing feels. Through these small, safe losses, children learn to accept defeat and try again.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 아이와 게임할 때 부모는 늘 최선을 다해 이겨야 한다.
아이의 자신감을 위해 게임에서 늘 이기게 해 주어야 한다.
학교에서의 경쟁은 아이의 정서 발달에 해롭다.
아이가 게임에서 가끔 지게 해 패배를 받아들이는 법을 배우게 해야 한다.
카드 게임보다 야외 놀이가 아이의 발달에 더 도움이 된다.
items.exp: 늘 이기게 해 주면 중요한 교훈을 빼앗을 수 있으니, 가끔은 지게 하고 그 기분을 차분히 이야기하며 작고 안전한 패배를 통해 패배를 받아들이고 다시 도전하는 법을 배우게 하라는 것이 요지예요. 다섯 살 아이를 상대로 전력을 다하라는 뜻은 아니라고 했으므로 ①은 지나쳐요.

items.passage: A slime mold is a strange yellow creature that lives on rotting logs in the forest. It has no brain, no eyes, and not even separate cells; it is basically one giant cell that can spread out like a thin, moving net. Yet it can do things that seem to require intelligence. When scientists placed oat flakes, its favorite food, at two ends of a maze, the slime mold at first stretched into every passage. Soon, however, it pulled back from the dead ends and kept only the shortest tube connecting the food. In another experiment, pieces of food were arranged like the cities around Tokyo, and the slime mold grew a network of tubes surprisingly similar to the region's real train lines. Researchers are now studying how such a simple organism solves these problems, hoping to design better transport and computer networks.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: reasons slime molds prefer to live on rotting logs
dangers that slime molds pose to forest trees
the history of building train lines around Tokyo
ways brain cells send messages to each other
the ability of a brainless organism to find efficient routes
items.exp: 뇌도 없는 하나의 거대한 세포인 점균이 미로에서 가장 짧은 길만 남기고, 도쿄 주변 철도망과 비슷한 연결망을 만든다는 내용이에요. 그래서 뇌 없는 생물이 효율적인 경로를 찾는 능력이 주제예요. ③은 실험 비교 대상일 뿐이고, ①은 첫 문장의 세부 정보예요.

items.passage: Long before humans began to plant crops, some ants were already farmers. Leafcutter ants, found in the forests of Central and South America, spend their days cutting pieces of leaves and carrying them back to their underground nests in long lines. Surprisingly, they do not eat the leaves. Instead, they chew them into a soft paste and use it to grow a special fungus, which is the colony's main food. The ants take great care of their gardens. They remove harmful molds, and they even carry a kind of helpful bacteria on their bodies that acts like a natural medicine against disease. Different ants have different jobs: large ants cut and carry leaves, while tiny ones tend the fungus deep inside the nest. A single colony can include millions of ants, all working together to keep their farm alive. In many ways, their system is as organized as a human farm.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Ants Prefer Leaves to Other Foods
Harmful Molds: The Enemy of the Forest
Tiny Farmers Under the Forest Floor
How Humans Learned Farming from Insects
The Largest Insects in South America
items.exp: 잎꾼개미가 잎을 먹는 것이 아니라 잎으로 균을 길러 먹으며, 역할을 나누어 체계적으로 '농사'를 짓는다는 글이에요. 그래서 '숲 바닥 아래의 작은 농부들'이 알맞아요. 개미는 잎을 먹지 않으므로 ①은 틀리고, ④는 글에 없는 내용이에요.

items.passage:
Greenhill Youth Paper Airplane Contest 2027

Fold, throw, and fly! Show us how far and how long your paper airplane can fly.

• When: Saturday, October 9, 2027, 1:00 p.m. – 5:00 p.m.

Categories

Rules

Sign up at the sports center's front desk by October 1.
items.q: Greenhill Youth Paper Airplane Contest 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 테이프는 사용할 수 있지만 풀은 사용할 수 없다.
신청은 스포츠 센터 안내 데스크에서 한다.
items.exp: 규칙에 테이프와 풀 모두 사용할 수 없다(Tape and glue are not allowed)고 했으므로 ④가 안내문과 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 장소와 시간, 대상, 참가비, 신청 방법과 일치해요.

items.passage: If you look at photographs from the 1800s, you will notice that almost nobody is smiling. Many people think this is because life ①[being] hard back then, but the real reasons are more interesting. Early cameras needed a long time to capture an image, so people had to stay perfectly still for several seconds or even longer. Holding a natural smile for that long ②[is] very difficult, and a smile that slowly faded would look blurry. In addition, photographs were expensive, and most people had their picture taken only a few times in their lives. They wanted to look serious and dignified, much like the people in the formal paintings ③[that] had come before photography. As cameras became faster and cheaper in the early 1900s, people began taking pictures of everyday moments, and smiling ④[gradually] became the normal way to pose. Today, it seems strange to see a family picture ⑤[taken] without a smile.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ① because 뒤에는 주어와 동사를 갖춘 절이 와야 하므로 being을 was로 고쳐야 해요. ② 동명사구 주어 Holding a natural smile은 단수라 is가 맞고, ③ that은 the formal paintings를 받는 관계대명사, ④ gradually는 동사 became을 꾸미는 부사, ⑤ taken은 사진이 찍힌 것이므로 과거분사가 맞아요.

items.passage: Have you ever noticed that milk and eggs are almost always found at the back of the supermarket? This is not an accident. These are items that most shoppers need on nearly every visit, so placing them far from the entrance ①[forces] customers to walk past many other products. Along the way, shoppers often see things they had not planned to buy and put them in their carts. Stores also place the most expensive brands at eye level, where they are ②[easiest] to notice, while cheaper options are put on the lowest shelves. Sweets and small snacks are usually displayed near the checkout, where people waiting in line have time to feel ③[tempted]. Even the music matters: slow background music can make shoppers walk more ④[slowly] and spend more time in the store. Knowing these tricks can help you shop more wisely. A shopping list, for example, makes it ⑤[harder] to stick to what you really need.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 가게의 판매 전략을 알면 더 현명하게 쇼핑할 수 있다고 했으므로, 장보기 목록은 꼭 필요한 것만 사는 일을 '더 쉽게' 해 줘요. ⑤ harder를 easier로 바꿔야 해요. ① 입구에서 멀리 두어 걷게 만들고, ③ 계산대 앞에서 사고 싶어진다는 것은 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: Why can't you tickle yourself? Run your fingers along the bottom of your own foot, and you will probably feel very little, yet the same touch from a friend can make you scream with laughter. The answer lies in how the brain handles our own movements. Whenever you move, a part of your brain receives a copy of the movement command and uses it to guess what you are about to feel. Because the sensation of your own fingers is completely ___, the brain turns down its reaction to it. A friend's touch, on the other hand, comes without warning, so the brain treats it as important news. This system is actually useful: it allows us to notice an insect landing on our arm even while we are busy scratching our own head.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 뇌는 움직임 명령의 사본으로 곧 느낄 감각을 미리 짐작하므로, 자기 손가락의 감촉은 완전히 예측 가능해서 반응을 줄인다고 했어요. 친구의 손길은 예고 없이 온다는 대조도 단서예요. unfamiliar(낯선)는 오히려 친구의 손길에 해당해요.

items.passage: Many people imagine that translation is simply a matter of replacing each word with its partner in another language, as if every language were just a different set of labels for the same things. Translators know better. The Korean word jeong, for example, refers to a warm, lasting bond that slowly grows between people who share their lives, but no single English word captures it; affection sounds too light, and love sounds too strong. Even everyday words cause trouble. English uses the one word rice for what Korean divides into the plant in the field, the raw grain, and the cooked meal on the table. A translator must therefore decide, again and again, which part of a meaning to keep and which to let go, knowing that something is always lost and something new is often added. For this reason, every translation is, in a sense, ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a perfect copy that can fully replace the original text
a list of labels that match each other one by one
a series of choices that reveals the translator's judgment
a simple task that machines will soon finish for us
a failure that readers should avoid by learning the original language
items.exp: 정이나 쌀처럼 낱말이 일대일로 대응하지 않으므로 번역가는 의미의 어느 부분을 살리고 버릴지 계속 결정해야 한다고 했어요. 그래서 번역은 번역가의 판단이 드러나는 선택의 연속이에요. ②는 글이 반박하는 통념이고, ⑤처럼 원어를 배워 번역을 피하라는 주장은 글에 없어요.

items.passage: Honey is one of the few foods that can last almost forever. Jars of honey found in ancient tombs thousands of years old were reportedly still safe to eat. ① One reason is that honey contains very little water, so the bacteria that spoil most foods cannot survive in it. ② Honey is also slightly acidic, which makes it an even harder place for germs to grow. ③ In addition, bees add a natural substance to the nectar that slowly produces a small amount of hydrogen peroxide, a well-known germ killer. ④ Bees must visit millions of flowers to make a single kilogram of honey, which is why it was once considered a luxury. ⑤ Because of these properties, honey has been used for centuries not only as a sweetener but also to protect wounds from infection. However, if honey is left open to moist air, it can take in water and begin to spoil, so it should be kept in a tightly closed container.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 꿀이 거의 상하지 않는 이유(적은 수분, 산성, 과산화수소)와 그 성질의 활용, 보관법을 다루는 글이에요. ④는 꿀을 만드는 데 많은 꽃이 필요해 귀했다는 내용이라 꿀이 상하지 않는 이유라는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
Tall buildings are not as still as they look. On a windy day, the top of a skyscraper can move back and forth by more than half a meter.

(A) To reduce this problem, engineers place a huge weight, sometimes as heavy as several hundred tons, near the top of some buildings. When the building leans one way, this weight swings the other way.

(B) By moving against the building's motion, it cancels out much of the swaying. The building still moves a little, but the people inside can hardly feel it.

(C) This movement is actually planned. A building that bends slightly is less likely to crack than one that is completely stiff. Still, if the swaying is too strong, people on the upper floors may feel dizzy or even sick.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 고층 건물이 흔들린다는 주어진 글 뒤에 This movement로 받아 의도된 것이지만 너무 심하면 어지러울 수 있다는 (C)가 와요. 이 문제(this problem)를 줄이려고 거대한 추를 단다는 (A)가 이어지고, 그 추(it)가 반대로 움직여 흔들림을 상쇄한다는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Water alone cannot wash grease off your hands, because oil and water do not mix. ( ① ) Soap solves this problem thanks to the special shape of its molecules. Each soap molecule has two very different ends. One end is attracted to water and easily mixes with it. ( ② ) When you wash your hands, these oil-loving ends push into the grease and surround tiny drops of it, while the water-loving ends stay pointed outward. ( ③ ) The result is a small ball with the grease trapped inside and water-loving ends covering the outside. ( ④ ) Because its surface is attracted to water, the whole ball can be carried away when you rinse. ( ⑤ ) This is also why you should rub your hands for at least twenty seconds: rubbing breaks the grease into drops small enough to be surrounded.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

The other end, however, is attracted to oil and grease and tends to avoid water.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 The other end는 앞에서 말한 물을 좋아하는 한쪽 끝(One end)과 짝을 이루므로 그 뒤에 와야 해요. 또 ② 뒤의 these oil-loving ends는 주어진 문장에서 처음 나오는 기름을 좋아하는 끝을 가리키므로 ②가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Gardeners who grow seedlings indoors often notice that the young plants become tall and thin, then fall over when they are moved outside. One simple way to prevent this surprises many people: gently brushing the tops of the seedlings with a hand or a piece of cardboard for a minute each day. Scientists have found that plants can sense being touched, bent, or shaken by the wind. In response, they slow their upward growth and put more energy into building thicker, tougher stems. A plant that grows on a windy hill, for example, is usually shorter and sturdier than the same kind of plant raised in a quiet greenhouse. This reaction makes sense, because a short, strong stem is less likely to snap in a storm. In other words, a little rough treatment prepares plants for the real world.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

When plants are physically (A) ___, they respond by growing in a more (B) ___ form that helps them resist damage.
items.exp: 식물은 손길이나 바람에 건드려지고 흔들릴 때(disturbed) 위로 자라는 것을 늦추고 줄기를 굵고 단단하게 만들어 키 작고 튼튼한(compact) 모습이 된다고 했어요. 조용한 온실처럼 보호받는(protected) 식물은 오히려 가늘고 길게 자라므로 ①, ②는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Over the past two hundred years, the average human life span has roughly doubled in many countries. When people think about the reasons for this, they usually imagine modern hospitals, skilled surgeons, and powerful medicines. These have certainly saved many lives. Yet historians of public health point out that some of the (a)[greatest] gains came from something far less exciting: clean water and proper sewers.

In the crowded cities of the nineteenth century, human waste often flowed into the same rivers and wells that people drank from. Diseases such as cholera and typhoid spread quickly, killing thousands of people, especially young children. Doctors at the time could do very (b)[little] to cure these illnesses once people were infected. What finally reduced them was not a new treatment but a change in the city itself. Governments built systems to carry waste away and to filter drinking water, and death rates (c)[fell] sharply.

This history teaches an important lesson. Treating sick people one by one is necessary, but preventing illness for a whole population can be even more (d)[effective]. Public health measures such as clean water, safe food rules, and vaccination programs work quietly in the background, so people rarely notice them. When they succeed, nothing dramatic happens; people simply do not get sick. Perhaps for this reason, such measures are often (e)[praised] when budgets are planned, even though they protect far more lives than any single hospital can.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Pipes and Filters: The Quiet Heroes of a Longer Life
How Hospitals Doubled the Human Life Span
The Spread of Cholera in Modern Cities
Why Doctors Failed to Cure Typhoid
Planning a Budget for a New Hospital
items.exp: 수명이 늘어난 큰 이유는 병원과 약보다 깨끗한 물과 하수도 같은, 눈에 잘 띄지 않는 공중보건 조치였다는 글이에요. 그래서 '관과 필터: 더 긴 수명의 조용한 영웅들'이 알맞아요. ②는 필자가 흔한 생각으로 소개한 뒤 반박한 내용이에요.

items.passage:

In the crowded cities of the nineteenth century, human waste often flowed into the same rivers and wells that people drank from. Diseases such as cholera and typhoid spread quickly, killing thousands of people, especially young children. Doctors at the time could do very (b)[little] to cure these illnesses once people were infected. What finally reduced them was not a new treatment but a change in the city itself. Governments built systems to carry waste away and to filter drinking water, and death rates (c)[fell] sharply.

This history teaches an important lesson. Treating sick people one by one is necessary, but preventing illness for a whole population can be even more (d)[effective]. Public health measures such as clean water, safe food rules, and vaccination programs work quietly in the background, so people rarely notice them. When they succeed, nothing dramatic happens; people simply do not get sick. Perhaps for this reason, such measures are often (e)[praised] when budgets are planned, even though they protect far more lives than any single hospital can.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 공중보건 조치는 조용히 작동해 사람들이 잘 알아채지 못하고, 'even though'로 더 많은 생명을 지킨다고 이어지므로 예산을 짤 때 '무시된다'는 내용이어야 해요. (e) praised를 ignored로 바꿔야 해요. (b) 당시 의사들은 거의 손쓸 수 없었고, (c) 사망률이 크게 떨어졌다는 것은 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
On a rainy afternoon, Junho borrowed an old book of poems from the school library. As he turned the pages at home, a folded piece of paper slipped out and fell onto his desk. It was a letter, yellow with age and dated May 1979. "Dear Sunhee," it began. "I am sorry I could not say goodbye. My family is leaving for Brazil tomorrow, and I did not know how to tell you. Please don't be angry. You will always be my best friend. Mira." (a)[He] read it twice and wondered whether Sunhee had ever seen it.

(B)
A month later, the librarian handed Junho a postcard covered in bright stamps. It was from Mrs. Han. With her grandson's help, she had searched online and found Mira, who now lived in São Paulo. "We talked on the phone for three hours," she wrote. "After forty-eight years, we laughed as if we were still fifteen. Thank you to (b)[the kind boy] who did not throw away an old piece of paper." Junho smiled and pinned the card above his desk.

(C)
The next day, Junho showed the letter to Ms. Oh, the librarian. She checked the library's old records and found that the book had been donated ten years earlier by a former student named Han Sunhee. "She runs a flower shop near the bus terminal," Ms. Oh said. "Everyone in town knows her." That Saturday, (c)[he] put the letter in an envelope and set off for the shop.

(D)
The shop was full of roses and the smell of wet earth. When Junho explained why he had come, the gray-haired woman behind the counter opened the letter with shaking hands. As she read, tears ran down her cheeks. "Mira borrowed this book from me the week before she left," she said softly. "I thought she had gone without a word. I was angry with her for years." Not knowing what to say, (d)[he] just stood quietly beside her. Finally, Mrs. Han wiped her eyes, squeezed his hand, and (e)[she] whispered, "You have given me back my friend."
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 편지를 발견한 (A) 뒤에, 다음 날(The next day) 사서에게 보여 주고 기증자를 찾아 토요일에 꽃가게로 출발하는 (C)가 와요. 꽃가게에서 Mrs. Han이 편지를 읽고 우는 (D), 한 달 뒤(A month later) 친구를 찾았다는 엽서가 오는 (B) 순서예요.

items.passage:

It was a letter, yellow with age and dated May 1979. "Dear Sunhee," it began. "I am sorry I could not say goodbye. My family is leaving for Brazil tomorrow, and I did not know how to tell you. Please don't be angry. You will always be my best friend. Mira." (a)[He] read it twice and wondered whether Sunhee had ever seen it.

items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 가리키는 대상이 나머지 넷과 다른 것은?
items.exp: (a), (b), (c), (d)는 모두 Junho를 가리키고, (e)는 Junho의 손을 잡고 속삭인 Mrs. Han을 가리켜요.

items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Junho는 학교 도서관에서 빌린 시집 속에서 오래된 편지를 발견했다.
한 달 뒤 Mrs. Han이 학교로 직접 찾아와 고맙다고 말했다.
사서는 도서관의 옛 기록을 확인해 책을 기증한 사람을 알아냈다.
Mrs. Han은 버스 터미널 근처에서 꽃가게를 하고 있었다.
Mrs. Han은 편지를 읽으며 눈물을 흘렸다.
items.exp: (B)에서 Mrs. Han은 직접 찾아오지 않고 도서관으로 엽서를 보냈다(the librarian handed Junho a postcard)고 했으므로 ②가 글과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 (A), (C), (D)의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Mr. Palmer,

My name is Yerin Choi, and I am the president of the film club at Riverside High School. This year, our twelve members have written, filmed, and edited six short films, each about ten minutes long. The stories are all set in our own neighborhood, and some scenes were even shot on the street in front of your theater. Until now, we have shown our films only in a classroom, using a small screen and borrowed speakers. Our dream is to share them on a real cinema screen with our families and neighbors. I understand that Moonbridge Cinema is usually closed on Monday mornings. Would it be possible for us to use one of your screening rooms on a Monday in December for about two hours? We would gladly pay for the cleaning afterward, and we would love to invite you as our special guest.

Sincerely,
Yerin Choi
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 영화 동아리의 새 회원 모집을 알리려고
단편 영화 상영을 위해 극장 상영관 대여를 요청하려고
극장 앞 거리에서의 촬영 허가를 받으려고
월요일 오전 극장 휴관 이유를 문의하려고
items.exp: 동아리가 만든 단편 영화들을 가족과 이웃에게 보여 주고 싶다며 월요일에 상영관 하나를 두 시간 정도 쓸 수 있는지 묻고 있어요. 극장 앞 거리에서 촬영했다는 말은 이미 한 일을 소개한 것이고, 월요일 휴관은 요청의 근거로 든 것이에요.

items.passage: At exactly 8 p.m., Somin clicked the button on the ticket website, her heart pounding. She had waited six months for her favorite band's first concert in Seoul. The screen froze for a moment and then showed a single gray line: "All tickets are sold out." She refreshed the page again and again, but nothing changed. Somin closed her laptop slowly and buried her face in her pillow. The posters on her wall suddenly seemed to be laughing at her. A little later, there was a knock on the door. Her older brother walked in, holding his phone behind his back. "I entered a radio contest last week," he said casually, "and they just called me." He turned the screen toward her. It showed two tickets in the front row. Somin screamed, jumped off the bed, and hugged him so hard that he almost dropped the phone.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Somin의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 표가 매진되었다는 문구를 보고 베개에 얼굴을 묻을 만큼 낙담했다가, 오빠가 라디오 이벤트로 받은 맨 앞줄 표 두 장을 보여 주자 소리를 지르며 껴안았으므로 heartbroken → overjoyed가 알맞아요. 마지막에 크게 기뻐하므로 lonely나 nervous로 끝나는 보기는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Every day, we see people crossing the street with their eyes fixed on a phone screen. Many of them believe they are safe because they can still see the road out of the corner of their eye. Research suggests otherwise. When people read or type while walking, they move more slowly, drift from side to side, and look left and right far less often before stepping into the road. Their ears do not help much either, especially when they are wearing earphones. In studies of busy crossings, distracted walkers were much more likely to miss an approaching car or a signal that had just changed. A message can almost always wait thirty seconds, but an accident can change a life in a moment. So when you reach a crosswalk, put your phone in your pocket, take out your earphones, and give the road your full attention until you reach the other side.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 길을 건널 때는 휴대폰을 넣고 도로에 온전히 주의를 기울여야 한다.
보행자의 안전을 위해 횡단보도 신호 시간을 늘려야 한다.
운전자는 보행자가 많은 곳에서 속도를 줄여야 한다.
이어폰 대신 주변 소리가 들리는 기기를 사용해야 한다.
메시지에는 가능한 한 빨리 답장하는 습관을 들여야 한다.
items.exp: 횡단보도에 이르면 휴대폰을 주머니에 넣고 이어폰을 빼서 건너편에 닿을 때까지 도로에만 집중하라는 마지막 문장에 주장이 드러나 있어요. 이어폰 이야기는 주의를 빼앗는 예로 든 것이지 다른 기기를 쓰라는 주장이 아니에요.

items.passage: Two towns at the same distance from the equator can have very different winters. One sits in the middle of a continent, and the other lies on the coast. In January, the inland town may freeze while the coastal town stays mild. The reason lies in the water. Compared with land or rock, water needs a great deal of energy to warm up, and it gives that energy back very slowly. All summer long, the ocean quietly absorbs heat from the sun without growing much warmer. Then, as autumn and winter arrive, the land cools quickly, but the sea goes on releasing its stored warmth into the air above it, and winds carry that warmth over the coast. In spring, the process works the other way, keeping coastal towns cooler while inland areas heat up. In a sense, coastal residents spend their winters [living on heat the sea saved from summer].
items.q: 밑줄 친 [living on heat the sea saved from summer]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: enjoying vacations at warm beaches far from home
paying more for heating than people in inland towns
being warmed by heat the ocean stored and slowly released
moving to the coast to escape the summer heat
using sea water to produce energy for their homes
items.exp: 바다는 여름 내내 열을 흡수했다가 겨울에 그 열을 천천히 내놓고, 바람이 그 온기를 해안으로 실어 온다고 했어요. 그러니 밑줄은 바다가 저장했다가 천천히 내놓는 열 덕분에 따뜻하게 지낸다는 뜻이에요. ⑤는 바닷물로 에너지를 만든다는 말이라 지문과 관계없어요.

items.passage: Every year, strong winds lift hundreds of millions of tons of dust from the Sahara Desert in Africa and carry it high into the sky. Much of it travels west across the Atlantic Ocean, a journey of several thousand kilometers that can take about a week. Some of this dust finally falls over the Amazon rainforest in South America. This may seem like a strange connection between a dry desert and one of the wettest forests on Earth, but it is an important one. Heavy rains in the Amazon constantly wash nutrients out of the soil, especially phosphorus, which plants need to grow. Much of the desert dust comes from the bed of an ancient lake and is rich in this nutrient, so it helps replace what the rain takes away. In this way, the world's largest hot desert helps feed the world's largest rainforest, showing how distant parts of the planet are linked through the air.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the reasons deserts are spreading toward rainforests
the harm that dust storms cause to human health
how heavy rain creates new soil in the Amazon
the long history of trade between Africa and South America
how desert dust carried by wind nourishes a distant forest
items.exp: 사하라 사막의 먼지가 바람을 타고 대서양을 건너 아마존에 떨어지고, 비에 씻겨 나간 인 같은 영양분을 채워 준다는 내용이에요. ③은 많은 비가 오히려 영양분을 씻어 낸다는 글의 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Most people need seven or eight hours of sleep a night, but a giraffe in the wild often sleeps less than two hours a day. This is not because giraffes need little rest. It is because sleeping is risky for an animal of their size. A giraffe that lies down takes a long time to get back up. It must swing its heavy neck forward and push itself up on its long legs, which leaves it almost helpless for several seconds. For a lion hiding in the grass, those seconds are a perfect chance to attack. So giraffes usually rest standing up, dozing in short naps throughout the day and night. When they do fall into deep sleep, they lie down, bend their long necks back, and rest their heads on their own bodies, but only for a few minutes at a time. In zoos, where there are no lions, giraffes tend to sleep much longer.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How Lions Hunt in the Tall Grass
Short Naps for Safety: How Giraffes Sleep
Why Long Necks Help Giraffes Find Food
Zoos Change the Way Animals Eat
Deep Sleep: The Secret to a Long Life
items.exp: 야생 기린은 눕고 일어나는 데 시간이 걸려 포식자에게 위험하기 때문에 서서 짧게 졸고 깊은 잠도 몇 분씩만 잔다는 내용이므로 ②가 알맞아요. 사자는 기린이 짧게 자는 이유로 등장할 뿐 글의 중심이 아니에요.

items.passage: Marguerite Delmas was born in 1874 in Lyon, France, the daughter of a silk weaver. As a girl, she collected scraps of ribbon and cloth from her father's workshop and used them to decorate dolls' hats. At sixteen, she moved to Paris and worked as an assistant in a well-known hat shop, where she learned to shape straw and felt. In 1901, she opened her own small shop near the river. Her hats were famous for being light and simple at a time when most fashionable hats were heavy and covered with feathers. Delmas refused to use the feathers of rare birds, and she spoke publicly against the trade that was killing them. Her designs became popular across Europe, and in 1925 she won a gold medal at an international exhibition. She closed her shop in 1938 and spent her last years teaching young designers.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 열여섯 살에 파리의 모자 가게에서 조수로 일했다.
희귀한 새의 깃털로 장식한 무거운 모자로 유명했다.
items.exp: 그녀의 모자는 가볍고 단순한 것으로 유명했고, 희귀한 새의 깃털은 쓰기를 거부했다(refused to use the feathers of rare birds)고 했으므로 ④가 글과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 아버지의 직업, 파리에서의 조수 생활, 1901년 개업, 1925년 금메달로 모두 일치해요.

items.passage: Hiccups can seem to come from nowhere, but each one ①[begin] with a sudden tightening of the diaphragm, the large muscle under the lungs that helps us breathe. When this muscle pulls down without warning, air rushes into the throat. Less than a second later, the vocal cords snap shut, ②[producing] the familiar "hic" sound. Eating too quickly, drinking fizzy drinks, or feeling suddenly excited can all trigger this reaction, though often no clear cause can be found. Most cases of hiccups stop on their own within a few minutes, and the many home remedies people swear by, such as holding one's breath or drinking water upside down, have rarely been tested ③[scientifically]. Interestingly, babies hiccup even before they are born. Some scientists believe that hiccups ④[help] unborn babies exercise the muscles they will later use for breathing, while others think the reflex may be left over from our distant ancestors, ⑤[who] breathed with both lungs and gills.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ①은 주어 each one이 단수이므로 begins로 고쳐야 해요. ②는 앞 절의 결과를 나타내는 분사구문, ③은 동사 tested를 꾸미는 부사, ④는 복수 주어 hiccups에 맞는 동사, ⑤는 사람 선행사 ancestors를 받는 관계대명사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Many shoppers believe that buying in large quantities is always the smart choice. A giant bag of rice or a box of forty yogurts usually costs ①[less] per item than a small package, so it seems like an obvious way to save money. However, the savings are real only if everything is actually ②[used]. Fresh foods such as fruit, bread, and milk can spoil before a small family finishes them, and the money spent on the wasted part is simply ③[lost]. Large packages can also change how we consume. Studies suggest that when people have plenty of snacks at home, they tend to eat them more ④[freely], so a bigger box may just disappear faster. Buying in bulk makes the most sense for items that last a long time and that we use regularly, such as soap or toilet paper. For everything else, the smallest package is sometimes the most ⑤[wasteful] choice.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 대량 구매는 상하거나 더 빨리 먹어 버리게 되어 오히려 손해일 수 있다는 흐름이므로, 마지막 문장은 작은 포장이 더 경제적인 선택일 수 있다는 뜻이 되어야 해요. 따라서 ⑤ wasteful을 economical로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: Why do so many people decide to start a diet on a Monday, join a gym in January, or promise to study harder at the beginning of a new semester? Psychologists suggest that such dates work as mental dividing lines. They allow us to separate our old self, who made mistakes, from a new self who can do better. Once a new week, month, or year begins, past failures feel as if they belong to someone else, and we feel freer to try again. Researchers have found that online searches for the word "diet" and visits to gyms rise sharply right after these points in the calendar, and even after birthdays. In other words, people treat certain moments on the calendar as ___, chances to close one chapter and open another with a clean page.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 새로운 주·달·해가 시작되면 과거의 실패를 이전의 나에게 돌리고 다시 시도한다고 했고, 빈칸 뒤에서도 한 장을 닫고 깨끗한 새 장을 연다고 했으므로 fresh starts가 알맞아요. deadlines는 무언가를 끝내야 하는 기한이라 새 출발의 의미와 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: My grandmother's recipe for bread, written on a small card, reads in its entirety: "Flour, water, salt, yeast. Knead until it feels right. Bake until done." To her, these few words were perfectly complete. To a beginner, they are nearly useless. How should the dough feel? How can you tell when the bread is done? The gap lies not in the words themselves but in what the reader brings to them. Every instruction, however carefully written, rests on a large background of unspoken knowledge. A laboratory manual assumes that the student knows how to hold a test tube; a sewing pattern assumes that the reader can already thread a needle. Simply adding more words does not solve the problem, either. A guide that explains every tiny step for the beginner quickly bores and slows down the expert. Thus, how clear an instruction is depends less on the text itself than on ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the number of steps it describes in detail
the fit between its words and the reader's experience
the authority of the person who wrote it
the precision of the measurements it gives
the time its writer spends revising it
items.exp: 할머니의 짧은 조리법은 할머니에게는 완전하지만 초보자에게는 쓸모없고, 모든 지시는 말하지 않은 배경지식에 기대며, 단어를 늘리면 전문가에게는 오히려 방해가 된다고 했어요. 따라서 지시의 명확성은 글과 읽는 사람의 경험이 얼마나 맞는가에 달려 있어요. ①과 ④는 단어를 더 늘리면 된다는 생각으로, 지문이 부정한 내용이에요.

items.passage: A golf ball is covered with hundreds of small dents called dimples, and they are not there just for decoration. They help the ball travel much farther through the air. ① Early golf balls were smooth, but players noticed that old, scratched balls often flew farther than new ones. ② The reason lies in the thin layer of air that flows around a ball as it moves. ③ On a smooth ball, this air separates from the surface early, leaving a wide pocket of swirling air behind the ball that pulls it back. ④ Golf is one of the oldest ball games still played today, and many of its basic rules were written in Scotland centuries ago. ⑤ Dimples make the air hug the surface a little longer, so the pocket behind the ball becomes smaller and the ball meets less resistance, allowing it to fly up to twice as far as a smooth one.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 골프공의 딤플이 공 뒤쪽의 공기 소용돌이를 줄여 공을 더 멀리 날게 한다는 흐름인데, ④는 골프의 오랜 역사와 규칙 이야기로 딤플의 원리와 관계가 없어요. ⑤는 ③에서 말한 매끈한 공의 문제를 딤플이 어떻게 해결하는지 설명하므로 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage:
In the center of Antarctica, the snow that falls each year almost never melts. Instead, it is buried by the next year's snow, and over time the layers are pressed into solid ice more than three kilometers thick.

(A) By measuring the gases in the bubbles from each layer of a core, researchers can learn how much carbon dioxide the air contained hundreds of thousands of years ago, long before anyone was there to record it.

(B) These bubbles are, in effect, samples of the ancient sky. To reach them, scientists drill deep into the ice and pull up long cylinders of it called ice cores.

(C) This ice is far more than frozen water. As the snow was pressed down, tiny bubbles of the air from that time were trapped inside it.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 두꺼운 얼음을 This ice로 받아 그 속에 공기 방울이 갇혔다는 (C)가 먼저 와요. 그 공기 방울을 These bubbles로 받아 얼음 기둥, 즉 ice cores를 뽑아 올린다는 (B)가 이어지고, a core의 각 층에서 기체를 측정한다는 (A)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: In most of East Asia, people eat with chopsticks, but the chopsticks are not the same everywhere. ( ① ) In China, they are usually long and made of wood or bamboo, which makes it easy to reach dishes shared in the middle of a large table. ( ② ) Japanese chopsticks are shorter and have pointed tips, which help diners remove small bones from fish, a common part of Japanese meals. ( ③ ) Several explanations have been offered for this choice. ( ④ ) Some historians point out that royal families once used silver chopsticks, since silver was believed to change color when it touched poison. ( ⑤ ) Others note that metal is easy to clean and lasts for many years, and that a flat shape keeps the chopsticks from rolling off the table.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Korea, however, stands out because its chopsticks are usually flat and made of metal.
items.exp: 중국과 일본 젓가락을 설명한 뒤 대조의 however로 한국의 납작한 금속 젓가락을 소개하는 ③이 알맞아요. ③ 뒤의 this choice는 금속 젓가락을 가리키고, 이어지는 은수저와 위생·모양 이야기는 그 이유를 설명해요.

items.passage: People often wave their hands while they talk, and we usually assume they do it for the listener. Yet people gesture even when no one can see them. Watch someone talking on the phone, and you will probably see their hands moving in the air. Even people who have been blind from birth, and who have never seen anyone gesture, move their hands when they speak, including when they talk to other blind people. In one experiment, researchers asked people to describe a complicated route or object while keeping their hands still. Compared with those who were free to move, these speakers paused more often, used more filler words like "um," and had more trouble finding the right words. Such findings suggest that gestures are not just signals for others. They seem to help speakers organize their thoughts and bring words to mind.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Hand movements during speech appear to benefit not only those who watch them but also those who (A) ___ them, since restricting them makes it (B) ___ to express ideas.
items.exp: 보는 사람이 없을 때나 시각 장애인끼리 말할 때도 손짓을 하고, 손을 움직이지 못하게 하면 말이 막히고 단어를 찾기 어려워졌다고 했어요. 따라서 손짓은 그것을 만드는 사람(produce)에게도 도움이 되고, 제한하면 생각을 말로 옮기기가 더 어려워진다(harder)가 알맞아요.

items.passage:
Roads connect towns and cities, but for wild animals they can be deadly barriers. Every year, millions of deer, foxes, frogs, and other creatures are killed while trying to cross highways. Roads also (a)[divide] animal populations into small groups that cannot meet. When animals cannot travel to find food or mates, these groups slowly become weaker.

To solve this problem, many countries have begun building wildlife crossings. These are bridges or tunnels designed especially for animals. A bridge over a highway may be covered with soil, grass, and even small trees, so that it looks like a (b)[strange] part of the forest to the animals using it. Fences along the road guide animals toward the crossing instead of onto the traffic lanes.

At first, some people doubted that wild animals would use them. Cameras placed on the crossings have shown the opposite. In one national park in Canada, bears, wolves, elk, and even shy mountain lions have crossed thousands of times. In the Netherlands, dozens of such bridges help badgers and deer move (c)[safely] across a crowded country. In some areas, accidents involving large animals have (d)[dropped] by as much as eighty percent.

Wildlife crossings are expensive, and a single bridge can cost millions of dollars. Yet supporters point out that crashes with large animals also cost a great deal in car repairs, hospital bills, and sometimes human lives. In the long run, helping animals cross the road may be one of the (e)[wisest] ways to protect both wildlife and drivers.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Deer Are Dangerous to Drivers
The High Cost of Road Repairs
How Cameras Help Count Wild Animals
Bridges for Animals: A Safer Way Across the Road
items.exp: 도로가 동물에게 위험한 장벽이 되자 동물 전용 다리와 터널을 만들었고, 실제로 많은 동물이 이용해 사고가 크게 줄었다는 내용이에요. 그래서 ⑤가 제목으로 알맞아요. ④의 카메라는 효과를 확인한 수단일 뿐이에요.

items.exp: 다리를 흙과 풀, 나무로 덮는 것은 동물에게 숲의 '자연스러운' 일부처럼 보이게 하려는 것이므로 (b) strange는 natural로 바꿔야 해요. (a)는 도로가 개체군을 나눈다는 뜻이고, (d)는 사고가 줄었다는 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
On a gray October afternoon, the phone rang at the Pine Valley Mountain Rescue station. A sixteen-year-old hiker named Owen had become separated from his group near Eagle Ridge. (a)[He] had twisted his ankle and could no longer walk. Thick fog was already rolling down the slopes, and the temperature was dropping quickly. Ruth Harlan, the team leader, grabbed her backpack and turned to the newest member of the team. "Leo, you're coming with me," she said. It was Leo's first real rescue, and his heart was racing.

(B)
At the station, Owen's parents were waiting, and his mother hugged him so tightly that he laughed through his pain. A doctor later confirmed that his ankle was badly sprained but not broken. Two weeks later, a letter arrived for the whole team. In it, Owen wrote that the sound of Leo's voice calling his name through the fog was the moment he stopped being afraid. Ruth handed it to Leo with a smile. (b)[He] folded it carefully and put it in his locker, where it stayed for many years.

(C)
The trail grew steeper, and soon the fog was so thick that they could see only a few meters ahead. Before the phone call ended, Ruth had told Owen to stay where he was and blow his whistle every five minutes. Now the mountain was silent. Leo stopped and held his breath. Far to the left, (c)[he] heard a thin, high sound. "There!" he shouted. Ruth hesitated, since the sound seemed to come from the wrong direction, but she trusted (d)[her new teammate] and followed him off the trail.

(D)
Ten minutes later, their flashlights found Owen sitting under a large rock, shivering and pale. "I knew someone would come," he whispered. While Ruth examined his ankle, Leo wrapped him in a thermal blanket and poured him a cup of hot tea from a flask. Then the two rescuers lifted Owen onto a light stretcher. The way down was long and slippery in the dark, but Leo never once let go of (e)[his] side of the stretcher, even when his arms began to ache.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 구조 요청을 받고 출발한 (A) 다음, 안개 속에서 호루라기 소리를 듣고 따라가는 (C), Owen을 찾아 들것에 싣고 내려오는 (D), 구조대 기지에서 부모를 만나고 편지를 받는 (B) 순서예요. (D)의 Owen 발견은 (C)의 수색 뒤에 와야 하고, (B)의 기지 도착은 하산 뒤에 와야 해요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Bennett,

I am Daniel Cho, a member of the photography club at Lakeside High School. Our club is planning a small exhibition next spring called "Faces of Our Town," and we would like to include portraits of local shop owners, bus drivers, and other people who make our community special. While searching through old newspapers, we discovered that your bakery has been on Main Street for over forty years. Many of our members grew up eating your bread, and we think your story would be a wonderful part of the exhibition. With your permission, two of our members would like to visit your bakery one morning next month and take a few photographs of you at work. The visit would take less than an hour, and we would be careful not to disturb your customers. We hope to hear from you soon.

Best regards,
Daniel Cho
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 사진 동아리의 신입 회원 모집을 알리려고
빵집에서 사진을 찍어도 되는지 허락을 구하려고
오래된 신문 자료의 열람 방법을 문의하려고
items.exp: 동아리 전시회에 빵집 주인의 사진을 넣고 싶다며, 허락해 준다면 다음 달 빵집을 방문해 일하는 모습을 찍고 싶다고 했으므로 촬영 허락을 구하는 글이에요. 전시회는 촬영 이유로 언급되었을 뿐 초대하는 글은 아니에요.

items.passage: It was Minjun's twelfth birthday, but the house was strangely silent when he came home from school. His mother had left for work early that morning without saying a word about it, and his older sister had not even sent a text. He dropped his bag on the floor and sat alone at the kitchen table. Nobody remembered, he thought, staring at the empty chairs around him. He was about to go up to his room when he heard a noise from the backyard. He opened the back door slowly. Suddenly, the lights came on, and his whole family, along with his three best friends, jumped out from behind the garden shed, shouting, "Happy birthday!" His grandfather was holding a chocolate cake covered with candles. Minjun burst out laughing, and his cheeks turned red as everyone gathered around him.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Minjun의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 생일인데 아무도 기억하지 못한다고 생각하며 빈 의자들을 바라보고 혼자 앉아 있을 때는 외로웠어요. 가족과 친구들이 깜짝 생일 파티를 열어 주자 웃음을 터뜨렸으므로 기뻐하는 마음으로 바뀌었어요. 그래서 lonely → delighted가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Every year, cities around the world tear down old buildings to make room for new ones. Some of these buildings have little value, but others hold more than bricks and wood. An old train station, a neighborhood theater, or a family-run market may be the place where three generations of residents met, worked, and celebrated. When such a place disappears, people do not just lose a building. They lose a shared reference point, a spot where they can say, "This is where my grandfather used to buy his newspaper." For this reason, some cities now try to reuse old structures instead of destroying them, turning factories into libraries or warehouses into art spaces. These projects keep the outer walls and character of the building while giving it a new purpose. In doing so, they allow a city to [grow without erasing its own diary].
items.q: 밑줄 친 [grow without erasing its own diary]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: expand its area while protecting natural parks
build new homes while keeping prices low
record its history in books for future citizens
develop while preserving places that hold shared memories
attract tourists by building modern landmarks
items.exp: 오래된 건물은 여러 세대 주민의 기억이 담긴 장소이며, 이를 허물지 않고 새 용도로 고쳐 쓰면 도시가 발전하면서도 공동의 기억을 지킬 수 있다고 했어요. diary는 도시의 기억이 담긴 장소를 비유한 것이에요. 책으로 기록한다는 ③은 diary를 글자 그대로 받아들인 오답이에요.

items.passage: Many people believe that a creative person is someone who has a sudden brilliant idea out of nowhere. In reality, most creative work grows from a large pile of ordinary attempts. A songwriter may write dozens of melodies before one is worth keeping, and a designer may sketch fifty versions of a chair before choosing the best. What separates these people from others is often not a special gift but a willingness to produce many ideas, including bad ones, without judging them too early. When we criticize every idea the moment it appears, we stop the flow before good ideas have a chance to show up. Studies of creative teams also show that groups that first generate many options and only later select among them tend to come up with more original solutions. Creativity, in this sense, is less about waiting for inspiration and more about the patient work of making many attempts.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 창의성은 타고난 재능이므로 훈련으로 키우기 어렵다.
창의적인 결과는 성급한 판단 없이 많은 시도를 하는 데서 나온다.
좋은 아이디어를 얻으려면 혼자보다 팀으로 일해야 한다.
아이디어는 처음부터 엄격하게 평가해야 질이 높아진다.
영감이 떠오를 때까지 충분히 기다리는 것이 중요하다.
items.exp: 창의적인 작업은 갑작스러운 영감보다 성급히 판단하지 않고 많은 아이디어를 내 보는 데서 나온다고 했고, 마지막 문장에서도 이를 다시 정리했어요. 팀 연구는 근거로 든 예이고, ④와 ⑤는 지문과 반대되는 내용이에요.

items.passage: Tomatoes are now so common in Italian food that it is hard to imagine pasta sauce or pizza without them. Yet tomatoes are not native to Europe at all. They first grew in South America and were brought to Europe by Spanish explorers in the sixteenth century. At first, many Europeans did not trust the strange red fruit. Because tomatoes belong to the same plant family as some poisonous plants, people grew them in gardens mainly as decoration. It took more than a century before cooks in southern Italy began to use them regularly in their dishes, and even longer for them to become a symbol of Italian cooking. The same pattern can be found with potatoes in Ireland and chili peppers in Korea. Foods that we now think of as deeply traditional were once newcomers that slowly won a place at the table.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: health benefits of tomatoes and potatoes
how foreign foods became part of local food traditions
the role of Spanish explorers in world trade
differences between Italian and Korean cooking
items.exp: 토마토, 감자, 고추처럼 지금은 전통 음식처럼 여겨지는 재료도 원래는 외부에서 들어와 서서히 그 지역 음식 문화의 일부가 되었다는 내용이에요. 독성 식물 이야기나 스페인 탐험가는 세부 내용일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: Only about one in ten people is left-handed, and in sports such as swimming or running, left-handers appear among top athletes at roughly the same rate. In sports where two players face each other directly, however, the picture is different. In fencing, table tennis, and boxing, left-handers are often found at the top level far more often than their share of the population would suggest. The reason seems to be not that they are naturally more talented, but that they are rare. A right-handed player spends most practice time against other right-handers, so the angles and spin of a left-hander's shots feel unfamiliar and are hard to read. Left-handed players, on the other hand, face right-handers every day and know exactly what to expect. Their advantage, in other words, comes from being unusual.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Is Being Left-Handed a Sign of Natural Talent?
Rare and Hard to Read: The Left-Hander's Edge in Sports
Tennis or Swimming: Which Sport Suits You Best?
How Coaches Turn Left-Handers into Right-Handers
items.exp: 상대와 마주하는 종목에서 왼손잡이가 유리한 것은 타고난 재능 때문이 아니라 드물어서 상대가 낯설고 읽기 어렵기 때문이라는 내용이에요. 그래서 ③이 알맞아요. 글은 왼손잡이가 재능의 표시가 아니라고 했으므로 ②는 답이 될 수 없어요.
